Single-finding cluster. The scan's file:line citations are accurate — no drift worth reporting (mutation uploadBlob putStreaming(namespace: .public) is at Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanPublicRepositoryMutationXRPC.swift:109-110; putBlobLocked at Sources/SwanSQLite/SwanSQLite.swift:7446; promotePermissionedBlobReferences at 9895-9968; the anonymous getBlob route at Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanPublicRepositoryReadXRPC.swift:839; the two cited tests start at Tests/SwanSQLiteTests/PermissionedBlobRepositoryReachabilityTests.swift:135 and :479).

Three controls the scan did NOT weigh, all of which cap the impact:
1. There is no CID-enumeration endpoint anywhere in the tree. `grep -rn "listBlobs" Sources/` returns nothing, and the public read surface is exactly four methods (Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanPublicRepositoryReadXRPC.swift:29-34: getBlob, getLatestCommit, getRepo, getRepoStatus). An anonymous reader must already hold the exact SHA-256 content address.
2. Permissioned blob CIDs are never broadcast. The public firehose outbox is written only from the public repository commit path (producers live solely in Sources/SwanSQLite/PublicFirehoseOutboxStore.swift:77; `public_event_outbox` appears nowhere in the permissioned `apply(space:author:...)` path at Sources/SwanSQLite/SwanSQLite.swift:3409-3500). So the CID of a permissioned blob leaves the server only to parties already authorized to read the record.
3. The behaviour is documented as a deliberate, explicitly-incomplete boundary, not an oversight. docs/superpowers/plans/2026-07-28-swan-public-blob-reference-isolation.md, section "Deliberate boundary": "The public upload endpoint establishes a public reference as part of the upload transaction... leaves garbage collection of unreferenced public uploads as a separate maintenance concern. A future staged-upload design may add atomic record-linked promotion, but it must preserve this fail-closed boundary." The permissioned promotion half of that future design has since landed (SwanSQLite.swift:9895); the GC half has not.

The scan's remediation string is the right shape but overreaches on the cheapest correct fix — see F01 remediation. Also note the whole cluster's "indefinitely" clause is really the GC gap, which is an availability/quota issue for public uploads as much as a confidentiality one (AccountBlobQuota 1 GiB / 10,000 refs, Sources/SwanStorage/SwanStorage.swift:23-26), and no sweeper exists (`grep -rn "unreferenced\|orphan" Sources/` finds only unrelated hits plus the comment at SwanSQLite.swift:7525).

findings.title: Permissioned blobs are uploaded into the anonymous public namespace and are CID-fetchable until a later permissioned commit promotes them; no expiry covers abandoned uploads, and same-CID re-upload recreates the public edge
findings.evidence:
Mechanism confirmed in full.

Only upload path: Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanPublicRepositoryMutationXRPC.swift:109-110 calls `blobStore.putStreaming(namespace: .public, ...)` unconditionally, and :137 rejects anything that does not come back `.public`. `grep -rn "namespace: \.space" Sources/` finds no HTTP writer — the space-scoped route Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanSpaceBlobXRPC.swift is read-only (`ComAtprotoSpaceGetBlob`, :50-115). Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanSpaceXRPC.swift:750/776/855 registers space.createRecord/putRecord/applyWrites but no space.uploadBlob. So a permissioned blob has no way into the store except through the public namespace.

Durable public edge at upload: putStreaming (SwanSQLite.swift:7127-7180) -> putBlobLocked (:7446) -> `INSERT INTO blob_namespace_references(cid, namespace_kind, space_uri)` (:7566-7571) with kind 'public' from blobNamespaceColumns (:9798-9807).

Anonymous sink has no record-reachability predicate: publicBlobMetadataIfReachable (SwanSQLite.swift:7925-7975) and publicBlob (:7247-7259) join `blob_payloads` to `blob_namespace_references` on namespace_kind='public' only. The route comment at SwanPublicRepositoryReadXRPC.swift:836-838 states the design intent plainly: "Like `resolveHandle` it needs no repository *generation*: a blob is content-addressed and carries no MST revision, so it stays out of the admission machinery the other routes depend on." So an unauthenticated GET /xrpc/com.atproto.sync.getBlob?did=...&cid=... (route at :839) serves any staged upload.

Promotion is the only cleanup: SwanSQLite.swift:3496-3499 calls promotePermissionedBlobReferences inside the permissioned apply transaction; :9927-9938 deletes the public edge only when `publicRepositoryContainsBlobCIDWithoutGate(cid)` is false. Nothing else removes it. No sweeper exists (`grep -rn "unreferenced\|orphan" Sources/` yields no blob GC; the only near-hit is a comment at SwanSQLite.swift:7525).

The unsafe intermediate state is asserted as intended by the suite: Tests/SwanSQLiteTests/PermissionedBlobRepositoryReachabilityTests.swift:515-518 does `let publicAfterReupload = try await database.publicBlobExists(cid: firstUpload.cid); XCTAssertTrue(publicAfterReupload)` — i.e. a test positively documents that re-uploading identical content restores anonymous reachability. :133-188 (testPermissionedRecordPromotesUploadedBlobIntoPrivateNamespace) proves only eventual isolation after a successful apply.

Where the scan is overstated (hence PARTIALLY, not CONFIRMED):
- No enumeration. `grep -rn "listBlobs" Sources/` -> zero hits; served public methods are exactly the four at SwanPublicRepositoryReadXRPC.swift:29-34. The attacker must supply the exact SHA-256 CID.
- No CID leak channel to an unauthorized party. public_event_outbox is produced only by Sources/SwanSQLite/PublicFirehoseOutboxStore.swift:77 on the public repository path; the permissioned apply (SwanSQLite.swift:3409-3500) never touches it. Everyone who legitimately learns a permissioned blob's CID is already authorized to stream it via com.atproto.space.getBlob.
- Therefore, against a party who has never been authorized, the primitive is a possession-confirmation oracle for content the attacker already holds byte-for-byte — not a read of unknown private bytes. The genuine confidentiality delta is against a *formerly* authorized reader (revoked space member) who retains the CID and polls while an abandoned or re-uploaded staging edge exists. That is real, and it is the case I would fix, but it is not the "private-intended bytes exposed to the anonymous internet" framing the HIGH rating implies.
- "Deliberately incomplete", not missed: docs/superpowers/plans/2026-07-28-swan-public-blob-reference-isolation.md "Deliberate boundary" names both the upload-time public reference and the missing GC, and pre-authorizes exactly the fix the scan proposes. The reasoning given there (avoid implicitly promoting a private blob into the public namespace via a record write) holds and is enforced by validatePublicBlobLinks (SwanPublicRepositoryMutationXRPC.swift:184); it just never covered the reverse direction.
findings.remediation:
Two changes, in this order.

1. Close the confidentiality gap at its source — do not let a permissioned blob enter the public namespace at all. Add `com.atproto.space.uploadBlob` alongside the existing read route in Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanSpaceBlobXRPC.swift (mirror AuthenticatedGetSpaceBlobHandler's authorization at :64-77 and the stream-admission lease at :74-84), and have it call `putStreaming(namespace: .space(uri))` — SwanSQLite.swift:7127 already accepts an arbitrary BlobNamespace, and the schema CHECK at SwanSQLite.swift:1043-1048 already permits 'space'. `promotePermissionedBlobReferences` (SwanSQLite.swift:9895) then becomes a no-op for these CIDs: its private INSERT at :9949-9956 is already `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`, and the public DELETE at :9929-9937 harmlessly matches nothing. No promotion window, no abandoned-upload edge, no re-upload edge — for permissioned data. This is cheaper and lower-risk than the scan's proposal because it needs no third namespace_kind and no schema migration.

I disagree with the scan's "add a staged namespace served by nobody" as the primary fix: it requires relaxing the CHECK at SwanSQLite.swift:1043-1048 (schema migration on a live single-account DB), a promotion step in the *public* record commit path that does not exist today, and it re-opens the exact hazard the design doc's "Deliberate boundary" was written to prevent (a record write implicitly promoting a blob into the public namespace). Direct space-namespace upload gets the same confidentiality result with a strictly smaller blast radius.

2. Independently, add the GC the design doc already flagged as owed. A periodic sweep that deletes public references older than a bounded age whose CID fails `publicRepositoryContainsBlobCIDWithoutGate` (SwanSQLite.swift:9921) and has no space reference, reusing the existing reclamation logic in removeBlobReference (SwanSQLite.swift:7284-7330). This is what actually addresses "indefinitely", and it also caps the quota leak against AccountBlobQuota (Sources/SwanStorage/SwanStorage.swift:23-26): today an interrupted upload permanently consumes unique-bytes and reference budget with no operator recourse.

What I would NOT do: gate anonymous getBlob on public-MST reachability at SwanSQLite.swift:7925. It closes all three sub-cases in one place, but it puts an MST scan on the hot network-facing image path (the route comment at SwanPublicRepositoryReadXRPC.swift:892-901 shows how carefully that path was budgeted) and it diverges from reference-PDS behaviour, which serves unreferenced blobs. Only worth it if a maintainer wants public unreferenced uploads unfetchable as a policy.
findings.risk:
Change 1 is a wire-format addition: a new NSID under com.atproto.space.*, which means a public protocol profile bump and re-pinning (Tests/SwanInteropTests/PublicProtocolProfileVerifierTests.swift:10-22 pins profile + lexicon + generated-wire SHA-256 triples; Tests/SwanPublicWireTests/SwanPublicWireTests.swift:144,170-173 pins public-data-testing-2026-08-06). Every permissioned client must be updated to call the new route — until they are, they keep using com.atproto.repo.uploadBlob and the exposure persists, so this is not fully mitigating until clients move. It does not change com.atproto.repo.uploadBlob semantics, so federation/AppView blob serving is untouched.

Change 2 risks deleting a public edge that a client legitimately staged and has not yet committed; the age threshold must comfortably exceed the longest realistic upload->putRecord gap, and the sweep must not race putBlobLocked (take withPrivateBlobLifecycleLock, as removeBlobReference does at SwanSQLite.swift:7286). It will also cause previously-fetchable orphan CIDs to start 404ing — client-visible, though only for blobs no record references.

Both changes will require updating Tests/SwanSQLiteTests/PermissionedBlobRepositoryReachabilityTests.swift:515-518, which currently asserts the unsafe state is present.
findings.needsHumanDecision: Two decisions are the maintainer's, not mine. (a) Is adding a new com.atproto.space.uploadBlob NSID — with the profile/lexicon/generated-wire re-pin it forces and the client migration it implies — acceptable, or should this wait for the "future staged-upload design" the 2026-07-28 plan reserved? (b) Should anonymous com.atproto.sync.getBlob continue to serve public blobs that no public record references (current behaviour, matches the reference PDS), or should Swan diverge and require record reachability? That is a deliberate-design question with federation and performance consequences, and the answer determines whether fix 2 is a GC sweep or a read-path predicate.

clusterNotes:
Single-finding cluster. The cryptographic mechanism the scan describes is exactly right and every cited line is accurate (only F02's `SwanSpaces.swift:518-527` needs a note: 518-528 is `sign`, and 530-582 is the verify pair + `contentBinding` + `encodedContext` — no meaningful drift).

The one concrete code defect worth fixing is a two-line comment at `Sources/SwanSpaces/StreamingSpaceCARRecovery.swift:305-308` that calls the pair "authenticated the exact commit root".

findings.title: Permissioned commit-context signature excludes the commitment; the content-binding MAC is recomputable from the envelope's disclosed IKM
findings.evidence:
Mechanism confirmed exactly as described. `Sources/SwanSpaces/SwanSpaces.swift:573-582` (`encodedContext`) covers only the domain string plus length-prefixed space, author, rev, ikm — never the commitment; `:518-528` (`sign`) signs that payload and separately computes `contentBinding(ikm:context:commitment:)`; `:557-571` derives the MAC key by one-block HKDF-Expand from the 32-byte IKM alone; `Sources/SwanSpaces/SwanSpaces.swift:1476-1488` (`encodeCommit`) puts `ikm` on the wire in cleartext next to `mac` and `sig`. Acceptance is at `Sources/SwanSpaces/StreamingSpaceCARRecovery.swift:294-298` (`contextSignatureVerifier(envelope)` && `verifyContentBinding(envelope)`), and the separately fetched freshness witness at `Sources/SwanInterop/PermissionedRemoteReplicaHTTPProvider.swift:211-252` uses the identical construction and yields only `(wireRevision, commitment)`, compared at `Sources/SwanSQLite/SQLitePermissionedRemoteReplicaRecovery.swift:780-787`. So yes: an observer of one valid envelope for a given (space, author, rev) can swap the commitment and recompute a passing MAC.

Impact is overstated for four independently sufficient reasons.
(1) DELIBERATE, EXTERNALLY PINNED DESIGN. This is a faithful port of the pinned reference implementation, not a Swan construction. `Swan/.interop-cache/atproto-3f6c96d5d2d25438bd40fa89d6ecc37865f8e354/packages/space/src/commit.ts:35-37`: "The signature covers only (space, rev, ikm), never the repo hash — that is what makes a rebroadcast commit non-probative"; :23-25: "Symmetric — anyone holding the commit can do this, which is what gives a leaked commit its deniability." That commit is the `referenceImplementationCommit` in `Profiles/public-data-testing-2026-08-06.json`. Swan's own comments say the same and are load-bearing: `Sources/SwanSpaces/SwanSpaces.swift:530-531` ("Verifies only the author signature over `(space, author, rev, ikm)`. It intentionally does not claim that the author signed repository data.") and `:546-547` ("This must never be called a signature: every reader can derive its key from the public IKM"). `docs/threat-boundaries.md:15-17` states it as a project invariant.
(2) TESTS DOCUMENT IT AS INTENDED. `Tests/SwanSpacesTests/SwanSpacesTests.swift:181-196` asserts the two checks are separate APIs; `:198-232` is a pinned cross-implementation KAT over the exact expand construction. Both would have to be rewritten to change the format.
(3) NOT REACHABLE ON THE DEPLOYED SURFACE. `verifyStreamingRecovery` production callers are `Sources/SwanInterop/PermissionedRemoteReplicaRecoveryOrchestrator.swift:241`, `Sources/SwanInterop/LiveInterop.swift:3482`, `Sources/SwanAccountExport/SwanOperatorAccountRestore.swift:613`, `Sources/SwanAccountExport/SwanPortableExport.swift:439`, invoked only from `swan lab ...` (`Sources/swan/SwanCommand.swift:4234-4239, 4467, 4857, 6919`) and `swan restore` (`:1570, :1634`). No SwanHTTP handler calls it. `swan restore` reads a local operator-supplied export file (`SwanOperatorAccountRestore.swift:601-604`), not the network.
(4) CONTROLS THE SCAN DID NOT CREDIT. The source origin must be HTTPS (loopback-only exception) and is canonicalized and durably pinned together with a SHA-256 fingerprint of the operator-configured verification key: `Sources/SwanStorage/PermissionedRemoteReplicaRecoveryStore.swift:132-165`, bound at `PermissionedRemoteReplicaHTTPProvider.swift:133-137` and persisted at `PermissionedRemoteReplicaRecoveryStore.swift:194, 207, 211`. A freshness witness is mandatory even on first bootstrap (`PermissionedRemoteReplicaRecoveryStore.swift:197-201`). Installation is additionally gated by high-water and equivocation checks: `Sources/SwanSQLite/SQLitePermissionedRemoteReplicaRecovery.swift:1541-1548` rejects any rev below the local head and any equal rev with a different commitment (also enforced at `:901-917`), tested at `Tests/SwanSQLiteTests/PermissionedRemoteReplicaRecoverySQLiteTests.swift:602` and `:2131`. So a replayed envelope can only install content at a rev strictly newer than anything the replica already holds, from the exact pinned HTTPS origin, under the exact pinned author key.

Residual real defect: one comment overstates what was proven. `Sources/SwanSpaces/StreamingSpaceCARRecovery.swift:305-308` says the checks "have authenticated the exact commit root"; they have not — they authenticate that the author signed *some* commit for that (space, rev, ikm) and that whoever produced this envelope knew the IKM. `Sources/SwanInterop/PermissionedRemoteReplicaHTTPProvider.swift:44-49` ("first it authenticates the source's current signed commit") is similarly loose.
findings.remediation:
Reject the scan's primary remediation ("bind the exact commitment into the writer-authenticated signature"). That is not a Swan-local change and it destroys the property the format exists to provide. The signed bytes are fixed by `bluesky-social/atproto@3f6c96d5.../packages/space/src/commit.ts:60-75` (`encodeCtx`), pinned by `Profiles/public-data-testing-2026-08-06.json` `referenceImplementationCommit` + `Profiles/*.lexicons.sha256` + `Profiles/*.generated-wire.sha256`, mirrored in `interop/reference-pds-overlay/reference-pds-recovery.patch`, and locked byte-exact by the KAT at `Tests/SwanSpacesTests/SwanSpacesTests.swift:198-232`. Signing the hash would make every leaked commit third-party-probative — the exact outcome proposal-0016 rejects.

Adopt the scan's second clause only, as documentation-level work:
1. `Sources/SwanSpaces/StreamingSpaceCARRecovery.swift:305-308` — rewrite the comment. Replace "have authenticated the exact commit root" with something true, e.g. that the author signature authenticates the (space, author, rev, ikm) context and the deniable MAC proves the producer of this envelope knew the IKM, so exact-content authority rests with the pinned serving origin, not with the author signature. This is the only line I would call a defect.
2. `Sources/SwanInterop/PermissionedRemoteReplicaHTTPProvider.swift:44-49` — soften "authenticates the source's current signed commit" the same way, and note explicitly that the freshness witness and the CAR come from the same origin so the witness is a freshness check, not an independent authority.
3. `docs/threat-boundaries.md` — add one line after :17 stating that for permissioned remote-replica recovery the pinned HTTPS source origin is the exact-content integrity authority; the author signature scopes it to a (space, rev) the author actually produced, and equivocation/high-water (`Sources/SwanSQLite/SQLitePermissionedRemoteReplicaRecovery.swift:1541-1548`) bound replay to strictly-newer revisions.
4. Optional regression test in `Tests/SwanSpacesTests/StreamingSpaceCARRecoveryTests.swift`: build a CAR whose commitment/records are substituted and whose MAC is recomputed from the replayed IKM, assert `verifyStreamingRecovery` *accepts* it (documenting the delegated-integrity property so a future reader does not mistake it for a bug), then assert the SQLite publish path rejects it via `.equivocation` when the local head already holds that rev. Pair it with the existing coverage at `Tests/SwanSQLiteTests/PermissionedRemoteReplicaRecoverySQLiteTests.swift:602`.
Do NOT add a rejection in `verifyStreamingRecovery` — there is nothing available there to reject on.
findings.risk: Items 1-3 are comments and docs: zero runtime, wire, or schema risk. Item 4 adds tests only. The rejected remediation is what carries risk: changing `encodedContext` in `Sources/SwanSpaces/SwanSpaces.swift:573-582` is a WIRE-FORMAT BREAK that invalidates every already-signed space commit, breaks interop with the pinned reference PDS and its overlay, fails `Tests/SwanSpacesTests/SwanSpacesTests.swift:198-232`, and requires regenerating/re-pinning `Profiles/*.lexicons.sha256` and `Profiles/*.generated-wire.sha256` plus the Petrel-generated `ComAtprotoSpaceDefs.SignedCommit` type used at `Sources/SwanInterop/PermissionedRemoteReplicaHTTPProvider.swift:212`.
findings.needsHumanDecision: Does Swan accept the pinned proposal-0016 trust model — the serving PDS origin is the sole authority for exact permissioned repository content, and the author signature is deliberately non-probative about that content — as a documented, permanent boundary? Changing it is an upstream protocol decision at bluesky-social/atproto (packages/space/src/commit.ts), not a Swan-local fix; if the answer is no, the ask is an upstream proposal-0016 amendment plus a coordinated re-pin, not a patch to Sources/SwanSpaces.

clusterNotes:
All four findings share one root: a space credential is a bearer capability whose claim set (`iss/sub/iat/exp/jti`, Sources/SwanOAuth/SwanOAuth.swift:370-376) carries no reader, client, membership, or policy identity, so every post-issuance authorization decision (Sources/SwanOAuth/SpaceCredentialAuthority.swift:861-908 -> Sources/SwanSpaces/SwanSpaces.swift:244-254) is signature+space+time only.

Line citations in this cluster are unusually accurate — every cited range resolves to the code the scan describes in the current tree. I found no drift.

Ordering / subsumption is the most important cross-finding fact: **F08 and F14 are strict subsets of F03 as long as F03 stands.** If a credential minted 1 ms *before* removal is valid for 2 h anyway, winning a race to mint one 1 ms *after* removal buys an attacker nothing. Do not spend effort on F08 as an independent defect; fix F03 first, and F08 collapses to "the read-time watermark now also covers the mint race" for free. F14 is the one exception worth fixing on its own merits, because it is a different asset (authority signing-key generation, not space policy) and its fix is a five-line mirror of a fence the same file already implements twice.

The scan's proposed remediations for F08 and F14 are the same boilerplate string ("Linearize lifecycle/generation authorization with the signing, streaming-adoption, or SQLite commit point..."), and F39's remediation is boilerplate lifted from a DID-binding finding whose controls are *already implemented* in the cited file (DID binding at PLCSpaceCredentialPublicKeyResolver.swift:354, issuer allowlist at :346, audit-chain-authenticated fetch + durable continuity CAS at :422-433). Treat F39's remediation string as noise; it does not address the TTL claim at all.

Deployed-configuration reality: `--enable-local-space-interop` IS set on swan.place (docs/superpowers/plans/2026-08-11-swan-place-migration-completion-record.md:36-38), and the space routes register off `PermissionedData0016.methods` independent of the public profile (Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanHTTP.swift:874-981), so `getSpaceCredential` and Bearer-credential reads are genuinely live endpoints on the box. But with local-only key resolution (Sources/swan/SwanCommand.swift:838-841 — no `--notification-config`, hence no pins and no PLC resolver), the only delegation Swan can verify is one signed by a *local* account, and there is exactly one account, which is necessarily the space owner, and owners cannot be removed (Sources/SwanSQLite/SwanSQLite.swift:6423-6425). So nothing in this cluster is exploitable on the box as it stands today; all four become reachable the moment a second local account, a pin, or a notification-config PLC resolver is added.

Shared helper worth introducing once: a single "credential freshness watermark" check consumed by all four credential-verifier call sites (Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanSpaceXRPC.swift:665, SwanSpaceBlobXRPC.swift:232, SwanSpaceRepositorySyncXRPC.swift:316, SwanSpaceNotificationXRPC.swift:534). Building it once closes F03 and F08 across record, blob, CAR, oplog, and notification reads; building it per-route is how one of those five surfaces gets missed.

findings.title: Space credential remains a valid whole-space read capability after the holder is removed or its app policy is denied
findings.evidence:
Mechanism is exactly as described and every citation resolves. Claim set has no reader/policy binding: Sources/SwanOAuth/SwanOAuth.swift:370-376 (`SpaceCredentialClaims` = iss/sub/iat/exp/jti) and :343 (`spaceCredentialLifetime = 2*60*60`); minting encodes nothing else, Sources/SwanOAuth/SpaceCredentialAuthority.swift:744-751. Verification is signature+space+time only, Sources/SwanOAuth/SpaceCredentialAuthority.swift:861-899, producing a grant whose subject is the *authority*, :900-907. The read policy then accepts that grant for any read in the space with no membership lookup, Sources/SwanSpaces/SwanSpaces.swift:244-254. Removal deletes the row and bumps the revision but revokes nothing, Sources/SwanSQLite/SwanSQLite.swift:6429-6433; there is no issued-credential JTI store anywhere (the only replay store is for single-use *delegations*, Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanSpaceCredentialXRPC.swift:114-121). Sink confirmed at Sources/SwanSQLite/SwanSQLite.swift:10514-10520 -> :11043-11054. Same pattern on blobs (Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanSpaceBlobXRPC.swift:227-245) and repo sync (SwanSpaceRepositorySyncXRPC.swift:316).

Why PARTIALLY and not CONFIRMED: two load-bearing comments document the mint-time-only model as deliberate. Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanSpaceXRPC.swift:405-412: "A verified credential is intentionally different: it is the proposal's cross-member read grant and its exact space was already bound above." Sources/SwanSQLite/SQLitePreMigratedAccountDirectory.swift:609-613: policy "is intentionally sequenced *before*" key access, and Sources/SwanSQLite/SwanSQLite.swift:7028-7032: "Evaluates persisted policy facts in a read transaction **before the caller mints a transient read credential**." docs/threat-boundaries.md:13-14 states only that a credential is read-only, asserting no immediate-revocation invariant. So the scan's "violates immediate membership revocation expectations" is an expectation this codebase never states; what is real is a 2 h residual capability lifetime with no revocation channel at all.

Test coverage: the scan is right that none exists. Tests/SwanOAuthTests/SpaceCredentialAuthorityTests.swift:369-458 tests mint-time member/app/managing-app fail-closed only; `removeSimpleSpaceMember` appears in exactly one test file (Tests/SwanHTTPTests/SimpleSpaceLifecycleHTTPTests.swift) and never in a mint-remove-read sequence.
findings.remediation:
I disagree with the scan's first option. Do NOT add a membership/policy generation claim to the credential: the claim set is pinned to proposal 0016 and to a reference TypeScript PDS (Sources/SwanOAuth/SwanOAuth.swift:330-342, Profiles/*.json reference pins), and the credential structurally cannot carry reader identity, so a per-reader generation is unenforceable cross-host anyway.

The cheap correct fix needs no wire change and no migration, because the watermark already exists: `touchSimpleSpace` (Sources/SwanSQLite/SwanSQLite.swift:9165-9183) monotonically bumps `permissioned_simple_space_authorities.updated_at` on every membership and policy mutation, including the removal at :6433. Add a per-space freshness gate that rejects any credential whose `iat` is not strictly greater than that row's `updated_at`:
1. Add `issuedAt` to `SpaceGrant` (Sources/SwanSpaces/SwanSpaces.swift:194-207) — only 4 construction sites (SpaceCredentialAuthority.swift:901, SwanSQLite.swift:11330, SwanSpaces.swift:2040, SwanInterop/LocalSemanticInterop.swift:406) — and populate it from `claims.iat` at SpaceCredentialAuthority.swift:900-907.
2. Add one directory method `requireSpaceCredentialNotSuperseded(space:issuedAt:)` on SQLitePreMigratedAccountDirectory next to `authorizeSimpleSpaceCredentialRead` (Sources/SwanSQLite/SQLitePreMigratedAccountDirectory.swift:614-638), reading the same authority row.
3. Call it at all four verifier seams: Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanSpaceXRPC.swift:665, SwanSpaceBlobXRPC.swift:232, SwanSpaceRepositorySyncXRPC.swift:316, SwanSpaceNotificationXRPC.swift:534.
This revokes every outstanding credential for a space on any membership/policy change, at the authority's own host, with the claims that already exist.

Second, independently and immediately: expose `DurableSpaceCredentialAuthority.Configuration.lifetime` (Sources/SwanOAuth/SpaceCredentialAuthority.swift:659-676 — already validated and already ≤2 h) as a `swan serve` flag and default the deployment to something like 300 s. That converts an unbounded-feeling 2 h window into an explicitly chosen revocation window, which is the honest framing of the scan's second option.

Cross-host revocation is a protocol gap, not a Swan bug — do not try to close it here.
findings.risk: The watermark over-revokes by design: any addMember/removeMember/client-allowlist change invalidates every live credential for that space, so well-behaved clients must re-run the delegation exchange (Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanSpaceCredentialXRPC.swift:107-140) mid-session. That is client-visible behaviour and needs the maintainer's sign-off. `updated_at` is second-granularity (`simpleSpaceTimestamp`) and `iat` is seconds, so use a strict `iat > updated_at` comparison and accept that a credential minted in the same second as a removal is rejected. Adding `issuedAt` to the public Codable `SpaceGrant` is a source-compatible change if defaulted, but it is a public type in SwanSpaces. Shortening the lifetime is a behaviour change for any pinned interop fixture that assumes 2 h. No schema migration and no JWT wire change are required by this proposal.
findings.needsHumanDecision: Is mint-time-only revocation an accepted property of proposal 0016 space credentials (in which case the only work is shortening the lease and documenting the window), or does Swan want to enforce prompt revocation at its own read endpoints via the `iat` > `updated_at` watermark, accepting that every membership or policy edit forces all readers of that space to re-exchange a delegation?

findings.title: Membership/policy revocation can commit between the authorization transaction and credential signing
findings.evidence:
The window is real and the citations are accurate: `authorizeSimpleSpaceCredentialRead` commits its read transaction at Sources/SwanOAuth/SpaceCredentialAuthority.swift:732-737, then the issuer suspends on `signingKeys.signingKey(for:)` at :738 and signs at :744-751 with no policy revision, CAS, or second membership check. The policy read really is a self-contained transaction (Sources/SwanSQLite/SwanSQLite.swift:7044-7074) and the sequencing is explicitly deliberate: Sources/SwanSQLite/SQLitePreMigratedAccountDirectory.swift:609-613 — key access and credential creation "live in SwanOAuth and are intentionally sequenced *after* this read-only policy transaction commits."

The scan missed a partial control: `requireCredentialAuthorityStillAvailable` (Sources/SwanSQLite/SQLitePreMigratedAccountDirectory.swift:628, defined :2561-2572) re-checks authority-account activity and database existence *after* the policy transaction, so whole-space authority teardown and account deactivation are partially fenced; only the space-policy predicate is unfenced.

Impact is overstated because it is fully subsumed by F03. An attacker who wins this race obtains a credential identical to one they could have obtained legitimately microseconds earlier and which F03 keeps valid for 2 h regardless. There is no state an attacker reaches through the race that they cannot reach without it. Tests/SwanOAuthTests/SpaceCredentialAuthorityTests.swift:463 covers concurrent issuance only for JTI freshness and non-persistence, not for a concurrent policy transition — the scan is right that no test covers this.
findings.remediation:
Do not implement the scan's remediation as written; "linearize lifecycle authorization with the SQLite commit point" would mean holding a policy transaction open across an encrypted key-store read, which is exactly the coupling the comment at Sources/SwanSQLite/SQLitePreMigratedAccountDirectory.swift:609-613 deliberately avoids, and it would still not stop a removal that lands one millisecond later.

If F03's `iat` > `updated_at` watermark lands, this finding closes for free: a credential minted after a removal has `iat` >= the bumped `updated_at` only if it was minted in a later second, and the strict comparison rejects the same-second case. Ship nothing separately.

If F03 is deferred, the proportionate standalone fix is one extra read: re-invoke `policyDirectory.authorizeSimpleSpaceCredentialRead(...)` immediately after the signing key resolves, between Sources/SwanOAuth/SpaceCredentialAuthority.swift:743 and :744, and fail closed. That is ~6 lines and one extra read transaction per exchange, with no lock-holding across the key read.
findings.risk: The re-check variant doubles the policy read per credential exchange (one extra SQLite read transaction on a route that is already rate-limited at the edge) and turns a lost race into an opaque `notAuthorized` rather than a mint — a behaviour change visible to a client that legitimately raced its own owner's edit. No wire-format or schema change either way.

findings.title: Authority account lifecycle and key generation are not re-read after the async key-store fetch on the space-credential signing path
findings.evidence:
The unfenced suspension is exactly where the scan says. Sources/SwanOAuth/SpaceCredentialAuthority.swift:204-224: `signingKey(for:)` checks `account.status.authorizesAccount` and reads `keyReferences` at :207-209, awaits `keyStore.key(for: references.signing)` at :213, and returns at :220-223 without re-reading the account or the reference generation. The caller signs immediately at :744-751.

The scan's own counterevidence is the strongest argument for fixing it: the two verification resolvers in the same file implement precisely this fence, with the reasoning spelled out — Sources/SwanOAuth/SpaceCredentialAuthority.swift:304-317 and :397-410: "The directory does not currently expose one atomic account/key projection. Re-read the complete account generation and lifecycle after the external metadata read, and treat any intervening change as a terminal local negative." The signing path is the odd one out.

Impact is overstated. A credential signed with generation N as N+1 commits is *useless locally*: `LocalAccountSpaceCredentialPublicKeyResolver` requires `authorizesAccount`, requires `signing.generation == rotation.generation`, requires the current references to match, and re-reads the whole account afterwards (:262-317), so local verification fails closed. The token is only usable at a remote verifier holding a pin or a live PLC cache — and on swan.place no pinned or PLC credential resolver is constructed at all (Sources/swan/SwanCommand.swift:838-841 selects local-only resolvers when `--notification-config` is absent). The window is also narrowed upstream by `requireCredentialAuthorityStillAvailable` (Sources/SwanSQLite/SQLitePreMigratedAccountDirectory.swift:628, :2561-2572), which the scan does not mention.
findings.remediation:
Fix this one on its own merits — it is cheap, it is internally inconsistent today, and it belongs to the same family as the C12 signer findings (proxy service token, delegation token), so fix all of them with one pattern.

In Sources/SwanOAuth/SpaceCredentialAuthority.swift:213-224, after `keyStore.key(for: references.signing)` returns and before constructing `SpaceCredentialAuthoritySigningKey`, re-read `accounts.account(did: authority)` and `accounts.keyReferences(did: authority)` and require the account to be unchanged, still `authorizesAccount`, and the signing/rotation generations to still match the pre-read values; otherwise `throw SwanError.unavailable("space credential signing key is unavailable")` (the existing error at :218 already carries this meaning, so no new error case and no HTTP mapping change — SwanSpaceCredentialXRPC.swift:153-157 already maps `.unavailable`). Mirror the comment at :304-308 so the next reader sees why. ~8 lines.

Ignore the scan's "lease/CAS" framing: no lease exists on this path and inventing one would be disproportionate to a fence the file already demonstrates twice.
findings.risk: A concurrent legitimate key rotation now surfaces as a transient `unavailable` on getSpaceCredential instead of returning a credential signed with the old generation — that is the intended failure mode and matches how verification already behaves, but it is a new (rare) 503-class response on the exchange route. One extra pair of directory reads per credential mint. No wire-format or schema change.

findings.title: PLC-backed credential verification serves a cached pre-rotation authority key for up to the cache TTL
findings.evidence:
The caching behaviour is real and as cited: `CacheConfiguration.standard` uses a 60 s lifetime with a 300 s ceiling (Sources/SwanOAuth/PLCSpaceCredentialPublicKeyResolver.swift:136-173), and `state(for:now:)` returns the cached document with no refresh while `entry.expiresAt > now` (:390-392), feeding `publicKey` (:340-384) and then the verifier at SpaceCredentialAuthority.swift:861-899.

But this is documented deliberate bounded staleness, not an oversight — the type comment says so at PLCSpaceCredentialPublicKeyResolver.swift:105-106: "Cached state is used only until its short TTL ends; an expired entry is never used if PLC refresh fails," and the failure branch at :477-486 actively evicts rather than serving stale on refresh failure. Bounded key-cache staleness is a property of every PLC consumer; calling it a defect would require a no-cache design nobody runs.

The stated impact is also inflated relative to F03: an attacker holding a compromised prior authority key can mint credentials valid for 2 h regardless of the cache, so the cache TTL adds at most 60 s to the window in which *newly minted* forgeries are accepted — a rounding error next to the credential lifetime itself.

Not reachable as deployed: this resolver is constructed only from `--notification-config` with a `credentialKeyPLC` block (Sources/swan/SwanCommand.swift:161-188, :222-226), and swan.place runs local-only resolvers (SwanCommand.swift:838-841); the migration record shows only the six space/public-mutation flags (docs/superpowers/plans/2026-08-11-swan-place-migration-completion-record.md:36-38).
findings.remediation:
Reject the scan's remediation outright — it is boilerplate copied from a DID-binding finding and every control it asks for is already implemented in the cited file: fetched documents are bound to the requested DID (`guard state.did == issuer`, PLCSpaceCredentialPublicKeyResolver.swift:354-356), the issuer allowlist is enforced before any lookup (:344-349), the fetch is audit-chain-authenticated with a durable continuity CAS (:422-433), and a malformed dedicated method fails closed instead of downgrading (:365-382). Implementing it would be a no-op that teaches the next reader the controls were missing.

Recommended action: no code change. Optionally (a) document the 60 s propagation window as an accepted revocation latency alongside the credential lifetime in docs/threat-boundaries.md, and (b) if a deployment ever enables `--notification-config`, set `lifetime` explicitly rather than relying on the default. If someone insists on a control, the only one that actually helps is a targeted cache invalidation triggered by an authority-key continuity advance — but that is disproportionate to a 60 s window sitting behind a 2 h credential.
findings.risk: None for the no-change recommendation. A forced-refresh-per-verification variant would turn every permissioned read into a PLC round trip and hand a remote bearer token a network-amplification primitive — strictly worse than the current bounded cache, and it would fight the concurrency and rate limits at PLCSpaceCredentialPublicKeyResolver.swift:407-418.
findings.needsHumanDecision: Confirm that a bounded 60 s PLC key-propagation delay is an accepted revocation latency for cross-host credential verification; if yes, close this finding as documented-deliberate rather than carrying it as open residual risk.

clusterNotes:
Shared substrate: all three findings sit behind one gate — `SwanAuthenticatedSpaceNotificationsCapability`, built only when `spaceCredentialConfiguration` AND `spaceNotificationConfiguration` are both non-nil (Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanHTTP.swift:703-720). Route registration itself iterates the static `PermissionedData0016.methods` registry, not the active profile (Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanHTTP.swift:875), so the profile does NOT gate these routes — the capability does.

IMPORTANT — the task briefing's stated deployed configuration is wrong on one point. The live unit (`ssh netcup 'systemctl cat swan.service'`) runs `--profile /usr/local/share/swan/Profiles/permissioned-data-0016-2026-07-30.json`, not `public-data-testing-2026-08-06`. It also runs `--enable-local-space-interop`, `--enable-public-repository-mutations`, `--enable-public-firehose`, `--enable-oauth-authorization-server`, and has NO `--notification-config` and no managing-service-audience flag. Consequences that decide reachability for this whole cluster:
1. `ServePermissionedRuntime.compose` takes `case let (.some(local), nil)` (Sources/swan/SwanCommand.swift:838-841), so `servicePublicKeys` is a bare `LocalAccountSpaceServicePublicKeyResolver` — `CompositeSpaceServicePublicKeyResolver` is never constructed and there are zero pins. F16 has no code path in production.
2. `notificationConfiguration` IS non-nil (Sources/swan/SwanCommand.swift:872-886), so `/xrpc/com.atproto.space.notifyWrite` and `/xrpc/com.atproto.space.notifySpaceDeleted` ARE routed on swan.place.
3. `recipientBindings` falls back to `.empty` (Sources/swan/SwanCommand.swift:881; Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanSpaceNotificationRecipientBindings.swift:11-13), so `notifySpaceDeleted` always returns early at Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanSpaceNotificationXRPC.swift:216-220 with 200 OK and zero durable effect. F31's sink is unreachable today.
4. The only issuer any accepted token can carry is the single locally-managed active account's own DID, and forging one requires that account's KEK-wrapped signing private key. An attacker with that key already owns the repo.

Ordering: land F04 first — it is a ~4-line unconditional cap that shrinks the exploitation window for F16 and F31 simultaneously and needs no wire change. F16 second (self-contained, mirrors an already-written adjacent resolver). F31's cheap half (existence precondition) is independent; its expensive half is a protocol change that should not be attempted before the operator actually configures recipient bindings.

Two scan-quality notes: the F16 "Proposed remediation" string (PLC audit-chain, duplicate service IDs, peer pinning) is boilerplate lifted from an unrelated DID-resolution finding and has nothing to do with the cited code — discard it entirely. And the F16 entrypoint citation `Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanXRPCPipethrough.swift:409-440` is wrong: that code calls `capability.tokens.issueProxyServiceToken` (an outbound minting path in SwanOAuth/ProxyServiceAuthentication.swift) and never touches `SpaceServicePublicKeyResolver`.

findings.title: Service JWT with absent `iat` skips both freshness controls; `exp` is bounded only from below
findings.evidence:
Mechanism is exactly as described and the citations are accurate. `SpaceServiceJWT.Claims.iat` is optional (Sources/SwanOAuth/SpaceServiceAuthentication.swift:291). `validateShape` requires alg/typ/iss/aud/lxm/jti but never `iat` (Sources/SwanOAuth/SpaceServiceAuthentication.swift:456-466). In `verify`, the only unconditional time check is the lower bound `parsed.claims.exp >= nowSeconds - clockSkew` (Sources/SwanOAuth/SpaceServiceAuthentication.swift:405-407); the future-issuance check and the `exp - iat <= maximumLifetime` check both live inside `if let issuedAt = parsed.claims.iat` (Sources/SwanOAuth/SpaceServiceAuthentication.swift:408-419). A correctly signed token with no `iat` and `exp = Int64.max` therefore returns successfully, and `DurableSpaceServiceAuthenticationVerifier` propagates that distant expiry into `VerifiedSpaceServiceAuthentication.expiresAt` (Sources/SwanOAuth/SpaceServiceAuthentication.swift:217-223).

Adjacent-control asymmetry is real: Swan's own OAuth JWT verifier has an explicit `requireIssuedAt` constraint (exercised at Tests/SwanOAuthTests/SwanOAuthTests.swift:325-336), and the service verifier has no equivalent. Test coverage confirms the gap: `testSignedJWTVerifiersRejectExtremeTimeClaimsWithoutOverflowing` builds a service token with `iat: .min, exp: .max` and asserts rejection (Tests/SwanOAuthTests/SwanOAuthTests.swift:337-355) — i.e. an extreme *present* `iat` is covered, absent `iat` is not.

No comment anywhere states that absent `iat` is a deliberate interop allowance. The header comment at Sources/SwanOAuth/SpaceServiceAuthentication.swift:273-277 justifies tolerating `typ`, ES256K, and route-level `lxm` — it is silent on `iat`. Interop evidence points the other way: the pinned reference issuer always emits `iat` (`const iat = params.iat ?? Math.floor(Date.now()/1e3)`, .interop-cache/atproto-3f6c96d5d2d25438bd40fa89d6ecc37865f8e354/packages/xrpc-server/src/auth.ts:32) and the checked-in golden fixture payload is `{"iat":1750000000,...,"exp":1750000060,...}` (Tests/SwanOAuthTests/Fixtures/pinned-typescript-notify-write.json). The reference *verifier* checks only `exp` and never looks at `iat` at all, so Swan is already stricter than upstream.
findings.remediation:
Agree with the second half of the scan's remediation, disagree with the first half as the primary fix.

Primary (do this): add an unconditional upper bound next to the existing lower bound at Sources/SwanOAuth/SpaceServiceAuthentication.swift:405-407 — compute `latestExpiration = nowSeconds + skew + Int64(maximumLifetime)` with `addingReportingOverflow`, and reject when `parsed.claims.exp > latestExpiration`. This caps every accepted token at ~6 minutes regardless of whether `iat` is present, needs no wire change, and stays compatible with any issuer that legitimately omits `iat` (the reference default lifetime is 60s, well under the 300s policy). Keep the existing `if let issuedAt` block at :408-419 unchanged as a tighter check when `iat` is supplied.

Secondary (maintainer's call): additionally require `iat` by moving it into `validateShape` (Sources/SwanOAuth/SpaceServiceAuthentication.swift:456-466) and making `Claims.iat` non-optional at :291. Safe against the pinned reference issuer, which always emits it — but it is a genuine tightening relative to the reference verifier's tolerance, so it should be an explicit decision, not a side effect.

Tests: extend Tests/SwanOAuthTests/SwanOAuthTests.swift:337-355 with (a) no-`iat` + far-future `exp` → rejected, (b) no-`iat` + `exp` within policy → accepted (if only the primary fix lands) or rejected (if the secondary lands), (c) present-`iat` + `exp` beyond `maximumLifetime` → still rejected. The golden TypeScript fixture test (Tests/SwanOAuthTests/TypeScriptSpaceNotificationContractTests.swift:11-31) must stay green — it will, since that token carries `iat` and a 60s lifetime.
findings.risk: Primary fix: no wire-format change, no schema change, no client-visible behaviour change for any conforming issuer — it only shrinks the accepted `exp` window from unbounded to now+skew+maximumLifetime. The one way it could bite is a peer that mints service tokens with lifetimes over 5 minutes; the reference implementation does not. Secondary fix (requiring `iat`) is a real interop tightening and would reject any future non-reference issuer that omits `iat`.
findings.needsHumanDecision: Should Swan hard-require `iat` on service JWTs, diverging from the pinned reference verifier which never inspects `iat`? The unconditional `exp` cap closes the security gap without this, so requiring `iat` is a strictness preference, not a necessity.

findings.title: Local service-key resolver conflates inactive/unavailable managed accounts with unmanaged DIDs, permitting pin fallback
findings.evidence:
The mechanism is real and the asymmetry with adjacent resolvers is exactly as the scan describes, but the stated impact is overstated and the entrypoint citation is wrong.

Real part: `LocalAccountSpaceServicePublicKeyResolver.publicKey` collapses five distinct outcomes — unmalformed-issuer, account absent, account not active, key references missing, public key missing — into a single `return nil` through one `guard` (Sources/SwanOAuth/SpaceServiceAuthentication.swift:76-83). Only a corrupt key *encoding* throws (:84-88). `CompositeSpaceServicePublicKeyResolver.resolve` then feeds that `nil` to `uniqueVerificationKey`, which returns the pinned key when local is nil (Sources/SwanOAuth/PermissionedResolverComposition.swift:206-216, 224-234). The credential and delegation resolvers do exactly the opposite and say so in a comment: "Only a proven absence from the local account directory may fall through to an operator pin or remote PLC resolver" (Sources/SwanOAuth/SpaceCredentialAuthority.swift:253-254 and :347-348), throwing `…ResolutionError.unavailable` for inactive status, generation mismatch, missing references, missing public key, and any post-read lifecycle change (:262-268, :271-281, :283-293, :305-316). The composition comment at Sources/SwanOAuth/PermissionedResolverComposition.swift:83-85 states the contract the service resolver violates. No test covers the service resolver's inactive-account path — Tests/SwanOAuthTests/PermissionedResolverCompositionTests.swift:61-67 uses a `StaticServiceKeys` stub, and `LocalAccountSpaceServicePublicKeyResolver` appears nowhere under Tests/.

Overstated part: the startup preflight loop resolves every pin through the same composition (Sources/SwanOAuth/PermissionedResolverComposition.swift:189-195), so a pin overlapping an *active* local DID must already carry key material identical to that account's (`deterministicIdentity` equality, :229-233). The pin holder is therefore whoever holds the account's own signing key. The scenario reduces to: a suspended/deleted account whose own key the operator had separately pinned keeps producing valid service JWTs — a lifecycle revocation bypass, not a cross-identity forgery.

Unreachable as deployed: no `--notification-config`, so `ServePermissionedRuntime.compose` takes `case let (.some(local), nil)` and `servicePublicKeys = local.servicePublicKeys` (Sources/swan/SwanCommand.swift:838-841) — `CompositeSpaceServicePublicKeyResolver` is never constructed and `PinnedSpaceServicePublicKeyResolver` holds zero pins.

Citation error: the scan's entrypoint `Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanXRPCPipethrough.swift:409-440` is a different subsystem — it mints outbound proxy tokens via `capability.tokens.issueProxyServiceToken` (:411-418) and never consults `SpaceServicePublicKeyResolver`. The real entrypoints are Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanSpaceNotificationXRPC.swift:556-581 and Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanSimpleSpaceCheckUserAccessXRPC.swift:53.
findings.remediation:
Discard the scan's proposed remediation entirely — PLC audit chains, duplicate service IDs, and peer pinning are boilerplate from an unrelated finding and touch none of this code.

Actual fix: rewrite `LocalAccountSpaceServicePublicKeyResolver.publicKey` at Sources/SwanOAuth/SpaceServiceAuthentication.swift:76-89 to mirror Sources/SwanOAuth/SpaceCredentialAuthority.swift:246-318 — return `nil` only when `accounts.account(did:)` succeeds and yields no row (proven absence), and throw `SwanError.unavailable` for every other negative: malformed issuer, `!status.authorizesAccount`, directory error, missing key references, missing public key. A terminal throw already propagates correctly: `serviceAuthentication` maps `SwanError.unavailable` to a 503 rather than a fallthrough (Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanSpaceNotificationXRPC.swift:573-577).

If you want full parity with the credential resolver, also add its post-read re-check of the account row (Sources/SwanOAuth/SpaceCredentialAuthority.swift:305-316) so a suspension racing the key read is terminal. That is optional — the primary status guard is the load-bearing one.

Tests: add a case to Tests/SwanOAuthTests/PermissionedResolverCompositionTests.swift driving a real `LocalAccountSpaceServicePublicKeyResolver` over an in-memory directory: active account + matching pin → resolves; account then suspended → composite throws rather than returning the pin; DID never provisioned + pin present → resolves from the pin (fallthrough preserved).
findings.risk: Behaviour change on a configuration nobody currently runs, so production risk is nil today. In a lab that pins a key for a DID it also hosts, verification switches from succeeding via the pin to failing 503 once the account is deactivated — which is the intent. One thing to watch: the fix makes a transient directory read error terminal (503) instead of silently falling through to the pin, so a notification peer will see availability errors where it previously saw success. That matches the credential/delegation resolvers' already-shipped semantics. No wire-format or schema change.
findings.needsHumanDecision: Is an operator pin intended to survive local account suspension/deletion as a deliberate break-glass, or is terminal revocation the intent? The credential and delegation resolvers already answer "terminal revocation" in comments; confirm the service resolver was meant to match and is simply an oversight rather than a documented exception.

findings.title: notifySpaceDeleted JWT carries no space binding; body selects the space and the tombstone write has no local-participation precondition
findings.evidence:
Mechanism confirmed, with an important correction to the framing and one Swan-specific defect the scan did not name.

The token claim set is `iss/aud/iat/exp/lxm/jti` only (Sources/SwanOAuth/SpaceServiceAuthentication.swift:288-299) — there is no space claim, and the issuer never sees one (Sources/SwanOAuth/SpaceServiceAuthentication.swift:239-270). The handler reads `space` from the request body and checks only `service.issuer == space.authority` (Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanSpaceNotificationXRPC.swift:202-211), then maps `service.audience` through operator recipient bindings (:216-220). Persistence re-checks only `issuer == space.authority, audience == accountDID` (Sources/SwanSQLite/SwanSQLite.swift:6956-6959). Replay is not blocked: the receipt primary key is `(issuer, event_id, space_uri)` (Sources/SwanSQLite/SwanSQLite.swift:342-349), so the same `jti` against a second space is not a duplicate (:6970-6983). The effect is durable and irreversible — `permissioned_space_recipient_tombstones` has `space_uri` as PRIMARY KEY (:351-356), no code path anywhere deletes a row from it, and its presence permanently fails local repository open (Sources/SwanSQLite/SwanSQLite.swift:9254-9269) plus blob reads (:9288, :9322), and the same transaction wipes `permissioned_space_outbox` for that space (:7018-7021).

The attack path is stronger than "observe a token": Swan-as-authority mints these tokens itself and posts them to endpoints registered via `registerNotify` (Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanSpaceNotificationDelivery.swift:228-242). A registrant for space S1 legitimately receives an authority-signed, space-unbound deletion token addressed to recipient R and can replay it at R with `space` swapped to S2 under the same authority.

Correction the scan missed: this is upstream's design, not a Swan-invented flaw. The pinned reference handler does the identical thing — space from `input.body`, `auth.credentials.iss !== new SpaceUri(space).authorityDid` as the only authorization, recipient from `aud` (.interop-cache/atproto-3f6c96d5d2d25438bd40fa89d6ecc37865f8e354/packages/pds/src/api/com/atproto/space/notifySpaceDeleted.ts:10-33).

But Swan is strictly weaker than the reference in one respect the scan did not identify: the reference no-ops unless the recipient already knows the space (`const existing = await actorTxn.space.getSpace(space); if (!existing) return`, same file :30-32). `receiveSpaceDeletionNotification` has no such precondition — it writes a tombstone for ANY syntactically valid SpaceURI under the issuer's authority, including spaces the recipient has never participated in (Sources/SwanSQLite/SwanSQLite.swift:7008-7017). That both enables the cross-space replay to land on unrelated spaces and lets any accepted authority insert unbounded tombstone rows.

Unreachable as deployed: `recipientBindings` is `.empty` (Sources/swan/SwanCommand.swift:881), so the handler returns at Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanSpaceNotificationXRPC.swift:219 before any storage call. No test covers cross-space replay; Tests/SwanHTTPTests/SpaceNotificationHTTPTests.swift:700 covers only the unknown-recipient no-op.
findings.remediation:
Disagree with the scan's remediation as written. "Include the exact space URI in the signed service JWT" is a wire-format divergence from the pinned reference PDS, which emits no space claim — Swan would reject every genuine reference-issued deletion notification. Do not do this unilaterally.

Do this instead, in two independent steps.

Step 1 (cheap, no protocol change, do now): add the reference's own precondition to `receiveSpaceDeletionNotification` at Sources/SwanSQLite/SwanSQLite.swift:6960-7017 — before inserting the tombstone, require an existing local row for `(space_uri, author_did = accountDID)` in `permissioned_repository_state` (or the equivalent recipient-participation projection); if absent, return as a no-op exactly as upstream does. This removes arbitrary-space tombstone insertion and reduces the replay's blast radius to spaces the recipient genuinely participates in. It also aligns Swan with the pinned handler, so it is defensible as an interop fix rather than a divergence.

Step 2 (protocol change, gate on maintainer + upstream): if per-space binding is wanted, the right seam is the token, not the handler — add an optional space claim in Sources/SwanOAuth/SpaceServiceAuthentication.swift:288-299 and :239-270, thread it through Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanSpaceNotificationDelivery.swift:232-236, and enforce equality at Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanSpaceNotificationXRPC.swift:209-211 **only when present**, so reference-issued tokens still verify. Enforcing it unconditionally requires an upstream lexicon change first.

Do not bother with the scan's suggestion to make `jti` globally unique across spaces — that would break legitimate reordered/retried delivery, which the current `(issuer, event_id, space_uri)` key handles deliberately.

Tests: add to Tests/SwanSQLiteTests/SpaceNotificationSQLiteTests.swift a case where a valid `(issuer, jti)` deletion for space S1 is replayed with `space` = S2 under the same authority, asserting no S2 tombstone and no S2 outbox deletion; and to Tests/SwanHTTPTests/SpaceNotificationHTTPTests.swift a route-level equivalent with recipient bindings configured.
findings.risk: Step 1 changes observable behaviour: a deletion notification for a space the recipient does not participate in becomes a silent no-op instead of a durable tombstone. That matches upstream, but if any Swan flow relies on pre-emptively tombstoning a not-yet-joined space, it would regress — check whether the `permissioned_restored_repository_closures` / portable-restore paths (Sources/SwanSQLite/SwanSQLite.swift:9276-9305) depend on a tombstone existing before repository state. No schema migration is needed for Step 1. Step 2 is a wire-format change to a token shared with the reference PDS and must not ship without upstream coordination; making the claim optional-but-enforced-when-present avoids breaking existing peers but creates a downgrade path any non-emitting issuer can take.
findings.needsHumanDecision: Two. (1) Is Swan willing to diverge from the reference `notifySpaceDeleted` token shape by adding a space claim, or must it stay wire-identical to the pinned TypeScript PDS? (2) Was omitting the reference's `if (!existing) return` precondition in `receiveSpaceDeletionNotification` deliberate — i.e. is a tombstone for a never-joined space meant to be a valid pre-emptive closure — or is it an unintended divergence? The answer decides whether Step 1 is a bug fix or a behaviour reversal.

findings.title: Read-only space credential can write durable notification registrations (registerNotify)
findings.evidence:
Mechanism is real and the citations are accurate (no line drift). Route: Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanSpaceNotificationXRPC.swift:254-279 registers POST /xrpc/com.atproto.space.registerNotify; the handler at :110-137 authenticates only via credentialAuthorization (:523-554), which requires `case let .spaceCredential(grant)` with `grant.space == space` (:539-542) and nothing else. The verifier always mints a read-only grant with no reader identity: Sources/SwanOAuth/SpaceCredentialAuthority.swift:899-906 (`permissions: [.read]`, `subject: claims.iss` = the authority), documented at :825-831 ("proposal 0016 credentials intentionally contain no reader identity"). Sink: Sources/SwanSQLite/SwanSQLite.swift:6699-6780 — `try grant.allows(.read)` at :6721, then DELETE-expired (:6729-6735), 1024-row budget check (:6746-6761, cap at :1674), then INSERT ... ON CONFLICT(space_uri, endpoint) DO UPDATE (:6762-6777). Table has no owner/registrant column (schema Sources/SwanSQLite/SwanSQLite.swift:331-339, PK (space_uri, endpoint)).

Where the scan overstates:
1. "Replace its filter" has no security effect today. Write fanout is deliberately never enqueued — Sources/SwanSQLite/SwanSQLite.swift:6933-6939 ("Do not enqueue an authority-signed `notifyWrite` fanout…"), restated in Sources/SwanStorage/AuthorizedSimpleSpaceDirectory.swift:376-381. The only consumer of registrations is deletion fanout (Sources/SwanSQLite/SwanSQLite.swift:6594-6622), whose rows carry repo_did NULL (:6613), and the pre-delivery recheck returns true whenever the fanout row's repository is nil (Sources/SwanSQLite/SwanSQLite.swift:6814-6819). repo_did is therefore inert.
2. "Replace its expiry" can only extend, never shorten or revoke: the route pins expiry to now+24h unconditionally (SwanSpaceNotificationXRPC.swift:121-122, constant :51) and the store rejects anything outside (0,24h] (:6712-6715).
3. Not SSRF, as the scan concedes: a registered endpoint is only a key into an operator-configured static map — Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanSpaceNotificationDelivery.swift:10-14 and :41-47 ("A registration only acts as a key into this map; it cannot select an audience or make a new network destination live").
4. "Bypasses SpaceAuthorizationPolicy" is a category error. SpaceAuthorizationPolicy.require (Sources/SwanSpaces/SwanSpaces.swift:239-254) governs *repository record* operations; the notification registry is a separate control-plane surface with its own explicit rule. Space-credential-only registration is the documented intended contract, asserted by tests: Tests/SwanHTTPTests/SpaceNotificationHTTPTests.swift:69 (`testCredentialOnlyWriterDiscoveryRegistrationAndServiceNotifications`, 200 OK for a bearer space credential at :96-108) and Tests/SwanSQLiteTests/SpaceNotificationSQLiteTests.swift:240-282 (`testRegistrationReplacementAndDeletionCreateOnlyOpaqueFanout`, registers with `fixture.readCredential()` and asserts replacement semantics) and :284-360 (capacity budget asserted as intended, including expiry reclamation at :348-360). These tests document the behaviour as deliberate, not accidental.

What survives: the per-space budget of 1024 (SwanSQLite.swift:1674) is consumable by a single authorized reader with no per-registrant accounting and no owner column, and the attacker can refresh his own rows indefinitely (upsert extends expiry), so co-readers of the same space can be denied new registrations for as long as the attacker holds a credential. Availability only, scoped to one space, and today the only lost signal is a space-deletion notification.
findings.remediation:
Reject the scan's remediation. "Require an account/authority write-capable credential for registerNotify" would break the interop contract outright: the intended registrant is a *remote* reader/PDS that holds no account and no OAuth grant on this server — that is the entire purpose of the endpoint (Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanSpaceNotificationXRPC.swift:12-14, Tests/SwanHTTPTests/SpaceNotificationHTTPTests.swift:69). "Bind the registration to the authorized repository/client" is also not implementable as written: the proposal-0016 credential carries only iss/sub/iat/exp/jti (Sources/SwanOAuth/SwanOAuth.swift:371-375) and deliberately no reader subject (SpaceCredentialAuthority.swift:825-831), so there is no principal to bind to without a wire-format change.

What I recommend instead, targeting only the surviving budget-squatting issue:
1. Plumb the credential `jti` into the grant: add an optional `credentialID` to SpaceGrant (Sources/SwanSpaces/SwanSpaces.swift:194-214, defaulted so the memberwise init stays source-compatible) and populate it in DurableSpaceCredentialVerifier (Sources/SwanOAuth/SpaceCredentialAuthority.swift:899-906) from `claims.jti`.
2. Add a `credential_jti TEXT` column to permissioned_space_notification_registrations (Sources/SwanSQLite/SwanSQLite.swift:331-339) via a new migration, written on insert at :6762-6777.
3. In the `existing.isEmpty` branch of registerSpaceNotification (Sources/SwanSQLite/SwanSQLite.swift:6745-6761), enforce a per-jti *creation* sub-quota (e.g. 8 new endpoints per credential) alongside the existing 1024 per-space cap. Deliberately do NOT gate replacement of an existing (space, endpoint) row on a matching jti — space credentials are short-lived, so a legitimate remote PDS refreshing its registration presents a new jti each cycle and would otherwise lose the ability to renew its own row.
4. Optional, cheap: emit an operator-visible signal when a space crosses (say) 75% of the budget, since there is no reaper other than the prune-on-register at :6729-6735.
If the maintainer wants true per-registrant ownership rather than a sub-quota, that requires a reader-scoped claim in the proposal-0016 credential — an upstream wire-format change, not a local fix.
findings.risk: Adds a column and a migration to permissioned_space_notification_registrations (Sources/SwanSQLite/SwanSQLite.swift:331-339) — schema migration on the authority account DB. Behaviour change visible to clients: a legitimate remote PDS that registers more than the sub-quota of distinct endpoints under one credential would start receiving the existing 503 `notification registration capacity exhausted` (SwanSQLite.swift:6757-6759, surfaced as temporarily_unavailable via SwanSpaceNotificationXRPC.swift:637-638/653). Existing rows have no jti, so the migration must treat NULL jti as unattributed and exempt from the sub-quota or the first post-migration refresh of a legacy row is miscounted. Tests/SwanSQLiteTests/SpaceNotificationSQLiteTests.swift:284-360 will need updating since it creates 1024 endpoints under a single credential.
findings.needsHumanDecision: Two calls only the maintainer can make: (a) is a per-credential creation sub-quota acceptable given proposal-0016 says nothing about it — i.e. are we willing to diverge from the pinned TypeScript PDS on registerNotify admission, and should it be recorded in Profiles/permissioned-data-0016-*.json `intentionalDivergences`? (b) Do we want to pursue a reader-scoped claim in the space credential upstream (the only complete ownership fix), or accept bearer-with-no-subject as the permanent model and treat registration squatting as an accepted, credential-gated availability risk?

clusterNotes:
Single-finding cluster. Three things worth carrying to whoever triages the rest of the scan:

1. The scan's remediation string for F25 is the generic boilerplate pattern flagged in the brief ("require a write-capable credential, bind to the authorized repository/client"). Here it is actively wrong in both halves — it would break the remote-reader interop contract, and the binding it demands is impossible because the credential has no reader subject (Sources/SwanOAuth/SwanOAuth.swift:371-375, SpaceCredentialAuthority.swift:825-831). The scan itself notes "proposal credentials carry no reader subject" in its own reachability text and then proposes binding to one anyway.

2. The scan treats SpaceAuthorizationPolicy (Sources/SwanSpaces/SwanSpaces.swift:239-254) as a global read-only invariant that registerNotify "bypasses". It is not — it is the *record* authorization policy. Any other C-cluster finding that argues "policy X rejects space-credential writes elsewhere, therefore surface Y is a bypass" should be checked for the same conflation.

3. The dominant real control in this area is Sources/SwanSQLite/SwanSQLite.swift:6933-6939: write fanout is deliberately not enqueued because the pinned receiver requires iss == repo. That comment neutralises most notification-registry impact claims (repo filters are inert, deletion fanout ignores them). Cross-check C9/C12 findings that assume write fanout is live.

No ordering constraints and no shared helper to introduce; the recommended change is local to registerSpaceNotification and the SpaceGrant type.

Two of the three findings share one root cause and it is not "identity resolution": **a security control was written twice and the copies drifted.**

1. IP classifier duplicated. `OAuthIPAddress.isPublicInternetAddress` (Sources/SwanOAuth/OAuthRemoteFetch.swift:67-103) and `ATHandleIPAddress.isPublicInternetAddress` (Sources/SwanAccounts/ATHandleVerification.swift:74-115) are byte-identical for IPv4 and divergent for IPv6. `/usr/bin/git log -S "6to4"` shows the special-purpose table was added on 2026-07-27 in b5f1610 "fix(accounts): harden handle verification boundaries" — to the handle copy only. F10 is an un-back-ported hardening, not a design choice.

2. Request-target construction duplicated three times. `SwanProxyHTTPTransport.swift:215-229` gets it right (percentEncoded* plus a 0x21-0x7E charset guard) and carries the explaining comment; `NIOPeerPinnedOAuthDocumentTransport.swift:128-132`, `NIOPeerPinnedOAuthPostTransport.swift:205-209`, and `NIOPeerPinnedATHandleHTTPTransport.swift:159-163` all use the decoding `url.path` and none has the charset guard. F22 is the attacker-reachable instance of the same defect.

Recommended shape: hoist ONE `SwanPublicAddressPolicy` and ONE `originFormTarget(for: URL) throws -> String` into SwanCore and delete the copies. Adding a fourth private copy is how this cluster happened. NIOPeerPinnedOAuthDocumentTransport.swift already shares `OAuthDocumentResponseHandler` and `OAuthPeerPinnedNIOClientResources` with the proxy transport (documented at SwanProxyHTTPTransport.swift:102-110), so the sharing seam exists.

Ordering: fix F22 first — it is the only unauthenticated one and the only one that is exploitable today without an external compromise. F10 is a one-function copy that should ride along in the same commit. F07 is independent and lowest urgency.

F07 does not belong with the other two: its "missing control" is largely supplied by the canonical DID-to-URL derivation, and the remediation string attached to F07 was pasted verbatim onto F10 where it is nonsense (F10 is an IPv6 prefix table, not DID binding). Treat the scan's remediation strings in this cluster as boilerplate.

findings.title: DID document not bound to the requested DID; no PLC audit-chain verification for proxy targets
findings.evidence:
The two mechanical claims are true. `SwanServiceEndpointResolver.Document` decodes only `service` — there is no top-level `id` field (Sources/SwanOAuth/SwanServiceEndpointResolver.swift:21-28), and `endpoint(did:fragment:)` never compares one (:36-57). Service selection accepts the short form `"#\(fragment)"` (:48-50), which is the form real Bluesky DID docs use, so the `"\(did)#\(fragment)"` alternative provides no binding in practice; `services.first(where:)` also silently takes the first of duplicate matching ids. `SwanPeerPinnedDIDDocumentFetcher.documentJSON` is a bare `fetchJSON` with no audit-chain check (:92-95), while `PLCClient.fetchState` (Sources/SwanAccounts/PLCClient.swift:395-418) does re-derive terminal state from the audit log and compare rotationKeys/verificationMethods/alsoKnownAs/services — so the stronger control does exist elsewhere. No test asserts id equality (Tests/SwanOAuthTests/SwanServiceEndpointResolverTests.swift:24-91 covers fragment, scheme, malformed, fetch-failure only) and no comment claims the omission is deliberate.

The stated impact is overstated, for three reasons the scan did not weigh.
(a) The document URL is canonically derived from the requested DID: did:plc → `plcOrigin/<did>` after a base32-sortable charset check, did:web → `https://<host>/.../did.json` from the DID's own method-specific id (Sources/SwanOAuth/SwanServiceEndpointResolver.swift:99-149). For did:web the host *is* the DID authority, so there is no gap at all — an id check would be pure self-consistency. Only did:plc has a distinct authority.
(b) The DID is chosen by the authenticated caller, not by an attacker: the only path to `.resolvedService` is an explicit `atproto-proxy` header (Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanXRPCProxyRouting.swift:128-148), and Sources/SwanXRPCProxyRouting.swift:73-76 states the destination is deliberately open — "naming an arbitrary labeler, feed generator, or alternate AppView is the point of `atproto-proxy`". The default no-header route short-circuits to the configured AppView with no resolution at all (Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanXRPCPipethrough.swift:396-399).
(c) The leaked artifact is narrow: `issueProxyServiceToken` binds `aud` to the *requested* DID and `lxm` to the exact NSID (Sources/SwanOAuth/ProxyServiceAuthentication.swift:159-168, Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanXRPCPipethrough.swift:409-421), so a substituted endpoint receives a short-lived token replayable only against the very service the caller named, for one method.

Net: real but small. Exploitation requires compromising plc.directory itself, which is the AT Protocol's identity authority by construction and which the reference PDS also trusts unverified for pipethrough target resolution.
findings.remediation:
Do the cheap half, refuse the expensive half.

DO: add `let id: String?` to the `Document` struct at Sources/SwanOAuth/SwanServiceEndpointResolver.swift:21-28 and require `document.id == did` in the guard at :43-45. AT Protocol DID documents always carry a top-level `id`; atproto's own did-resolver enforces exactly this. ~4 lines.

DO: reject ambiguity instead of taking the first match at :47-50 — replace `services.first(where:)` with a filter and require exactly one match. A document with two `#bsky_appview` entries currently resolves silently to whichever the serializer emitted first.

DO NOT adopt the scan's "verify authenticated PLC audit-chain terminal state and durable continuity" for this path. It would add two extra HTTPS fetches plus a full signature-chain verification to every third-party pipethrough request, against an audit log with no size bound in this code path, for a threat (plc.directory serving a forged document) that Swan's own account-identity path already handles separately in PLCClient.fetchState and that the rest of the network does not defend against either. If the maintainer wants it, it belongs behind a cache keyed by DID, not inline in `SwanPeerPinnedDIDDocumentFetcher.documentJSON`.

The scan's "keep public-address peer pinning through the connected socket" clause is already satisfied — Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanXRPCPipethrough.swift:434-436 documents it and Sources/SwanOAuth/SwanProxyHTTPTransport.swift:66-72 enforces it.
findings.risk: The id-equality check is a behaviour change visible to clients: any DID document that omits `id`, or whose `id` differs in case/normalization from the requested DID string, stops resolving and the caller gets a 400 (`SwanXRPCPipethroughFailure.invalidRequest`, Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanXRPCPipethrough.swift:404-406). did:plc ids are canonical lowercase so this is safe there; did:web ids can differ in percent-encoding of a port (`%3A`), so compare against the requested DID string exactly as received and do not normalize. The duplicate-service rejection could break a malformed-but-currently-working third-party document. Neither is a wire-format or schema change. Add a test to Tests/SwanOAuthTests/SwanServiceEndpointResolverTests.swift alongside the existing cases.
findings.needsHumanDecision: Two questions. (1) Is plc.directory inside or outside Swan's trust boundary for *third-party* DIDs? docs/threat-boundaries.md says nothing about it, and PLCClient.fetchState treating it as untrusted for Swan's own account implies "outside" — which, taken literally, is an argument for the expensive fix I am recommending against. The maintainer should state the intended boundary in docs/threat-boundaries.md either way. (2) Does the id-equality check risk breaking any DID document Catbird actually proxies to today (labelers, chat.bsky, ozone)?

findings.title: OAuth/DID/proxy IP classifier accepts 6to4, ORCHIDv2 and 3fff::/20 while the sibling handle classifier rejects them
findings.evidence:
Mechanically exact. Sources/SwanOAuth/OAuthRemoteFetch.swift:96-101 admits any address with `(bytes[0] & 0xE0) == 0x20` and subtracts only 2001:db8::/32 (:99) and `2001:00xx` with `bytes[3] < 0x20`, i.e. 2001::/27 (:100). Therefore 2002::/16 (6to4), 2001:20::/28 (ORCHIDv2 — `bytes[3]` is 0x20-0x2F, just outside the `< 0x20` cut), and 3fff::/20 (RFC 9637 documentation, `bytes[0]==0x3F` passes the 0xE0 mask) all classify as public. Sources/SwanAccounts/ATHandleVerification.swift:100-113 rejects exactly those, with the comment "IANA IPv6 Special-Purpose Address Registry, last updated 2025-10-09. Swan deliberately rejects the whole 2001::/23 protocol-assignment umbrella…", and Tests/SwanAccountsTests/ATHandleVerificationTests.swift:81-101 asserts it for 2001::1, 2001:db8::1, 2002::1, 3fff::1, 3fff:fff::1. No equivalent test exists for OAuthIPAddress. `/usr/bin/git log -S "6to4" -- Sources/` returns exactly one commit, b5f1610 (2026-07-27) "fix(accounts): harden handle verification boundaries" — so this is an un-back-ported hardening of a duplicated control, not a documented deliberate choice.

The classifier is shared by all three outbound surfaces the scan names: OAuth metadata/JWKS (OAuthRemoteFetch.swift:581-585, 611-616), DID document fetch (SwanServiceEndpointResolver.swift:92-95 routes through the same fetcher), and authenticated XRPC pipethrough (SwanProxyHTTPTransport.swift:66-72).

The impact claim is where it thins out, and my reading is harsher than the scan's. To reach a special-purpose address the attacker needs either a DNS answer in that range or an IP-literal host. The literal route dies at TLS: NIOPeerPinnedOAuthDocumentTransport.swift:86-89 sets `serverHostname: hostname` for SNI and certificate-name verification, and no CA issues certs for 2002:: literals. The DNS route needs the deployment to actually route the prefix — `SystemOAuthHostnameResolver` sets `AI_ADDRCONFIG` (OAuthRemoteFetch.swift:358), so a container with no global IPv6 address gets no AAAA answers at all, and 6to4 needs a configured `sit` tunnel plus the 192.88.99.0/24 relay anycast, which this same policy rejects for IPv4 (OAuthRemoteFetch.swift:79). 3fff::/20 and 2001:20::/28 are non-routable by definition. So today this is a policy inconsistency with no reachable protected asset, and the honest label is defense-in-depth, not SSRF.
findings.remediation:
