Replace the IPv6 branch at Sources/SwanOAuth/OAuthRemoteFetch.swift:96-101 with the prefix-table form already proven at Sources/SwanAccounts/ATHandleVerification.swift:105-113, including the `ipv6(_:hasPrefix:bitCount:)` helper at :117-130. Better: hoist one classifier into SwanCore and have both `OAuthIPAddress` and `ATHandleIPAddress` delegate to it — the drift this finding documents is the cost of keeping two. Mirror Tests/SwanAccountsTests/ATHandleVerificationTests.swift:81-101 into Tests/SwanOAuthTests/ as `testProductionIPv6PolicyRejectsCurrentSpecialPurposeRanges`, asserting 2002::1, 2001::1, 2001:20::1, 2001:db8::1, 3fff::1, 3fff:fff::1 are rejected and 2606:4700:4700::1111 is accepted.

Ignore the remediation string the scan attached to this finding — it is F07's text pasted verbatim ("Bind every fetched document to the requested DID, verify authenticated PLC audit-chain terminal state…") and has nothing to do with an IPv6 prefix table.
findings.risk: Essentially none. No legitimate public host resolves into 2002::/16, 2001::/23 or 3fff::/20; the ranges are reserved or deprecated (6to4 was deprecated by RFC 7526). Not a wire-format or schema change. The only behaviour a fix could break is a lab fixture that pins a documentation-range address, and the explicit `OAuthRemoteNetworkAllowlist` escape hatch (OAuthRemoteFetch.swift:108-114, consulted first in `permits` at :167) still covers that case.

findings.title: OAuth document transport emits a percent-DECODED request target, enabling CRLF injection into the outbound request line
findings.evidence:
Confirmed, with one sub-claim refuted and the impact materially understated.

The defect: NIOPeerPinnedOAuthDocumentTransport.swift:128-132 builds the origin-form target from `url.path` and `url.query`. The sibling transport documents why that is wrong and does it correctly — Sources/SwanOAuth/SwanProxyHTTPTransport.swift:215-219: "Keep the origin-form target byte-identical to what the client sent: `URL.path` percent-decodes, which would silently rewrite an encoded path segment on the way to the upstream service" — and additionally guards the result with `uri.utf8.allSatisfy { (0x21...0x7E).contains($0) }` at :227-229, asserted by Tests/SwanOAuthTests/SwanProxyHTTPTransportTests.swift:141-142. The document transport has neither. Same defect, unreached today, at NIOPeerPinnedOAuthPostTransport.swift:205-209 and NIOPeerPinnedATHandleHTTPTransport.swift:159-163.

Sub-claim REFUTED: `url.query` does not percent-decode. Probed on Swift 6 Foundation with `xcrun --toolchain XcodeDefault swift`: for `https://victim.example/a%0d%0aX-Injected:%20yes%3Fq/b?x=1%26y=2`, `url.query` returned `"x=1%26y=2"` (encoded, identical to `percentEncodedQuery`) while `url.path` returned `"/a\r\nX-Injected: yes?q/b"`. Only the path half is defective. Same probe confirmed `absoluteString == raw` and `fragment == nil`, i.e. the input survives every upstream check.

Impact is worse than "a different same-origin resource". NIOHTTP1 writes the URI verbatim into the request line — .build/checkouts/swift-nio/Sources/NIOHTTP1/HTTPEncoder.swift:719-726 (`self.writeString(request.uri)`), swift-nio 2.101.3, no validation. So a decoded CR/LF becomes a literal CRLF on the wire: full request-line and header injection, and with enough encoded bytes a second pipelined request with its own method and body.

And the path is UNAUTHENTICATED. `POST /oauth/par` is registered unconditionally whenever the authorization server is configured (Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanHTTP.swift:811-824) and reaches `clientMetadataLoader.load(clientID: form.clientID)` at SwanOAuthAuthorizationServerHTTP.swift:233 after only a DPoP nonce dance any caller can perform (:208-231). `oauthServerExactURL` requires `url.absoluteString == raw` (:968-973) — which percent-escapes satisfy — and `validateHTTPSClientID` checks only scheme/host/port/user/fragment (OAuthClientMetadata.swift:421-428). No charset constraint on the client_id path anywhere. `jwks_uri` reaches the same transport via OAuthClientMetadataLoader.swift:306-309 and its validator (`validateHTTPSURL`, OAuthClientMetadata.swift:430-436) is weaker still — it permits an explicit port.

The scan's own "proof gap" (needing a same-origin endpoint that returns usable metadata) applies only to the metadata-confusion framing: `validateResponseIdentity` (OAuthClientMetadata.swift:241-246) does require the fetched document's `client_id` to equal the requested URL string, so response confusion is hard. But the injected bytes leave the process before any response is validated, so the side effect at the victim host does not depend on that at all. The scan also correctly notes that `responseURL` is reported as the original `requestURL` (NIOPeerPinnedOAuthDocumentTransport.swift:248-251), which makes the exact-URL check at OAuthRemoteFetch.swift:606-610 tautological and blind to the rewrite.
findings.remediation:
Sources/SwanOAuth/NIOPeerPinnedOAuthDocumentTransport.swift:128-132 — replace with the proxy transport's construction. `components` is already in scope from :40, so:

    let encodedPath = components.percentEncodedPath
    let path = encodedPath.isEmpty ? "/" : encodedPath
    guard path.hasPrefix("/") else { throw SwanError.malformed("OAuth document path is not origin-form") }
    let target = components.percentEncodedQuery.map { $0.isEmpty ? path : "\(path)?\($0)" } ?? path
    guard target.utf8.allSatisfy({ (0x21 ... 0x7E).contains($0) }), target.utf8.count <= 8_192 else {
        throw SwanError.malformed("OAuth document request target is invalid")
    }

The charset guard is the part that actually closes CRLF injection and must not be dropped as "redundant" — percentEncodedPath alone would fix path confusion but a raw control byte reaching `URL` by another route would still be written verbatim by NIO. Apply the identical change to NIOPeerPinnedOAuthPostTransport.swift:205-209 and NIOPeerPinnedATHandleHTTPTransport.swift:159-163 in the same commit; neither is attacker-reachable today, but leaving two known-defective copies is what produced this finding.

Also fix the blind spot at NIOPeerPinnedOAuthDocumentTransport.swift:248-251: report the emitted target in `responseURL` (or carry it as a separate field) so OAuthRemoteFetch.swift:607's exact-URL comparison stops comparing a value against itself.

The scan's "use one canonical URL representation" framing is right in spirit but underspecifies: the canonical representation must be the percent-ENCODED one, and validation must additionally reject bytes outside 0x21-0x7E. Do NOT implement its "reject encodings whose decoded path/query changes the validated identity" as a comparison of decoded vs encoded forms — that is a fragile blacklist; constructing the target from the encoded form makes the comparison unnecessary.

Regression test: a `SwanProxyConnectionPlan`-style unit test is not available here (the document transport has no extracted plan type), so add a test asserting the target-construction helper — extract it as an internal free function — maps `https://h/a%0d%0ab` to a thrown error and `https://h/a%2Fb?x=%3A` to `/a%2Fb?x=%3A`. Mirror it in Tests/SwanOAuthTests/ next to SwanProxyHTTPTransportTests.swift:141-142.
findings.risk: Client-visible in one narrow way: a client_id or jwks_uri whose path contains a percent escape currently gets fetched at the DECODED path and will, after the fix, be fetched at the ENCODED path. Any real client relying on that would already be broken, because `validateResponseIdentity` (OAuthClientMetadata.swift:241-246) requires the served document to declare the original encoded client_id — so the decoded fetch can only succeed where the server serves the same bytes at both paths. Practically zero deployed impact, and Swan hosts one account. Not a wire-format or schema change; no migration. The charset guard newly rejects client_ids containing encoded control bytes or spaces with a 400 from PAR, which is the intended outcome. Extracting the helper for testability touches three transports, so build all of SwanOAuth and SwanAccounts.
findings.needsHumanDecision: Should Swan additionally reject at admission any client_id/jwks_uri whose `percentEncodedPath != path` — i.e. any path carrying an escape at all (Sources/SwanOAuth/OAuthClientMetadata.swift:421-428 / :430-436)? That is stricter than the AT Protocol client-metadata spec requires and would refuse client_ids that are currently accepted, so it is a maintainer call. My recommendation is no: fix the transport, leave the grammar alone. Separately: `validateHTTPSURL` permits an explicit port on `jwks_uri` while `validateHTTPSClientID` forbids one on `client_id` — intentional, or a second drift?

clusterNotes: Both findings sit on the same route (`/xrpc/**` fallback, `Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanXRPCPipethrough.swift:260-300`) but share no root cause and should not be fixed together. Shared reachability fact that both scan entries under-weight: the route is gated at `SwanXRPCPipethrough.swift:358-364` → `authorizedPipethroughSubject` → `SwanOAuthResourceAuthorizer.authorize` (`Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanOAuthResourceAuthorization.swift:76-155`), which requires `Authorization: DPoP ` (`:161-165`), a server-issued nonce, an `ath` binding, and `.accountOAuth` with the `atproto` scope (`SwanXRPCPipethrough.swift:524-527`). No browser navigation, ``, or link click can produce that. On the deployed configuration there is exactly one account and invite codes are on, so every "authenticated attacker" in this cluster is the operator's own account or a client the operator's account deliberately proxied to. Second shared fact: the proxy never follows a redirect itself. `SwanNIOPeerPinnedProxyTransport.makeRequest` (`Sources/SwanOAuth/SwanProxyHTTPTransport.swift:258-335`) writes one request head and reads one response, and the DID-document fetcher separately requires `redirectCount == 0` (`Sources/SwanOAuth/OAuthRemoteFetch.swift:606-608`, documented at `SwanServiceEndpointResolver.swift:68-70`). There is therefore no server-side SSRF component to F35 — the scan correctly says so, and I confirm it. Ordering: F35's fix is a one-line deletion with a test edit; F40's fix touches a shared control in SwanOAuth used by OAuth metadata and DID resolution. Do F35 first and independently. Cross-cluster note (not in this file, but it changes how F40 should be prioritised): the "shared DNS capacity" half of F40 does not need the pipethrough at all. `/oauth/par` loads arbitrary client metadata from a caller-supplied `client_id` host at `Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanOAuthAuthorizationServerHTTP.swift:233` after only a self-generated DPoP proof — no account. That reaches the same `SystemOAuthHostnameResolver` serial queue. So if the DNS-queue stall matters, it must be fixed at `OAuthRemoteFetch.swift:347`, not at the pipethrough.

findings.title: Upstream Location relayed verbatim by the XRPC pipethrough
findings.evidence:
Mechanism confirmed, citations accurate. `pipethroughResponse` (Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanXRPCPipethrough.swift:709-738) builds the client-facing response; the forwarded set at :722-725 includes `("location", .location)` and the copy loop at :726-732 checks only single-valued, <=256 bytes, printable-ASCII. No scheme/host/origin parse — the scan is right about that.

Where the scan overstates: (1) The route cannot be traversed by a lured victim. `SwanXRPCPipethrough.swift:358-364` authenticates before any outbound work, and `SwanOAuthResourceAuthorization.swift:76-155` requires a DPoP-bound access token (`Authorization: DPoP` parsed at :161-165), a server nonce (:89-92), an `ath` hash binding (:113), and account status (:145-149); `SwanXRPCPipethrough.swift:524-527` further requires `.accountOAuth` + `atproto` scope. A browser following an attacker's link sends none of that and gets 401 + nonce challenge, so the classic open-redirect lure (unauthenticated victim traverses Swan's origin) is structurally unavailable. (2) The destination is chosen by an upstream the *same caller* named in `atproto-proxy` (routing at Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanXRPCProxyRouting.swift:122-158; the comment at :74-76 states the destination set is deliberately open) or by the operator-configured AppView (SwanXRPCPipethrough.swift:396-399). A caller that can pick the upstream already controls where its own next hop points; no privilege is gained.

What is genuinely real, and what the scan did not identify: a `Location` value is resolved by the client against the *response* URL, which is `https://swan.place/...`. A relative or scheme-relative value from a hostile labeler/feedgen therefore steers the caller's next request back onto Swan's own origin with the caller's Swan credentials attached (a same-origin onward-request steer), not off it. Nothing at :726-732 rejects a relative value.

Deliberate-design evidence: the comment at :718-721 ("`location` is here because without it an upstream 3xx reaches the client bodyless and unfollowable") and the test `testUpstreamLocationIsForwardedAndOtherHeadersAreNot` at Tests/SwanHTTPTests/SwanXRPCPipethroughTests.swift:884-914, which asserts Location IS relayed and Set-Cookie is not. This is intended behaviour, so any change is a maintainer decision.

Counter-evidence to the stated design rationale: the upstream reference PDS does not relay Location at all — atproto/packages/pds/src/pipethrough.ts:527-531 forwards only `atproto-repo-rev`, `atproto-content-labelers`, `retry-after`, plus content-* at :533-548. Every AT Protocol client already copes with a proxy that drops upstream 3xx metadata, so the stated justification does not hold against ecosystem practice.
findings.remediation:
Preferred (and I disagree with the scan's "allow only same-origin/same-service canonical destinations" — a same-host restriction would forbid the exact CDN case the existing test invents, and per-case allow-listing here has no principled boundary): delete `("location", .location)` from the forwarded tuple at Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanXRPCPipethrough.swift:724, rewrite the comment at :718-721 to state that upstream 3xx metadata is dropped for parity with atproto/packages/pds/src/pipethrough.ts:527-531, and invert Tests/SwanHTTPTests/SwanXRPCPipethroughTests.swift:884-914 into `testUpstreamLocationIsNotForwarded` (keep the Set-Cookie and content-type assertions unchanged so the narrowing of the set is still pinned).

If the maintainer wants to keep relaying it, the minimum correct hardening at :726-732 is: parse the value with `URLComponents`, require `scheme == "https"`, a non-empty host, no user/password, and reject anything that is not absolute. That kills the relative-Location same-origin steer and the `javascript:`/`data:` family in one check while preserving the cross-host CDN case. Do not add a host-equality check.
findings.risk: Client-visible wire behaviour change: any client that today follows a 3xx returned through `/xrpc/**` would instead see a bodyless 3xx with no Location. I found no Swan or Catbird code depending on it, and the upstream PDS never emitted it, but this is a maintainer call, not a mechanical fix. No schema or storage change. The `cache-control: no-store` and dropped-header behaviour is unaffected.
findings.needsHumanDecision: Do you want to keep relaying upstream `Location` at all? Dropping it matches upstream PDS behaviour and removes the finding outright; keeping it means accepting the absolute-https-only hardening instead and knowingly diverging from atproto/packages/pds/src/pipethrough.ts:527-531.

findings.title: Proxy sender resolves DNS outside any caller deadline while holding a pipethrough lease
findings.evidence:
Mechanism confirmed and citations accurate. `SwanPeerPinnedProxySender.send` awaits `resolver.resolve(host:)` bare at Sources/SwanOAuth/SwanProxyHTTPTransport.swift:67, before the timeout-bounded `transport.send` at :69-72 — the `timeout` argument only ever reaches the transport. Production wires the real resolver there: `SwanPeerPinnedProxySender(policy:resolver: SystemOAuthHostnameResolver(), transport:)` at Sources/swan/SwanCommand.swift:2797-2807. `SystemOAuthHostnameResolver.resolve` (Sources/SwanOAuth/OAuthRemoteFetch.swift:351-398) dispatches blocking `getaddrinfo` (:366) onto a **serial** `DispatchQueue` (:347) after taking one of four process-wide leases (:353, admission at :192-229). The asymmetry the scan names is real: `OAuthRemoteDocumentFetcher.fetchJSONWithoutAdmission` wraps both of its resolutions in `resolveOAuthHostname(..., timeout: policy.timeout)` (:582-584, :602-604), and that helper (:303-341) is declared `private` at file scope, i.e. fileprivate — so SwanProxyHTTPTransport.swift cannot call it even though it is in the same module. The lease is held across the whole thing: acquired at Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanXRPCPipethrough.swift:385-388, released only on scope exit after step 8. No global request-deadline middleware exists (only a 60s connection idle timeout, Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanHTTP.swift:1148).

Where the scan is wrong or overstated: (1) "beyond the advertised 10-second request timeout" invents an invariant the code never claims. `SwanXRPCPipethroughLimits.timeout` is documented at SwanXRPCPipethrough.swift:22-26 as the bound the *transport* can hold a request for, and it is passed only to `sender.send(...)` at :439-443. Nothing advertises a whole-request deadline; step 5 alone (DID document fetch, two deadline'd resolutions at 5s each plus a 5s transport, OAuthRemoteFetch.swift:124-129 policy default) can already exceed 10s on the existing code paths. (2) "one blocked serial getaddrinfo can stall queued callers while leases remain held" is wrong about the admission gate: `OAuthBlockingDNSAdmission.acquire` throws `SwanError.unavailable` immediately when full (:206-211) and never queues — pinned by `testBlockingDNSAdmissionRetainsTimedOutWorkUntilLibcCompletion`, Tests/SwanOAuthTests/OAuthRemoteFetchAdmissionTests.swift:12-32. It is right about the *serial queue*, which is the real amplifier and which the scan does not name: one stalled `getaddrinfo` blocks every subsequent DNS lookup in the process regardless of admission. (3) `getaddrinfo` is not unbounded — glibc bounds it by `resolv.conf` timeout/attempts (order tens of seconds, Linux x86_64 target), so this is lease retention for ~10-40s per request, not indefinite.

Reachability split: the cited entrypoint is account-gated (see cluster notes), so on the deployed one-account configuration the pipethrough half is self-DoS. The shared-DNS half is anonymously reachable through a different door — `/oauth/par` loads a caller-supplied `client_id` host at Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanOAuthAuthorizationServerHTTP.swift:233 behind only a self-generated DPoP proof (:208-230) — and that door is not on `/xrpc/*`, so the Cloudflare 600 req/10s rule does not cover it. No test asserts a resolution bound on the sender path; Tests/SwanOAuthTests/SwanProxyHTTPTransportTests.swift:29-34 uses an instantly-returning `StubResolver`.
findings.remediation:
Two independent changes; the scan's boilerplate remediation ("move the missing security check to the closest shared control, fail closed") describes only the first and, applied alone, fixes nothing about the shared-capacity impact it claims.

1. Bound the sender's resolution. Change `private func resolveOAuthHostname` at Sources/SwanOAuth/OAuthRemoteFetch.swift:303 to internal, and at Sources/SwanOAuth/SwanProxyHTTPTransport.swift:67 replace `try await resolver.resolve(host: host)` with `try await resolveOAuthHostname(resolver, host: host, timeout: policy.timeout)`. `policy` is already a stored property (:46) and `OAuthRemoteFetchPolicy.timeout` defaults to 5 (OAuthRemoteFetch.swift:124-129). This releases the pipethrough lease (SwanXRPCPipethrough.swift:385-388) and the client socket on schedule. Regression test: a resolver stub that sleeps 30s, asserting `SwanPeerPinnedProxySender.send` throws within ~policy.timeout — add to Tests/SwanOAuthTests/SwanProxyHTTPTransportTests.swift next to the existing stub at :29.

2. If the shared-DNS stall is to be addressed at all, it must be fixed at Sources/SwanOAuth/OAuthRemoteFetch.swift:347 by making that queue `attributes: .concurrent`, leaving `OAuthBlockingDNSAdmission.shared` (limit 4, :193) as the sole concurrency bound. The comment at :187-191 already states plainly why the deadline cannot help here ("A timed-out caller cannot cancel the libc call, so its lease is released only when that blocking operation actually returns") — that reasoning holds, and it is exactly why change 1 alone leaves the cross-surface impact untouched. With a serial queue, one hostile authoritative nameserver degrades OAuth login metadata and DID resolution for everyone; with a bounded-concurrent queue, at most four stalls coexist and the fifth caller fails fast.

I would land change 1 (cheap, strictly correct) and treat change 2 as the one that actually matters, prioritised against the `/oauth/par` entrypoint rather than the pipethrough.
findings.risk:
Change 1: `resolveOAuthHostname` abandons the resolver task on deadline (OAuthRemoteFetch.swift:309-329), so a slow-but-successful DNS answer now becomes a 502 (`SwanXRPCPipethroughFailure.badGateway`, SwanXRPCPipethrough.swift:444-446) instead of a slow success. With `policy.timeout` at 5s that is a behaviour change for genuinely slow third-party service hosts. No wire format, schema, or client-visible contract change.
Change 2: makes the DNS queue concurrent, so up to four dispatch threads can be blocked in `getaddrinfo` simultaneously instead of one. Bounded by the existing admission limit, but it does raise blocked-thread count under attack and touches a control shared by OAuth metadata loading, JWKS fetching, and DID resolution — rerun Tests/SwanOAuthTests/OAuthRemoteFetchAdmissionTests.swift in full, not just the DNS test.
findings.needsHumanDecision: Is the process-wide serial DNS queue (OAuthRemoteFetch.swift:347) deliberate — e.g. chosen to cap blocked dispatch threads at one — or incidental? If deliberate, change 2 is a reversal of that choice and the residual cross-surface stall should be accepted and documented at :187-191 instead.

findings.title: Permissioned route installation iterates the build-wide registry instead of the selected profile's endpoint inventory, while describeServer advertises the profile id
findings.evidence: Mechanism is real and already a documented open backlog item. Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanHTTP.swift:875 `for descriptor in PermissionedData0016.methods` — the build-wide registry, never `profile.endpoints`; describeServer at SwanHTTP.swift:860-867 emits `swanProfile: profile.id`. The design comment at SwanHTTP.swift:869-873 states the deliberate intent — "The checked-in wire registry is the sole source for this coverage: every profile method gets an explicit, method-correct closed handler until its authenticated implementation is ready" — which explains why the registry (not the profile) drives the loop, but does not justify ignoring a narrower profile. Recorded as knowingly unfixed: docs/superpowers/records/2026-08-12-swan-production-readiness/task-10-report.md:300-303 and README.md:38-40 ("D10's 'the permissioned surface correctly iterates the loaded profile' — it does not"). IMPACT OVERSTATED, three ways. (a) The scan's framing conflates two profile families: Sources/SwanCore/SwanCore.swift:80 requires `id.hasPrefix("permissioned-data-")`, so `--profile` structurally cannot name a public profile, and the public surface IS profile-selected via `--public-profile` → `Self.resolvePublicRouteSurface(selector: publicProfile)` at SwanCommand.swift:2298-2301. The defect is confined to the permissioned surface. (b) The two checked-in permissioned profiles are endpoint-identical — verified by decoding both: 25 endpoints each, symmetric difference empty. (c) Every branch of the loop is capability-gated (`if let authenticatedGetSpace`, `if let authenticatedSpaceRecords`, … SwanHTTP.swift:876-981); a method absent from a narrowed profile still needs its capability configured, and the else branch at :980 installs a 503 gate. An existing tripwire already guards divergence: Tests/SwanHTTPTests/ServePermissionedRuntimeCompositionTests.swift:217-222 asserts `profileSet == generatedSet` and `PermissionedData0016.methods.count == 25`, so the day a profile narrows, CI fails before the router does. Citation drift: the scan cites SwanCommand.swift:1799-1800 for the source; the actual `--profile` declaration is SwanCommand.swift:1798-1799 and the load is at :2295.
findings.remediation: Two separate changes, only the first is security-relevant. (1) SwanHTTP.swift:875 — iterate `PermissionedData0016.methods.filter { profile.endpoints.contains($0.nsid) }`, and add a startup refusal near SwanCommand.swift:2295 rejecting any `profile.endpoints` entry with no matching registry descriptor. Fail-closed both directions: a narrowed profile narrows the surface, an unknown endpoint refuses to boot rather than silently serving nothing. Keep the :980 unavailable-gate else branch and the :989 unknown-method guard exactly as they are — they are the reason no method can become an accidental public fallback, and the scan misreads them as the problem. (2) Separately close the advertising gap the report records at task-10-report.md:305-308: describeServer currently advertises the *permissioned* profile id while the live public surface is the default `public-data-testing-2026-08-06`, so nothing on the wire names the contract a relay or AppView actually gets. I disagree with the scan's remediation string, which bundles this with F17's lab-trust concern; they share no code.
findings.risk: Change (1) is behaviour-preserving today because both permissioned profiles carry the same 25 NSIDs — the filter is a no-op on every checked-in profile, which makes it safe to land now and valuable later. It will, however, make ServePermissionedRuntimeCompositionTests.swift:217-222 redundant as a divergence tripwire; keep the assertion. Change (2) adds a field to ServerDescription (SwanHTTP.swift:861-866) — that IS a wire-format change on a federated endpoint, and swan.place is live and federated with bsky.network, so it needs maintainer sign-off separately from (1).
findings.needsHumanDecision: Adding a public-surface identifier to `com.atproto.server.describeServer` is a wire-format addition on a live federated endpoint. Confirm whether the public route surface should be advertised at all, and under what field name, before touching SwanHTTP.swift:861-866. Change (1) needs no such decision and can land alone.

findings.title: Lab notification config with laboratory=true is baked into every runtime image and composable with ordinary serve
findings.evidence: The composability half is real: Dockerfile:21-23 unconditionally `COPY Swan/interop/notification-config.json /etc/swan/interop/notification-config.json` into the runtime stage of every image, and that file sets `"laboratory": true` (interop/notification-config.json:15-18). SwanCommand.swift:170-174 and :207-211 select `PLCClientConfiguration.laboratory(origin:allowlistedHost:)` from the JSON boolean alone — there is no process-wide production/laboratory mode gate, and nothing correlates it with the HTTPS `--public-url`. THE STATED IMPACT IS REFUTED. The scan's root cause claims "the shown boundary does not independently authenticate the first observed PLC history" and that an on-path attacker "could substitute the initial authority key". That control exists and the scan missed it: Sources/SwanAccounts/PLCOperation.swift:374-384 `verifyGenesis` requires `genesisDID(for: operation) == expectedDID` and then `verify(operation, authorizedRotationKeys: regular.rotationKeys)`. PLC DIDs are self-certifying hashes of the genesis operation, so substituting the genesis rotation key changes the CID and therefore the DID, and the check fails. The whole audit chain is verified op-by-op with prev linkage and nullification handling at PLCClient.swift:667-727 (`verifyGenesis` at :670, `PLCOperationCodec.verify` at :691/:700/:709, prev-is-active at :681-687), and fetchState cross-checks state against the active audit terminal at PLCClient.swift:409-416. The resolver's own consistency checks are at PLCSpaceCredentialPublicKeyResolver.swift:509-521. A transport downgrade to HTTP therefore buys an attacker nothing on key substitution. Three further bounds the scan understates: the baked file is inert unless `--notification-config` names it (SwanCommand.swift:130-138 is the only entry point); its `allowlistedHost` is `reference-plc` (interop/notification-config.json:18), a Docker-network name that does not resolve outside the lab; and `allowedIssuers` is derived from authorityDestinations (SwanCommand.swift:162-165), which contains exactly one placeholder DID `did:plc:abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwx` (interop/notification-config.json:6), so no attacker-chosen issuer is resolvable even if the file were loaded in production. Origin validation is also tighter than described: PLCClient.swift:249-264 requires http + literal-loopback OR exact allowlist match, plus a port in 1024...65535.
findings.remediation: Reject the scan's remediation string outright — "bind every fetched document to the requested DID, verify authenticated PLC audit-chain terminal state and durable continuity, reject duplicate/ambiguous service IDs" names four controls that all already exist (PLCClient.swift:409-416, :633-635, :667-727; PLCOperation.swift:374-384). Implementing it would be a no-op and would teach the next reader that these checks were missing. The real fix is deployment hygiene plus one startup interlock: (1) Dockerfile:21-23 — drop the `mkdir -p /etc/swan/interop`, `touch`, and `COPY` of the lab notification config from the runtime stage entirely; mount it as a lab-only file in docker-compose.yml:104-105 instead. The base compose comment at docker-compose.yml:102-103 already asserts this file is lab-only, so removing it from the image makes the code match the comment. Note Scripts/verify-interop-lab.sh:560 currently *rejects* a host bind for that path, so switching to a config volume rather than a bind keeps that assertion intact. (2) SwanCommand.swift:170-174 and :207-211 — refuse to boot when `plc.laboratory == true` and the resolved `--public-url` is an https origin whose host is not loopback. That is the missing process-wide gate, and it is ~6 lines at each site.
findings.risk: Removing the COPY breaks any lab or acceptance flow that relies on /etc/swan/interop/notification-config.json existing inside the image — Scripts/run-forum-live-demo.sh and the acceptance runners write their own configs into .interop-live and pass absolute paths, so they are unaffected, but docker-compose.yml:104-105 must be converted in the same commit or the base lab topology fails to start. The startup interlock could break a hypothetical operator running a lab PLC behind an https public URL; nothing checked in does that.
findings.needsHumanDecision: The laboratory=true interlock in (2) is a deliberate-design boundary: it removes an operator's ability to point a public HTTPS deployment at an HTTP lab PLC. Confirm no interop or staging deployment relies on that combination before landing it.

findings.title: --oauth-allow-metadata-ip allowlists a bare IP and permits it for any hostname resolving there, composable with the public authorization server
findings.evidence: The host-agnostic allowlist is real and is the crux: Sources/SwanOAuth/OAuthRemoteFetch.swift:166-169 `permits(_ address:forHost:)` returns true on `networkAllowlist.addresses.contains(address)` before ever consulting `host`, so any attacker-chosen hostname resolving to an allowlisted address passes both validateURL (:151-155) and validateResolved (:159-164). Composability confirmed: SwanCommand.swift:1860-1861 declares the flag; :2442-2443 makes the metadata loader (and therefore the allowlist) active whenever `enableOAuthAuthorizationServer || enableLocalSpaceInterop`; :2447-2461 folds the literal IPs into OAuthRemoteFetchPolicy with no requirement of a loopback listener or a laboratory mode. Production runs --enable-local-space-interop (docs/superpowers/plans/2026-08-11-swan-place-migration.md:383,:388), so the flag WOULD be accepted there — the scan is right about composability. But it is fail-closed by default and no checked-in configuration sets it: SwanCommand.swift:1861 defaults to `[]`, and :2480-2484 hard-rejects the flag when neither subsystem is enabled. The counter-control the scan itself cites is real and I verified it exists: Tests/SwanHTTPTests/RemoteOAuthAuthorizationServerHTTPTests.swift:626 `testUnsafeRemoteMetadataNeverActivatesAClientOrContactsTransport`. Remaining bounds hold as stated: 256 KiB body cap and 5 s timeout (OAuthRemoteFetch.swift:125-126), HTTPS required (:148-150), peer pinning via NIOPeerPinnedOAuthDocumentTransport. Impact if enabled is blind SSRF to one exact operator-chosen internal address, with TLS still having to validate the attacker's hostname.
findings.remediation: The scan's remediation string here is a copy of F13's ("make the selected profile constrain the installed parser/routes…") and has nothing to do with OAuth metadata fetching — ignore it. Preferred fix: pin host together with address. Change `OAuthRemoteNetworkAllowlist.addresses` (OAuthRemoteFetch.swift:108-114) from `Set<OAuthIPAddress>` to a set of (host, address) pairs, make `permits(_:forHost:)` at :166-169 require both to match, and change the CLI parse at SwanCommand.swift:2448-2454 to require `host@ip` syntax rather than a bare literal. That removes the entire attacker-chosen-hostname degree of freedom while keeping the lab escape hatch working. Cheaper alternative if the maintainer does not want a CLI syntax change: add a guard near SwanCommand.swift:2447 refusing a non-empty allowlist when the resolved `--public-url` is a non-loopback HTTPS origin — same shape as the F17 interlock, and the two should be written to look alike. Do not remove the flag; the lab genuinely needs it.
findings.risk: The host@ip change is a breaking CLI syntax change for any lab operator currently passing a bare IP — grep shows no checked-in invocation uses the flag, so blast radius is developer muscle memory plus Tests/SwanHTTPTests CLI parse tests. It also touches OAuthRemoteFetchPolicy's Equatable conformance (OAuthRemoteFetch.swift:116-135), so existing policy-equality assertions in SwanOAuthTests will need updating. No wire format, no schema, no client-visible behaviour.
findings.needsHumanDecision: Whether to take the CLI syntax change (host@ip) or the cheaper HTTPS-public-URL refusal. The first is structurally correct; the second is two lines and consistent with F17's interlock. Maintainer's call on how much lab ergonomics to spend.

clusterNotes:
Single shared root cause: `/xrpc/com.atproto.sync.subscribeRepos` is the only public route in Swan with no resource accounting of any kind. Every other anonymous surface goes through an explicit lease (`PublicRepositoryJSONReadAdmission`, see the Task-7 record `docs/superpowers/records/2026-08-12-swan-production-readiness/task-7-report.md:410-440`, which fixed the identical "concurrency bounded only by maximumConnections (256, never overridden)" shape for resolveHandle); the WebSocket route was never given one. There is no router middleware at all (`Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanHTTP.swift:759` builds the router with zero middleware registrations), so nothing in-process bounds this endpoint.

All three findings land in two files (`PublicFirehoseStreamingRoute.swift`, `SwanHTTP.swift`). Recommended order:

1. **F11 first — it is a one-line change with no design content.** `maxFrameSize` at `SwanHTTP.swift:1171` is *inbound-only* (proved below); lowering it to 4096 deletes F11's entire mechanism today, before the F05 work starts.
2. **F05 second** — the admission lease. Put the acquire at the top of `publicFirehoseOnUpgrade` (`PublicFirehoseStreamingRoute.swift:245`), not in `shouldUpgrade`, because a lease taken in `shouldUpgrade` has no release site (Hummingbird gives `shouldUpgrade` no handle on the eventual session; `RouterShouldUpgrade.dontUpgrade` also hard-codes a 405 response — `hummingbird-websocket/Sources/HummingbirdWebSocket/WebSocketRouter.swift:92-93` — which is a wrong status for capacity).
3. **F33 last** — reuse `PublicReadDiagnosticThrottle`.

**Operational stopgap available today, ahead of any code change:** the deployment already terminates at Cloudflare with a per-IP rule on `/xrpc/*` that explicitly *excludes* subscribeRepos. Adding a concurrent-connection / connection-rate rule scoped to that one path is a same-day mitigation for F05 and F33 and does not wait on a release. Note that per-peer limiting *inside* Swan is near-useless in this deployment: every socket arrives from a Cloudflare address, so the only usable client identity is the `X-Swan-Client-IP` header already parsed by `Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanLoginClientIdentityPolicy.swift:21-56` — which is why the global cap, not the per-principal cap, is the load-bearing control here. That is a direct disagreement with the scan's remediation string, which leads with "per-principal".

One correctness hazard for whoever implements F11: Swan's outbound path currently uses `outbound.write(.binary(...))` (`PublicFirehoseStreamingRoute.swift:416`), which ignores `maxFrameSize` entirely. If anyone ever switches that call to `writeBinaryMessage`, a lowered `maxFrameSize` would silently fragment `#commit` frames into continuation frames and break the AT Protocol frame contract. The replacement test should pin "`.binary` write is used and outbound frames are not fragmented", which is what the current test at `Tests/SwanHTTPTests/PublicFirehoseStreamingHTTPTests.swift:1550-1556` was actually trying to protect.

findings.title: Anonymous subscribeRepos sockets have no route-level admission and can consume the entire shared listener budget
findings.evidence:
The upgrade decision is the only gate and it checks nothing but syntax: `publicFirehoseUpgradeDecision` (Sources/SwanHTTP/PublicFirehoseStreamingRoute.swift:177-210) validates the `Upgrade` header, rejects `#`, bounds the query at 8 KiB, and parses at most one strictly-decimal `cursor`. No count, no lease, no peer identity. It is wired straight to `.upgrade([:])` at :148-153. There is no router middleware anywhere (Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanHTTP.swift:759 builds the router with none), and the checked-in lab proxy adds no limits either (interop/Caddyfile:8-12 is a bare `reverse_proxy` plus a client-IP header).

The hub has no capacity check: `subscribers` is a plain dictionary (Sources/SwanHTTP/PublicFirehoseWakeupHub.swift:17) and `subscribeWithFinish` inserts unconditionally (:58-74).

I closed the scan's stated proof gap — "whether upgraded sockets remain charged". They are. `MaximumAvailableConnections` is installed as the listener's `availableConnectionsDelegate` (Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanHTTP.swift:1133-1136) and the handler charges on accept and refunds only on channel close: `.build/checkouts/hummingbird/Sources/HummingbirdCore/Server/AvailableConnectionsHandler.swift:96-108`. A WebSocket upgrade does not close the channel, so an idle subscriber holds its slot for its whole lifetime. When the count reaches the cap the handler stops calling `context.read()` on the accept socket (:111-117), i.e. the server stops accepting *any* new TCP connection — for login, OAuth, public reads, permissioned routes, and the relay's own reconnect alike.

The budget is 256 and is not operator-tunable: default at Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanHTTP.swift:132, and `swan serve` constructs the configuration without it (Sources/swan/SwanCommand.swift:3040-3045). There is no `--max-connections` flag anywhere in Sources/swan.

Per-connection state confirmed as described: two firehose DB reads for cursor resolution (PublicFirehoseStreamingRoute.swift:263-264), a hub subscription (:312), a forwarder task (:320-324), and a two-task group (:330-359).

Sub-claims I judged separately:

(a) "non-reading" clients — largely REFUTED by an existing control the scan under-weighted. Auto-ping is enabled at 30 s with a 15 s close timeout (Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanHTTP.swift:1167-1176); the loop closes the channel on a missed pong (.build/checkouts/swift-websocket/Sources/WSCore/WebSocketHandler.swift:238-260), and a test pins exactly this: `testPublicFirehoseAutoPingClosesAClientThatDoesNotPong` asserts `.goingAway` / "Ping timeout" (Tests/SwanHTTPTests/PublicFirehoseStreamingHTTPTests.swift:1392-1420). A client that stops reading cannot pong and is evicted in ~60 s.

(b) "responsive idle" clients — CONFIRMED and unmitigated. Nothing evicts a socket that answers pings and consumes nothing. This is the whole finding.

(c) "maximumWriteDuration is evaluated only after a write returns" — CONFIRMED as written. Sources/SwanHTTP/PublicFirehoseStreaming.swift:228-233 awaits `outbound(row.frameBytes)` and only then measures. `backfillElapsed` is likewise only updated between pages (:236-241), so a write suspended inside a page is bounded by nothing in Swan. Anonymously reachable via `?cursor=0`, which streams the whole retained window (`PublicFirehoseCursorPolicy.resolve` :84, route :297) to a peer that can then stop reading. Whether the write actually stalls depends on the retained window exceeding the kernel socket buffer, and in the current deployment (one account, low write volume) the window is small — so this is a real code defect whose exploitation today is uncertain.

(d) "O(attacker subscribers) per event" — OVERSTATED. The fan-out is one `continuation.yield` per subscriber into a 1-slot buffer (PublicFirehoseWakeupHub.swift:28-30, :40-42). At N=256 that is 256 non-blocking yields per repository event.

(e) "~two SQLite reads per 250 ms per connection" — CONFIRMED arithmetically but minor. The idle path calls `retainedFromSeq()` then `events(after:)` and sleeps `idlePollInterval` = 0.25 s (PublicFirehoseStreaming.swift:186-199; limit at :24). Both are single-row/indexed lookups (Sources/SwanSQLite/SQLiteFirehoseDatabase.swift:467-493, :439-460). All firehose work serializes through one actor with one connection (:65, :71) behind an unbounded-FIFO gate (:782-803), so 256 pollers add latency to the sequencer's `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` appends rather than failing them — the gate has no waiter cap, so unlike the control database this cannot produce an admission-exhaustion error.

No test anywhere asserts a subscriber ceiling: the only `subscriberCount()` assertions are for 0, 1, and 2 (Tests/SwanHTTPTests/PublicFirehoseStreamingHTTPTests.swift:695, :754, :1276; Tests/SwanHTTPTests/PublicFirehoseServiceWiringTests.swift:240, :470-473). No design comment claims the absence of a cap is deliberate.
findings.remediation:
I raise this above the scan's MEDIUM. The consequence is not "cross-route starvation" in the abstract — it is total loss of the listener, including federation, from one host opening ~256 sockets.

1. Add a firehose-specific subscriber lease modelled on `PublicRepositoryJSONReadAdmission` (the precedent and its rationale are in docs/superpowers/records/2026-08-12-swan-production-readiness/task-7-report.md:410-440). Acquire at the top of `publicFirehoseOnUpgrade`, Sources/SwanHTTP/PublicFirehoseStreamingRoute.swift:245-246, with `defer { lease.release() }` — before the cursor reads at :263, before `hub.subscribeWithFinish()` at :312, and before the task group at :330. On refusal, close immediately and return, mirroring the existing FutureCursor exit at :271-280. A refused socket returns its listener slot at once, so refusals cost nothing durable.

   Do NOT put the acquire in `shouldUpgrade` (:147-154): there is no release site there, and `.dontUpgrade` hard-codes 405 (hummingbird-websocket/.../WebSocketRouter.swift:92-93), which misrepresents capacity as method.

2. Size the cap as a reservation, not a ceiling: at most ~25% of `maximumConnections` (64 of 256) so ≥192 slots always remain for HTTP, OAuth, and the relay's reconnect.

3. Add `--max-connections` plumbing to `SwanHTTPConfiguration` at the `swan serve` call site (Sources/swan/SwanCommand.swift:3040-3045). Today an operator under attack has no knob at all.

4. Fix the write deadline properly at Sources/SwanHTTP/PublicFirehoseStreaming.swift:228 — wrap the `await outbound(...)` in a timeout (task group with a `Task.sleep(for: limits.maximumWriteDuration)` racer) so a suspended write is cancelled rather than measured after the fact. Keep the existing post-hoc check as the fast path.

I disagree with the scan's remediation ordering: "per-principal quota" is close to useless here because every socket arrives from a Cloudflare address. If a per-peer dimension is wanted, key it on the already-parsed `X-Swan-Client-IP` (Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanLoginClientIdentityPolicy.swift:21-56) and treat it as secondary to the global cap.

Regression test to add alongside: open cap+1 concurrent live subscriptions against `app.test(.live)` and assert the last one is refused while `hub.subscriberCount()` stays at the cap and a plain HTTP route still answers 200.
findings.risk: The refusal signal is client-visible and needs a maintainer decision. The subscribeRepos lexicon defines only `FutureCursor` and `ConsumerTooSlow`; emitting a new `#error` name is a wire-surface addition that relays may treat as fatal rather than retryable. Safer alternative: close with WebSocket code 1013 ("try again later") and no error frame, which standard relay clients back off on. Either way, capping subscribers means a legitimate relay can be refused when attacker sockets hold the budget — the cap bounds the blast radius, it does not make the endpoint attack-proof, and that trade should be stated explicitly. Adding `--max-connections` is additive and safe. The write-deadline change alters when a slow consumer is dropped (at the deadline rather than after the write completes), which is a behaviour change clients could notice, but it is the behaviour the existing `maximumWriteDuration` name already promises.
findings.needsHumanDecision: Two: (1) On capacity refusal, close with WS code 1013 and no frame, or add a new `#error` name to the subscribeRepos error set? The second is a lexicon-visible wire change. (2) What fraction of the 256-slot listener budget may firehose subscribers hold — I recommend 25%, but that is a federation-capacity/availability trade only the maintainer can set.

findings.title: Admitted anonymous sessions can pin ~5 MB each in the inbound frame decoder; the 5 MB frame ceiling protects nothing
findings.evidence:
Mechanism confirmed. The drain loop is `for try await _ in inbound {}` (Sources/SwanHTTP/PublicFirehoseStreamingRoute.swift:333-350, the loop itself at :338): every client data frame is accepted and discarded with no count, byte, or rate budget. Because Swan iterates `next()` rather than `nextMessage(maxSize:)`, each frame materialises a `WebSocketDataFrame` whose init does `self.data = frame.unmaskedData` (.build/checkouts/swift-websocket/Sources/WSCore/WebSocketDataFrame.swift:24-33) — a full allocate-plus-XOR copy of up to 5,000,000 bytes per frame before it is dropped. `maxFrameSize: 5_000_000` is set at Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanHTTP.swift:1171.

Two corrections to the scan, both material:

(1) The scan says the 5,000,000-byte maximum "exists for outbound commit frames but applies symmetrically inbound". That is backwards. On the server it is *inbound-only*. `NIOTypedWebSocketServerUpgrader(maxFrameSize:)` (wired at .build/checkouts/hummingbird-websocket/Sources/HummingbirdWebSocket/WebSocketChannel.swift:278) passes the value solely to the decoder: `.build/checkouts/swift-nio/Sources/NIOWebSocket/NIOWebSocketServerUpgrader.swift:323-325` adds an unconstrained `WebSocketFrameEncoder()` and a `WebSocketFrameDecoder(maxFrameSize:)`. Swan's outbound path calls `outbound.write(.binary(...))` (PublicFirehoseStreamingRoute.swift:416), and that case writes the frame straight through with no size consultation (.build/checkouts/swift-websocket/Sources/WSCore/WebSocketOutboundWriter.swift:29-46). Only `writeBinaryMessage`, which Swan does not call, consults `maxFrameSize`.

   Therefore the doc comment at Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanHTTP.swift:1159-1166 — "the 16 KiB default would fail every real #commit with messageTooLarge" — is wrong, and the test pinning it (`testWebSocketMaxFrameSizeAtLeastFrameLimit`, Tests/SwanHTTPTests/PublicFirehoseStreamingHTTPTests.swift:1550-1556, against `FirehoseFrameLimits.maximumFrameBytes` = 5_000_000 at Sources/SwanPublicFirehose/FirehoseFrameLimits.swift:7) is pinning a false premise. The setting buys the protocol nothing and is pure inbound attack surface.

(2) The dominant harm is memory pinning, not CPU. The decoder holds a partial frame in its accumulation buffer until the declared length arrives — `validateState` bounds the *declared* length against maxFrameSize (.build/checkouts/swift-nio/Sources/NIOWebSocket/WebSocketFrameDecoder.swift:200-205) and `readSlice(length:)` returns `.insufficientData` until the full payload is buffered (:187-190). So an attacker declares a 5,000,000-byte frame and drips payload at a byte per second, pinning ~5 MB per connection at negligible cost. Across the 256-slot listener that is ~1.28 GB. By contrast the CPU story the scan leads with is roughly 1:1 with attacker bandwidth (an XOR pass over bytes the attacker had to send), which is weak.

Note `validateUTF8: true` (SwanHTTP.swift:1174) is inert on Swan's path — it is consulted only in `getMessage(validateUTF8:)` on the `nextMessage` path (WebSocketInboundStream.swift:105, :121), which Swan does not use. Control frames are separately capped at 125 bytes by the decoder (:209-211), so pings are not a vector.

Existing coverage documents the *tolerant* behaviour as intended: `testSubscribeReposInboundDrainKeepsLoopAlive` sends a binary "client-hello" and comments "A client data message must be consumed by the server's inbound drain without disturbing the tailer" (Tests/SwanHTTPTests/PublicFirehoseStreamingHTTPTests.swift:624-668, comment at :641-643). That is evidence that silently swallowing client data is deliberate — so closing on any inbound data frame is a design reversal, while a size cap is not.
findings.remediation:
Reject the scan's remediation. "Charge actual bytes, enforce backpressure, add per-principal budgets" is a bookkeeping system for a problem that a single literal removes.

1. Lower `maxFrameSize` at Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanHTTP.swift:1171 from 5_000_000 to 4096. subscribeRepos defines no client-to-server data protocol, so no legitimate client — relay included — sends anything larger. This caps the decoder accumulation buffer at 4 KiB per connection (256 × 4 KiB ≈ 1 MB instead of 1.28 GB), and an oversize frame is rejected by NIO with `messageTooLarge` before Swan ever allocates or unmasks it. It does not touch outbound `#commit` frames, per the evidence above.

2. Rewrite the doc comment at Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanHTTP.swift:1159-1166 to say what the value actually governs ("the largest frame this server will accept FROM a client; outbound `#commit` frames are written unsplit via `.binary` and are not bounded by this"). Leaving the current text in place is worse than the bug — it will talk the next reader out of the fix.

3. Replace `testWebSocketMaxFrameSizeAtLeastFrameLimit` (Tests/SwanHTTPTests/PublicFirehoseStreamingHTTPTests.swift:1550-1556) with two tests: one asserting a >4 KiB client frame is closed with `messageTooLarge`, and one asserting a full-size stored `#commit` still arrives intact and unfragmented (that second one guards the `.binary`-vs-`writeBinaryMessage` hazard, which is the property the old test was groping for).

4. Only if the maintainer wants defence in depth: add a cumulative inbound-byte budget in the drain loop at :338 (e.g. close after 64 KiB total from one client). Optional once (1) lands; keep it well above the 12-byte "client-hello" so the existing drain test still passes.
findings.risk: Wire-visible in one direction: any client that sends a data frame larger than the new cap now gets closed with 1009 messageTooLarge instead of being silently ignored. No AT Protocol client should send client-to-server data on subscribeRepos at all, so I assess this as near-zero client impact — but it is a behaviour change on a live federated endpoint and should be stated in the change note. The real risk is the coupling described in evidence: if outbound ever moves from `.binary` to `writeBinaryMessage`, a small maxFrameSize would fragment `#commit` frames and break the frame contract. Mitigate with the replacement test in step 3, not with a comment.
findings.needsHumanDecision: Confirm no non-standard subscribeRepos consumer of swan.place sends client-to-server data frames above 4 KiB. I found none in-repo and the protocol defines none, but this is live federated traffic and only the operator can rule out a bespoke client.

findings.title: Unthrottled info-level open/close records let anonymous connection churn set journal growth rate
findings.evidence:
Mechanism confirmed exactly as described, and the cited lines are accurate. `PublicFirehoseSubscriptionObservation.log(to:)` ends in `logger.info(...)` (Sources/SwanHTTP/PublicFirehoseStreamingRoute.swift:85-99, the emit at :98). When no observer is injected the runtime installs that logger as the default (:126-132), and production takes exactly that path — `SwanCommand.swift:2855-2860` constructs `SwanPublicFirehoseStreamingRuntime` with `database/hub/limits/logger` and no `observeSubscription`. One `opened` record is emitted per successful upgrade (:255-259) and one `closed` per termination (:370-374), each with a fresh UUID (:255). There is no sampling, dedup, or rate limit on this path.

The scan's own severity framing is right and I did not find a control it missed. The fields are all server-generated enums plus a UUID, so there is no injection or disclosure dimension — this is purely rate-driven.

The repository-local precedent the scan alludes to is real and stronger than the scan states. `PublicReadDiagnosticThrottle` exists specifically because the maintainers already diagnosed this exact class on the public-read routes, and the doc comment says so in the strongest possible terms: "Every 503 on these routes writes a `.warning`, and every one of these routes is anonymous. A persistently unadmittable account therefore let any caller ... set the service journal's growth rate directly, with no ceiling. That is a disk-fill path on the production box, and it arrived through the very work that made these refusals loud." (Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanPublicRepositoryReadXRPC.swift:1385-1404; class at :1413-1455; 1-second window at :1461-1466; call site at :1362-1377.) The firehose lifecycle logger is the one anonymous-driven journal writer left outside that discipline.

Two qualifications that keep this LOW rather than higher. First, journald applies its own defaults on the deployed box — per-service rate limiting and size-capped rotation — so "durable growth at attacker request rate" is capped outside the source; the practical harm is log dilution and loss of forensic signal during an attack, not disk exhaustion. Second, the log line is not even the expensive part of a churn cycle: each upgrade also runs two serialized firehose-DB reads for cursor resolution (:263-264) before it logs `closed`.

One piece of doc/reality drift worth recording: the type comment at :11-14 says the connection identifier is "meaningful only for pairing the open and close records in local lab logs" — but this observer is wired in production, not just in a lab.
findings.remediation:
The scan's proposed remediation for this finding is boilerplate copied from an unrelated cluster — "Linearize lifecycle/generation authorization with the signing, streaming-adoption, or SQLite commit point using the existing active-account authorization transaction/lease pattern; re-read the generation after every suspension" has nothing to do with logging, and the finding's own `authorization-state-race` category label is likewise mis-assigned (the body describes resource exhaustion, and the two sibling findings are correctly categorised that way). Ignore both; fix the logging.

Use the in-repo pattern rather than inventing one:

1. Route the default observer at Sources/SwanHTTP/PublicFirehoseStreamingRoute.swift:129-131 through a `PublicReadDiagnosticThrottle`-shaped window keyed on the low-cardinality tuple — `(event, cursorMode)` for opens and `(event, closeCategory, closeReason)` for closes — folding the suppressed count into the next line as `suppressedRepeats`, exactly as SwanPublicRepositoryReadXRPC.swift:1372-1375 does. The key space is bounded by construction here too: every component is an enum raw value (:16-41), never request input.
2. Drop `connection_id` from throttled lines, or keep the pairing only when a line is actually written. Under throttling the UUID is what makes each record unique and therefore unsuppressable, so it must not participate in the key.
3. Reconcile the type comment at :11-14 with the fact that this observer runs in production.

If pairing open/close records is considered operationally necessary, the alternative is to demote both to `.debug` (:98) and emit a periodic aggregate — currently-live / opened-since / closed-by-reason — from the existing firehose services. That preserves the operator signal at fixed cost. Either shape is fine; the current unbounded one is not.
findings.risk: Observability regression, and that is the whole risk. Throttling breaks 1:1 open/close pairing by connection id, which is what the current design exists to provide; demoting to `.debug` removes the records from the production journal entirely. Neither affects client-visible behaviour, wire format, or any stored schema. Reusing `PublicReadDiagnosticThrottle` directly would make the firehose route share a process-wide window with the public-read routes — instantiate a separate throttle for the firehose so a saturating read failure cannot silence firehose lifecycle records, mirroring the separate-instance reasoning already applied to `publicHandleResolutionAdmission` in docs/superpowers/records/2026-08-12-swan-production-readiness/task-7-report.md:425-440.
findings.needsHumanDecision: Is per-connection open/close pairing (the unique `connection_id`) an operational requirement in production, or a lab-only affordance as the comment at PublicFirehoseStreamingRoute.swift:11-14 claims? The answer picks the fix: throttle-with-suppressed-counts if pairing is expendable, demote-to-debug-plus-periodic-aggregate if it is not.

clusterNotes:
Cross-finding observations.

1) F06 and F09 are in direct tension and cannot both be fixed by reordering. F06 says "claim the durable DPoP jti only after client identity is validated"; F09 says "do not let an unauthenticated caller trigger a remote client-metadata fetch". Client identity in PAR is established *by* the remote metadata fetch (SwanOAuthAuthorizationServerHTTP.swift:233), so moving the jti claim after it would put the attacker-controlled remote fetch first — strictly worse. The scan's remediation string for F06 ("move the missing security check to the closest shared control, fail closed before the sensitive operation") is boilerplate and not actionable here. The shared root cause of F06/F09/F19/F41 is the same and it is not ordering: **there is no per-peer admission on `/oauth/*` at all.** grep of Sources/SwanHTTP for rate limiting finds only two call sites, both account-scoped (SwanOAuthAuthorizationServerHTTP.swift:363, SwanLocalhostOAuthHTTP.swift:208); `SwanRequestBodyAdmissionConfiguration` (SwanHTTP/SwanJSONWriteBody.swift:80-83) is a concurrency lease, not a rate limit.

2) Deployment gap worth acting on before any code change: every OAuth authorization-server route is registered under `/oauth/*` (SwanOAuthAuthorizationServerHTTP.swift:125,129,135,140,148,164), **not** under `/xrpc/*`. The stated Cloudflare rule (600 req/10s per-IP on `/xrpc/*`) therefore does not cover PAR, token, revoke, authorize, or login. Extending that rule to `/oauth/*` is a zero-code mitigation that materially degrades F06, F09, F19 and F41 today. This should be done first; the code fixes below are the durable version of it.

3) Swan already contains the exact control F34 is missing, in the sibling subsystem: SwanSQLite/AccountLoginAdmissionStore.swift:239-251 — "A denied request must not allocate missing handle/pair keys: otherwise one already-limited peer could vary handles until it poisoned the global capacity bound." The email limiter (SwanHTTP/SwanAccountEmailXRPC.swift:124-145) deliberately does the opposite. Fixing F34 is a port of an existing, already-reasoned control, not new design.

4) F34 and F42 are both unreachable on the deployed configuration for the same reason: no `--enable-email-recovery` ⇒ `accountEmailXRPC == nil` (SwanCommand.swift:2650,2707) ⇒ `com.atproto.server.requestPasswordReset` is installed as an unavailable stub (SwanHTTP.swift:1047-1049,1068; SwanPublicUnavailableXRPC.swift:5-33) that never reaches the limiter or the store. They are latent, not live. Do not spend live-incident effort on them; fix them before email recovery is ever enabled.

5) Ordering constraint if all are taken: a single per-peer durable admission gate on `/oauth/par` (reusing `AccountLoginAdmissionService`'s bucket primitive, SwanAccounts/AccountLoginAdmission.swift:61-160) is the shared prerequisite for F06 and F19 and substantially blunts F09. Land that first, then the F19 abandon-ticket fix, then the F09 reservation. F41 is an independent one-line policy default.

6) Every "cap exhausted ⇒ reject" behaviour in this cluster is deliberate and has a passing test asserting it (OAuthControlStorageHardeningTests.swift:127-168; AccountEmailOutboxSQLiteTests.swift:1044-1088; OAuthRemoteFetchAdmissionTests.swift:393,490-500). The findings are not "a bound is missing" — the bounds are the point. In every case the real defect is that the bound is *global and unpartitioned*, so an unauthenticated peer can spend the whole budget. Frame the fixes as partitioning, not as adding limits.

findings.title: PAR durably claims a DPoP jti before any client identity is validated
findings.evidence:
Ordering is exactly as claimed. Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanOAuthAuthorizationServerHTTP.swift:215 runs `OAuthDPoPProofValidator(...).validate(...)`, and the client metadata load is not reached until :233. Inside the validator, Sources/SwanOAuth/OAuthProofValidation.swift:117-119 calls `tokenService.claimDPoP(...)` as the last step of validation, before returning; Sources/SwanOAuth/DurableOAuthTokenService.swift:922-936 forwards to `controlStore.claimDPoPReplay`, and Sources/SwanSQLite/OAuthControlStore.swift:1741-1797 inserts a durable row under the `dpopReplays` cap of 131_072 (Sources/SwanSQLite/OAuthControlStore.swift:121). The nonce is a stateless HMAC over a whole-second timestamp with a 300s window (Sources/SwanOAuth/SwanOAuth.swift:295-308), so one issued nonce is reusable for ~5 minutes by any caller — no account, no registered client, no token. The same primitive is reachable pre-identity on two more routes: /oauth/token (SwanOAuthAuthorizationServerHTTP.swift:519) and /oauth/revoke (:627). There is no per-peer admission on /oauth/* anywhere in Sources/SwanHTTP, and /oauth/* sits outside the deployed Cloudflare /xrpc/* rate-limit rule.

What is overstated: the stated end-state (fill 131_072 rows, deny DPoP globally). Rows expire at iat+300s (OAuthProofValidation.swift:115) and `purgeExpiredLocked` runs inside every control transaction (OAuthControlStore.swift:1751, 1644-1659), so the table reaches the cap only at ~440 sustained *distinct, validly ES256-signed* proofs/second. Every one of those is a serialized `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` on a single actor (OAuthControlStore.swift:1750-1751, `withConnectionGate`+`transaction`) that runs ~12 purge DELETEs plus a `SELECT COUNT(*)` over the whole replay table on each new key (OAuthControlStore.swift:1208-1216). At the traffic needed to approach the cap, the control store is already the bottleneck — the observable outcome is an ordinary write-saturation flood, and the row cap adds little marginal harm. No test asserts the safe ordering; OAuthControlStorageHardeningTests.swift:127-168 asserts only that the caps fail closed, which is intended.
findings.remediation:
Do not reorder — see clusterNotes(1); moving the jti claim after client validation would place an attacker-controlled remote fetch ahead of it and create F09 on the same route. Two changes, in this order:
1. Operational, today: extend the Cloudflare per-IP rate-limit rule from `/xrpc/*` to `/oauth/*`. No code change; directly caps the proof rate that this finding depends on.
2. Code: add a per-peer durable admission call at the top of `handleOAuthServerPAR` (Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanOAuthAuthorizationServerHTTP.swift:174, immediately after form parsing at :183 and before the DPoP validate at :215), and mirror it in `exchangeOAuthServerToken` (:519) and `revokeOAuthServerToken` (:627). Reuse the existing bucket primitive rather than inventing one: `AccountLoginAdmissionService` (Sources/SwanAccounts/AccountLoginAdmission.swift:61-160) already gives HMAC-keyed, process+durable, globally bounded per-peer buckets with the correct "do not allocate varied keys once limited" semantics; a new `AccountLoginRateLimitScope` value or a parallel service over the same table is enough. Peer identity should come from the same `SwanLoginClientIdentityPolicy.clientIPAddress(directPeer:headers:)` already used at :354-356, so the trusted-proxy header handling stays in one place.
I would NOT partition the DPoP replay namespace per client (implied by the scan's "pre-client-validation replay namespace"). RFC 9449 replay protection has to be global over the jti; per-client namespacing would let the same proof be replayed against a second client_id.
findings.risk: Adding admission ahead of DPoP validation changes the failure mode for a burst of legitimate clients from 401-with-nonce-challenge to 429/503. Clients that treat any non-201 PAR as fatal (rather than retrying) could regress — Catbird/Petrel behaviour on 429 at PAR should be checked before the default is set tight. The Cloudflare rule change risks breaking OAuth for a NAT'd population sharing one egress IP if the threshold is set low; start at the same 600/10s as /xrpc/*. No wire-format or schema change if the existing login rate-limit table is reused (its `scope` column is TEXT, so a new scope value needs no migration).
findings.needsHumanDecision: What per-IP PAR/token rate is acceptable for real Catbird clients, given retries and multi-account users behind one NAT? And is extending the Cloudflare rule to /oauth/* acceptable given it also covers the interactive browser login flow?

findings.title: Eight distinct slow attacker origins starve the process-wide OAuth remote-document budget
findings.evidence:
Mechanism confirmed in full. `OAuthRemoteFetchAdmission.shared` is a process-global, non-queueing 8-slot gate (Sources/SwanOAuth/OAuthRemoteFetch.swift:474-475, 486-496) and its own comment states the design: "One process-wide budget covers every outbound OAuth document... Admission is deliberately non-queueing: an attacker controlling many distinct URLs cannot turn the server into an unbounded waiter or connection factory" (:470-473). The loader adds a second global 8-slot gate on distinct client_ids (Sources/SwanOAuth/OAuthClientMetadataLoader.swift:86, 137-141). One lease is held across the metadata GET and the optional JWKS GET (:283-311), and each GET does two DNS resolutions plus a transport call, each bounded by `policy.timeout` (default 5s; Sources/SwanOAuth/OAuthRemoteFetch.swift:126, 578-604). Loads are `Task.detached` and deliberately survive caller cancellation (OAuthClientMetadataLoader.swift:145-160), so the attacker can fire and disconnect. Exact-URL singleflight is keyed on the full client_id string (:74-77, :130-133), so distinct URLs never share.

Blast radius on the deployed config is real: /oauth/token and /oauth/revoke call `revalidate` unconditionally, deliberately bypassing the cache ("A token endpoint always obtains a new document rather than trusting the PAR cache", SwanOAuthAuthorizationServerHTTP.swift:537-540; :645), so pool starvation denies token issuance AND refresh for the one real account. Space interop shares the same loader instance (SwanCommand.swift:2442-2444, 2527-2531). Cost to the attacker is ~8 requests per 5s ≈ 1.6 req/s, unauthenticated, and /oauth/* is outside the Cloudflare /xrpc/* rule.

Overstated in two places. (a) "DID or other security-critical remote fetches": the deployed AppView proxy path is `.configuredAppView` and performs no DID lookup at all (Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanXRPCPipethrough.swift:396-400); only `atproto-proxy` targets other than the configured AppView reach `SwanPeerPinnedDIDDocumentFetcher` (SwanCommand.swift:2807-2818), so AppView proxying is not affected today. (b) The fail-fast behaviour is not an oversight — Tests/SwanOAuthTests/OAuthRemoteFetchAdmissionTests.swift:393 and :490-500 drive 24 distinct slow client_ids and assert that at least 16 fail closed, "excess distinct metadata loads must fail closed instead of queueing without bound". The behaviour is deliberate and tested; what is missing is partitioning, not a bound.
findings.remediation:
The scan's remediation ("charge actual bytes/work rather than worst-case fixed reservations") is boilerplate and wrong for this code — the reservation is a connection slot, not bytes. The correct fix is to stop letting the attacker-reachable class of load consume the whole budget:
1. Reserve part of the budget for already-established clients. Split `OAuthRemoteFetchAdmission.shared` (Sources/SwanOAuth/OAuthRemoteFetch.swift:474-496) into a general pool and a reserved pool, and have `OAuthClientMetadataLoader.loadAndCache` (OAuthClientMetadataLoader.swift:283) request the reserved pool when the client_id already has a published freshness row. The store already knows this: `oauth_control_client_metadata_freshness.published_generation > 0` (OAuthControlStore.swift:1266-1279). That keeps /oauth/token and /oauth/revoke working for the real client while a stranger floods first-contact loads.
2. Cheaper complement: cap concurrent flights per host inside the loader. Flights are keyed by full URL (OAuthClientMetadataLoader.swift:74-77); add a host counter with a cap of 2 alongside `maximumConcurrentFlights` at :86 so one origin cannot hold 8 of 8.
3. Do NOT raise the limit or add queueing — that reverses the documented decision at OAuthRemoteFetch.swift:470-473 and re-opens unbounded socket growth.
findings.risk: Splitting the pool changes which requests fail under load; the assertions in Tests/SwanOAuthTests/OAuthRemoteFetchAdmissionTests.swift:393 and :503 count successes against a flat budget of 8 and will need updating — verify the update still asserts fail-closed, do not relax it to fail-open. A per-host cap can throttle a legitimate multi-tenant client-metadata host if one ever serves several distinct Swan clients. No wire-format or schema change.
findings.needsHumanDecision: How the reserved budget is split (e.g. 5 general / 3 reserved) and whether "established client" should mean "has a published freshness row" or a stricter "has an active token family". Both are policy calls that decide who gets denied first under attack.

findings.title: Failed metadata fetches leave one-hour freshness rows; 8,192 attacker client_ids block unseen and idle clients
findings.evidence:
Every step verifies. `OAuthClientMetadataLoader.loadAndCache` issues the ticket at Sources/SwanOAuth/OAuthClientMetadataLoader.swift:285-292, before the first network call at :293 (`admittedFetcher.fetchJSON`) and before `decodeValidated` at :296. `beginClientMetadataFetch` (Sources/SwanSQLite/OAuthControlStore.swift:398-413) calls `issueClientMetadataFetchTicketLocked` (:1225), which runs `requireInsertionCapacity` against `clientMetadataFreshness` = 8_192 (:1229-1234, cap at :117) and then upserts `retain_until = now + 3600` (:1235-1237, constant at :201). There is no abandon/rollback path: the only other writer is `markClientMetadataFetchPublishedLocked` on success (:1290), and the sole freshness deletion is in `purgeExpiredLocked` (:1527-1544), which requires BOTH `retain_until <= now` AND a NULL join against `oauth_control_client_metadata` — so a never-published attacker row survives the full hour. `requireInsertionCapacity` (:1197-1222) throws `SwanError.unavailable` for any client_id without an existing row once the table is full; PAR maps that to 503 temporarily_unavailable (SwanOAuthAuthorizationServerHTTP.swift:275-281). Tests/SwanSQLiteTests/OAuthControlStorageHardeningTests.swift:156-168 asserts exactly this fail-closed behaviour on `beginClientMetadataFetch`, i.e. the cap is intended; the pre-validation allocation with 1h retention is what makes poisoning cheap.

The scan understates one thing. It says "already cached clients remain usable". The metadata cache expires after 300s (`cacheLifetime` default 300, OAuthClientMetadataLoader.swift:97-101) while the freshness row lives 3600s, so an actively used client survives — but after ~1h with no PAR/token traffic its freshness row is purged, and it is then indistinguishable from a new client and locked out. On a one-account PDS that means sustained poisoning eventually locks out the real user's client, not just strangers. Cost: 8,192 requests (~2 min at 60 req/s) then ~2.3 req/s to hold it, unauthenticated, on a route outside the Cloudflare /xrpc/* rule.
findings.remediation:
Add the missing abandon operation rather than a generic quota. Concretely:
1. Add `abandonClientMetadataFetch(ticket:now:)` to the `OAuthControlStore` protocol (Sources/SwanStorage/SwanStorage.swift, next to the existing begin/publish pair) and implement it in Sources/SwanSQLite/OAuthControlStore.swift beside `publishClientMetadata` (:415). It must delete the freshness row only when the ticket is still the latest AND nothing was ever published — i.e. `WHERE client_id = ? AND latest_generation = ? AND published_generation = 0 AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM oauth_control_client_metadata WHERE client_id = ?)`. Those guards preserve the publication-ordering invariant the existing comment at :450-453 protects, and make a concurrent second flight a no-op rather than a lost row.
2. Call it from `OAuthClientMetadataLoader.loadAndCache` (Sources/SwanOAuth/OAuthClientMetadataLoader.swift:285-336) on every failure path after the ticket is issued — wrap :293-311 so fetch failure, `decodeValidated` failure and JWKS failure all abandon.
3. Belt-and-braces, independent of (1): give a never-published client_id a short retention. At Sources/SwanSQLite/OAuthControlStore.swift:1235-1237, insert with a short `retain_until` (e.g. 60s — comfortably longer than the 5s×3 worst-case fetch) and extend it to the full 3600s only in `markClientMetadataFetchPublishedLocked` (:1290). This alone reduces the attack's hold time 60×, and it survives a missed abandon call.
The scan's generic "move the check to the closest shared control" is not the fix; the check is already in the right place, the allocation just has no compensating release.
findings.risk: The abandon delete must not race a concurrent successful flight for the same client_id — the `latest_generation = ?` and `published_generation = 0` guards are load-bearing; get them wrong and a valid publication is discarded. Tests/SwanOAuthTests/OAuthRemoteFetchAdmissionTests.swift:34 (`testNewerStartedFetchDoesNotStarveOlderValidPublication`) is the regression to keep green. Shortening the initial retention changes durable row lifetimes but not the schema (`retain_until` is already a plain column) and is invisible on the wire. Adding a protocol method touches every `OAuthControlStore` conformer including test doubles.
findings.needsHumanDecision: Whether to take both (1) abandon-on-failure and (3) short initial retention, or only one. I recommend both — (3) is two lines and covers any failure path a future edit forgets to wrap.

findings.title: Pre-password login admission lets one IP spend a victim handle's global 10-per-5-minute bucket
findings.evidence:
`admitLogin` runs at Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanOAuthAuthorizationServerHTTP.swift:359-365, before `authenticateForLogin` at :369 — so a wrong password still consumes the buckets. `AccountLoginAdmissionService.admit` (Sources/SwanAccounts/AccountLoginAdmission.swift:94-158) canonicalizes the handle (:110-116) and consumes handle, direct-peer and pair buckets on every call (:128-133). Defaults: handleAttempts 10, directPeerAttempts 100, pairAttempts 10, window 300s (:25-28). Reaching it needs only a self-service PAR plus GET /oauth/authorize to mint a browser session and CSRF token (:317-325), then repeated POSTs to /oauth/authorize with the victim's public handle — the session is not consumed by a failed login (the guard at :347 only requires `session.subject == nil`). The lockout renders as 429 (:363-364).

The precise structural defect, which the scan does not name: handleAttempts (10) equals pairAttempts (10). The pair bucket already caps a single IP at 10 attempts/5min, so the handle-wide bucket contributes zero additional brute-force protection against a single-IP attacker, while granting that single IP a global lock on the account. Ten requests every five minutes — roughly 0.03 req/s — sustains it indefinitely, and /oauth/authorize is outside the Cloudflare /xrpc/* rule. Tests/SwanAccountsTests/AccountLoginHardeningTests.swift covers bucket cardinality, durability and fail-closed capacity (:98, :202) but nothing asserts the handle/pair ratio, so this is not a documented deliberate choice.
findings.remediation:
Do not add another quota (the scan's boilerplate). Change the ratio so the handle bucket requires many distinct peers to exhaust, which is the only configuration in which a handle-wide bucket does useful work:
1. Sources/SwanAccounts/AccountLoginAdmission.swift:25 — raise the `handleAttempts` default from 10 to a value well above `pairAttempts` (100 is the natural pick, matching `directPeerAttempts`). With pairAttempts unchanged at 10, locking the handle then needs 10 distinct source IPs instead of one, while the global brute-force ceiling stays at 100 attempts / 5 min against an Argon2id verifier — still far below anything that threatens a real password.
2. Add a regression test in Tests/SwanAccountsTests/AccountLoginHardeningTests.swift asserting that a single peer exhausting its pair bucket leaves the handle bucket with headroom for a different peer. That is the invariant, and it is currently untested.
3. Optional and separable: reset the handle bucket on successful authentication. It does not fix an actively-sustained lockout, so do not treat it as the fix.
Do not move admission after password verification — that would remove the brute-force defence entirely.
findings.risk: This is a deliberate-looking security default being loosened, so it needs an explicit owner decision. Raising handleAttempts to 100 raises the global online-guessing ceiling for a single handle from 10 to 100 per 5 minutes (2,880 → 28,800 per day). Against Argon2id and a strong password that is not meaningful, but against a weak password it is a real 10× change. No schema, wire or client-visible change; `AccountLoginAdmissionPolicy` already validates 1...10_000 (:32).
findings.needsHumanDecision: Yes — this is an explicit brute-force-resistance vs. availability trade. Confirm that 100 handle attempts / 5 min is acceptable given the account's password strength, or pick a different number. Nothing should change without that decision.
