findings.title: Password-reset email buckets are allocated even after the peer bucket is limited, filling the shared 4,096-row table
findings.evidence:
The mechanism is real and the arithmetic checks out, but it is not reachable on the deployed configuration.

Mechanism: `SwanDurableAccountEmailXRPCRateLimiter.permits` deliberately consumes every rule after one reports limited — "Consume every applicable bucket even after one reports limited. This keeps the externally visible path independent of which dimension (DID, address, or peer) exhausted its budget" (Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanAccountEmailXRPC.swift:124-145). For `.requestPasswordReset` the rules are email/hour 5, email/day 15, peer/hour 15, peer/day 50 (:193-199), and the email rules are listed first, so a peer already over 15/hour still allocates two fresh email-scope rows per request. `consumeEmailRateLimit` (Sources/SwanSQLite/AccountControlStore.swift:1499-1587) inserts under a global 4_096 cap (:20) and returns `.limited` for any absent key once full (:1567-1571). 4096/2 ≈ 2,048 varied emails, matching the scan. Tests/SwanSQLiteTests/AccountEmailOutboxSQLiteTests.swift:1044-1088 fills the table with fresh digests and asserts a new digest is denied — the cap is intended ("the table must stop allocating before the process runs out of disk"), so the denial is the safe half; the unsafe half is that a limited peer can still allocate.

Not reachable as deployed: without `--enable-email-recovery`, `accountEmailXRPC` is nil (Sources/swan/SwanCommand.swift:2650, 2707), so `com.atproto.server.requestPasswordReset` is skipped by the install check at Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanHTTP.swift:1047-1049 and :1111-1123 and instead registered as a flat unavailable stub (SwanHTTP.swift:1065, SwanPublicUnavailableXRPC.swift:5-33). The stub touches neither the limiter nor the store. The finding is latent, not live.

Decisive extra evidence the scan missed: Swan already implements the exact control this path lacks, in the sibling login store — Sources/SwanSQLite/AccountLoginAdmissionStore.swift:239-251: "A denied request must not allocate missing handle/pair keys: otherwise one already-limited peer could vary handles until it poisoned the global capacity bound." The email limiter is inconsistent with a rule Swan already reasoned through and shipped.
findings.remediation:
Port the existing login-store control; do not invent a new quota (the scan's boilerplate). Two options, in preference order:
1. Preferred, at the storage boundary: give `consumeEmailRateLimit` (Sources/SwanSQLite/AccountControlStore.swift:1499) the same batched shape as `consumeLoginRateLimit` (Sources/SwanSQLite/AccountLoginAdmissionStore.swift:151-290) — take all rules for the operation in one transaction, evaluate every existing row first, and if any dimension is already limited return `.limited` WITHOUT inserting rows for the absent dimensions (the guard at AccountLoginAdmissionStore.swift:239-251). This preserves the anti-oracle property the comment at SwanAccountEmailXRPC.swift:124-127 protects — the wire response and the query count are unchanged — while removing the poisoning primitive.
2. Cheaper, at the caller: in `permits` (SwanAccountEmailXRPC.swift:121-145), order the peer rules before the email rules and, once `allowed` is false, call the store in a non-allocating mode (increment only if the row exists). This needs a flag on `consumeEmailRateLimit` and is strictly weaker than (1), because it cannot see the other dimensions inside one transaction.
Do this before `--enable-email-recovery` is ever turned on.
findings.risk: Option (1) changes the durable consume semantics for all four email operations, not just password reset — `requestEmailConfirmation` and `confirmEmail` share the helper (SwanAccountEmailXRPC.swift:176-192) and their existing tests assert per-rule counting; those will need review. There is a genuine anti-oracle constraint to preserve: whatever shape is chosen must keep the number and cost of the durable operations independent of which dimension was limited, or the timing floor logic in `passwordRecoverySuccess` (SwanAccountEmailXRPC.swift:695) becomes the only defence. No wire-format change; the `scope` column is TEXT so no migration.
findings.needsHumanDecision: Confirm that batching the email rules into one transaction does not violate the anti-oracle intent stated at SwanAccountEmailXRPC.swift:124-127 — that comment is load-bearing and its author should sign off on the reshaped version.

findings.title: Anonymous password-reset spends a victim address's email-only bucket and blocks legitimate recovery
findings.evidence:
Mechanism confirmed in source; unreachable as deployed, same gate as F34.

`requestPasswordReset` (Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanAccountEmailXRPC.swift:647-695) is unauthenticated, canonicalizes the attacker-supplied address (:664-669) and calls `admit(operation: .requestPasswordReset, did: nil, email:, ...)` (:671-678) before `recovery.requestPasswordRecovery` (:680). The policy for that operation is email/hour 5 and email/day 15 (Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanAccountEmailXRPC.swift:193-199) keyed solely on the address — `value(for:)` maps `.email` to `request.email?.value` with no peer component (:147-157). Five anonymous requests therefore spend the victim's hourly quota and fifteen spend the day, and each also sends a real reset email (spam). The blind/opaque response (:678-693 and the comment at :684-688) means the attacker learns nothing about account existence, which is the mitigation the scan credits.

Not reachable as deployed: no `--enable-email-recovery`, so the route is an unavailable stub (Sources/swan/SwanCommand.swift:2650, 2707; Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanHTTP.swift:1047-1049, :1111-1123; Sources/SwanPublicUnavailableXRPC.swift:5-33).

Structural gap worth naming, which the scan does not: the email limiter has no pair scope. `AccountEmailRateLimitScope` is `{did, email, directPeer}` (Sources/SwanStorage/AccountControlStore.swift:1094-1098), whereas the login admission it parallels has `{handle, directPeer, handlePeerPair}` (Sources/SwanStorage/AccountLoginAdmissionStore.swift:6-14) precisely so a per-source bucket can be tight while the global per-subject bucket stays loose. Password reset is missing that middle dimension, so the only per-subject limit is global.
findings.remediation:
Mirror the login admission's three-dimension design instead of adding a generic quota:
1. Add an `emailPeerPair` case to `AccountEmailRateLimitScope` (Sources/SwanStorage/AccountControlStore.swift:1094-1098) — the storage column is TEXT so no migration is required — and derive its value in `SwanDurableAccountEmailXRPCRateLimiter.value(for:request:)` (Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanAccountEmailXRPC.swift:147-157) as the HMAC of the email and peer digests, exactly as `AccountLoginAdmissionService` does at Sources/SwanAccounts/AccountLoginAdmission.swift:117-127.
2. In the `.requestPasswordReset` rule list (Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanAccountEmailXRPC.swift:193-199), keep the pair bucket tight (e.g. 3/hour) and raise the email-wide bucket well above it (e.g. 20/hour, 50/day) so a single source can no longer spend a victim's whole quota. This is the same ratio argument as F41; the email-wide bucket only does useful work if exhausting it requires many distinct peers.
3. Land this together with the F34 fix — both touch the same rule table and the same store method, and doing them separately means two passes over the same anti-oracle constraint.
Note that no fix eliminates targeted reset-email spam within the per-pair budget; that is inherent to an unauthenticated recovery endpoint and is correctly treated as a cost of the blind-recovery design.
findings.risk: Raising the email-wide cap increases the maximum number of reset emails a distributed attacker can direct at one address (delivery-infrastructure and reputation cost), which is the exact thing the current tight bucket protects. The pair bucket must be tight enough to keep the aggregate acceptable. Adding an enum case touches every switch over `AccountEmailRateLimitScope`. Storage is scope-agnostic (TEXT column) so no migration and no wire change.
findings.needsHumanDecision: The new per-pair and email-wide numbers are a spam-volume vs. availability trade against the SMTP sender's reputation budget — the operator should pick them. Also confirm this is worth doing now, given the route is not installed today; my recommendation is to fix it as a precondition of ever passing --enable-email-recovery, not as live work.

clusterNotes:
Citation quality: unusually good. Every cited file:line in this cluster resolves to the code the scan describes; the only drift is F20's `SwanSpaces.swift:1605-1661` (SpaceWriteLimits actually starts at :1613). Do not discount these on location grounds.

Shared root cause, two distinct shapes:
(A) Fixed worst-case spool reservations (F23, F29). Both reserve a constant before the real size is known, on `PublicRepositorySpoolAdmission` / `SpaceCARSpoolAdmission` whose defaults are 1 GiB global / 512 MiB per account (PublicRepositoryReadDirectory.swift:876-894, SwanSpaces.swift:666-678). Neither lease type has a resize API (PublicRepositoryReadDirectory.swift:961-982, SwanSpaces.swift:709+), so the scan's phrase "adjusted only after the actual content length is known" is factually wrong in both findings — nothing adjusts. The correct shared fix is a single `downsize(to:)` on both lease classes plus size-aware reservation, introduced ONCE. The codebase already contains the fixed pattern and the reasoning for it, verbatim, at SwanPublicRepositoryReadXRPC.swift:893-902 — that comment is the specification for F23's remediation.
(B) Durable ledgers with no expiry (F20, F21, F24, F27). Four tables, all missing a timestamp column: `permissioned_space_requests` (SwanSQLite.swift:991-998), `public_repository_blocks` (SwanSQLite.swift:434-437), `public_repository_mutation_requests` (SwanSQLite.swift:448-472), and completed `public_event_outbox` rows. The adjacent controls that DO exist prove the omission is an omission, not a philosophy: oplog retention (SwanSQLite.swift:3682-3710), global firehose retention (PublicFirehoseRetention.swift:19-24, 3d/1M rows/1 GiB), per-account blob quota (SwanStorage.swift:23-27, 1 GiB / 10k refs). Any fix needs ONE shared retention helper, not four ad-hoc DELETEs, and each has a documented constraint on what may be pruned (see per-finding risk).

Cross-finding gap the scan MISSED and that outranks most of what it did find: the F20 asymmetry (mutation path has no live-record cap, export path refuses >100,000 records at SwanSQLite.swift:4869) exists identically on the PUBLIC side, which is the side actually deployed. `PublicRepositoryReadLimits.maximumGenerationIndexEntries = 100_000` (PublicRepositoryReadDirectory.swift:528) is enforced on every public read admission (PublicRepositoryReadStore.swift:529-534) and on projection verification (PublicRepositoryStore.swift:945-948), but nothing in `applyPublicRepositoryMutation` (PublicRepositoryStore.swift:440-697) or the coordinator counts live records. ~100,001 `createRecord` calls — reachable inside the Cloudflare 600 req/10s budget in roughly 28 minutes — permanently break getRecord/listRecords/getLatestCommit/getRepo for that account while leaving writes working. That is the sharpest concrete impact in the cluster and should be filed as its own item; I recommend fixing it alongside F20 since it is the same missing check on the sibling surface.

Ordering: F26 first (only unauthenticated-reachable item, ~30 lines, no schema change). Then the public-side 100k live-record cap above + F21 block GC (same file, same transaction area). F23/F29 next as one shared lease-downsize change. F20/F24/F27 last — all require maintainer retention-policy decisions.

Deployed-config caveat applied throughout: with exactly one hosted account, every "exhaust shared storage / starve other accounts" framing collapses to self-DoS by the operator's own credentials. Invite codes are on, so a second account changes that; judge these as pre-conditions for opening signups, not as live incidents. F26 is the exception — it needs no account at all.

findings.title: Unauthenticated public-mutation bodies reserve from the shared authenticated JSON-write pool before authorization
findings.evidence: Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanPublicRepositoryMutationXRPC.swift:588-605 calls `withAdmittedJSONWriteResponse` with `capability.jsonWriteAdmission`; the lease is taken at Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanJSONWriteBody.swift:293-297 and held via `defer` across body collection, decode, AND `operation`, which is where `authorizedTarget` first runs (SwanPublicRepositoryMutationXRPC.swift:163, 234, 268, 309 -> :329-343). Authorization is header-only — `authorizedContext` (:352-364) calls `capability.authorizer.authorize(request:method:fixedPath:)` and never touches the body — so nothing forces this ordering. Pool defaults: 8 concurrent writes / 8 MiB (PublicRepositoryReadDirectory.swift:731-741); `publicMutationMaximumJSONBytes` is 1 MiB, so the concurrency dimension binds at 8. Hold time is the absolute 30 s deadline (SwanJSONWriteBody.swift:13-15), not resettable. The same instance is shared with permissioned space writes (SwanSpaceXRPC.swift:1077), simple-space writes (SwanSimpleSpaceXRPC.swift:552), account email (SwanAccountEmailXRPC.swift:352), actor preferences (SwanActorPreferencesXRPC.swift:121) and — relevant because AppView proxying is ON — the XRPC pipethrough (SwanXRPCPipethrough.swift:152). A chunked request with no Content-Length passes the pre-reservation header check (SwanPublicRepositoryMutationXRPC.swift:608-618 returns true on empty values). Counter-evidence considered and rejected: the maintainers demonstrably know this attack class and isolated two OTHER routes from it — PublicRepositoryReadDirectory.swift:703-724 spells out "a handful of anonymous chunked GETs could hold every lease and deny authenticated JSON commands" for `publicBlobReadProcessShared`, and :694-701 does the same for `managementRejectedProcessShared`. The JSON mutation routes were not given that treatment. `uploadBlob` in this very file is the corrected sibling: it authorizes from headers at :77-79 BEFORE reserving, and drains rejected bodies on a 1-byte lease (SwanJSONWriteBody.swift:236-244). Tests/SwanHTTPTests/PublicRepositoryMutationHTTPTests.swift:329-374 documents the 503-under-held-lease behaviour as intended, i.e. the exhaustion is known and accepted, but it uses a 1-lease pool and never asserts that authenticated capacity survives anonymous load.
findings.remediation: Disagree with the scan's boilerplate remediation ("add per-principal quota at the earliest unauthenticated boundary") — a per-principal quota is impossible here, the principal is unknown until after the reservation. Copy the sibling route instead. In `withPublicMutationInput` (Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanPublicRepositoryMutationXRPC.swift:565-605), hoist the header-only OAuth/DPoP check ahead of `withAdmittedJSONWriteResponse`: call `authorizedContext(request:method:path:)` (:352-364) first, and on failure drain with `drainRejectedRequestBody` (SwanJSONWriteBody.swift:230-255) exactly as `uploadBlob` does at :63-68 and :71-79. Keep the repo/selector binding check (:338-342) where it is, after decode. This requires threading `method`/`path` into `withPublicMutationInput` — both are already string literals at each call site. If the maintainer prefers not to reorder, the weaker fallback is a dedicated `publicMutationUnauthenticatedProcessShared` instance beside PublicRepositoryReadDirectory.swift:721, but that only shrinks the blast radius rather than removing it, and it leaves the AppView pipethrough sharing a pool with anonymous writes.
findings.risk: Client-visible error-precedence change: a request that is both unauthenticated and malformed currently returns 400 InvalidRequest (body validated first) and would return 401 Unauthorized. Check whether any interop/acceptance fixture pins that ordering before landing. No wire format, no schema, no migration. Second-order: hoisting auth means an unauthenticated caller no longer gets its body drained on the main pool, which is the intent — confirm the connection is still terminated via `context.jsonWriteBodyTermination` on the new failure path or a client can hold a listener slot without a lease.

findings.title: Public repository blocks accumulate forever — no reachability GC as heads advance
findings.evidence: Block insertion is Sources/SwanSQLite/PublicRepositoryStore.swift:556-571: every new CID is INSERTed into `public_repository_blocks`, whose schema (Sources/SwanSQLite/SwanSQLite.swift:434-437) is `(cid TEXT PRIMARY KEY, bytes BLOB)` — no generation, no refcount, no timestamp. `grep -rn "DELETE FROM public_repository_blocks"` across Sources/ returns nothing; there is no GC anywhere in the tree. Record updates/deletes only touch the index projection (:574-605), so replacing one rkey repeatedly with unique near-limit values keeps the live projection at 1 record while adding a new record block plus a fresh MST path per commit, capped only by the pinned 2,000,000-byte relevant-block budget per request (PublicRepositoryLimits.swift:12, :71). No `PRAGMA max_page_count` and no free-space check exist anywhere in Sources/. So the block half is fully confirmed. The outbox half is confirmed but DELIBERATE and documented: Sources/SwanSQLite/PublicFirehoseOutboxStore.swift:234-236 states completion "retain[s] its public material indefinitely as an exact-replay and conflict-detection anchor", and SwanSQLite.swift:2479-2482 adds "pruning requires a separately designed tombstone that preserves the same conflict checks". The scan is right that global retention (PublicFirehoseRetention.swift:19-24 — 3 days / 1M rows / 1 GiB) does not reach this account-local table. Downgraded from CONFIRMED because the stated impact — "exhaust SHARED storage", "impact can cross accounts that share a filesystem" — needs a second hosted account; today the only writer is the operator. But unlike the rest of the cluster this is not purely an attack finding: dead blocks accrue during normal posting, with no attacker at all.
findings.remediation: Two separable pieces; do not conflate them as the scan does. (1) Blocks: add a reachability sweep keyed off the committed head, run outside the mutation transaction. The exact walker already exists — `RepositoryMSTValidation.validateProjection` (Sources/SwanPublicRepository/RepositoryMSTValidation.swift:344-546) enumerates every reachable MST and record CID, and PublicRepositoryStore.swift:938-948 already drives it against the live state into a temp table. Reuse that temp index to DELETE the complement from the table written at PublicRepositoryStore.swift:556-571, gated behind a maintenance command rather than the write path. (2) Outbox: do NOT prune it as the scan proposes — SwanSQLite.swift:2479-2482 states the required design (a tombstone retaining source_key + digests so the exact-replay conflict check still fails closed). That is a design task, not a cleanup. File it separately.
findings.risk: Block GC is the highest-risk change in this cluster: deleting a still-reachable block silently corrupts the repository and breaks getRepo/CAR export with no error until a reader asks. Mandatory guards — run only against the durably committed head under the same connection gate, never delete a CID present in the freshly built temp index, and never run concurrently with an in-flight reservation (PublicRepositoryStore.swift:308-422 allocates a revision before the head advances, so a naive sweep can race a prepared-but-uncommitted block). Prefer mark-then-sweep-on-next-pass over immediate deletion. Outbox tombstones are a wire-adjacent change to idempotence semantics and need maintainer sign-off.

findings.title: Permissioned blob read reserves a fixed 256 MiB before learning the blob's real size
findings.evidence: Exactly as described. `maximumPermissionedBlobTransferBytes = 256 * 1024 * 1024` (Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanSpaceBlobXRPC.swift:12) is reserved at :77-82 immediately after authorization and BEFORE the directory lookup at :90-95 that produces `blob.body.contentLength` (first read at :109-110). The lease is released only when the response writer finishes (:165). Production wires the real directory instance, not a test stub: SwanCommand.swift:973 passes `directory.publicRepositorySpoolAdmission`, built with defaults at SQLitePreMigratedAccountDirectory.swift:228-229 -> PublicRepositoryReadDirectory.swift:876-894 (1 GiB global, 512 MiB/account, 64/16 leases). The byte budget binds long before lease count: 512/256 = 2 per account, 1024/256 = 4 globally. The public sibling route is the documented fix and its comment names this exact failure mode — SwanPublicRepositoryReadXRPC.swift:893-902: "Reserving the 256 MiB ceiling for every blob instead would make a 5 KiB avatar cost a quarter of the per-account budget: two concurrent image reads per account, four across the service... That bound was inherited from the old mutation-surface route" — and reserves `metadata.size` at :929-931 after a metadata-only lookup at :905-907. Two scan claims are wrong. (1) "adjusted only after the actual content length is known" — there is no adjustment; `PublicRepositorySpoolLease` (PublicRepositoryReadDirectory.swift:961-982) exposes only `release()`. (2) "four across authors" needs four accounts. Downgraded on deployed reachability: the route IS registered (SwanHTTP.swift:875-936 iterates `PermissionedData0016.methods` unconditionally, not gated by the active profile, and serve always passes the directory at SwanCommand.swift:956), but holding a lease requires an existing permissioned blob — `spaceBlob` reads a separate permissioned table (SQLitePreMigratedAccountDirectory.swift:1008-1043) — and every failure path releases via the `defer` at SwanSpaceBlobXRPC.swift:83-86. With no permissioned-space traffic, only transient reservations are achievable.
findings.remediation: Port the public route's shape verbatim. Add a metadata-only method to `AuthorizedSpaceBlobDirectory` (Sources/SwanStorage/AuthorizedSimpleSpaceDirectory.swift:271-278) mirroring `publicBlobMetadata`, call it in `prepare` between the authorization check (SwanSpaceBlobXRPC.swift:75) and the reservation (:77-82), validate `0 < size <= maximumPermissionedBlobTransferBytes` there, then reserve `size` instead of the constant. Keep the existing post-open length check but tighten it to `blob.body.contentLength == metadata.size` exactly as SwanPublicRepositoryReadXRPC.swift:958-965 does, releasing the lease on mismatch — otherwise the reservation can under-cover the transfer, which is strictly worse than today's over-reservation. Do not instead shrink the constant; a 256 MiB blob must remain servable.
findings.risk: Protocol-internal change to `AuthorizedSpaceBlobDirectory`, which is a public protocol — any out-of-tree conformer breaks. In-tree there is exactly one conformer (SQLitePreMigratedAccountDirectory.swift:22). New failure mode to guard: a metadata/body size disagreement must fail closed with the lease released, or an under-reserved stream escapes the budget. No wire format, no schema, no client-visible change on the success path.

findings.title: Permissioned writes have per-batch limits but no cumulative live-record or byte quota, so a repository can outgrow its own full-recovery export
findings.evidence: Per-batch bounds are real and enforced: `SpaceWriteLimits` (Sources/SwanSpaces/SwanSpaces.swift:1613-1660 — note the scan's :1605 is off by 8) caps 4,096 operations and 1 MiB aggregate value bytes, validated at SwanSQLite.swift:3422-3432. The apply transaction (SwanSQLite.swift:3474-3720) then performs replay-dedup, CAS, canonical-CBOR/CID validation and per-write inserts (:3531-3572) with no COUNT or SUM over `permissioned_space_records` anywhere in it — confirmed by reading the entire transaction. The asymmetry the scan identifies is the strongest part and is real: full-CAR production refuses a repository above 100,000 records at SwanSQLite.swift:4855-4871 (`SpaceCARProductionLimits.maximumRecordCount` -> `absoluteMaximumIndexEntries = 100_000`, StreamingSpaceCARRecovery.swift:59), plus logical-metadata and per-record byte budgets at :4873-4902. So writes the mutation path accepts can permanently strand full recovery. That a per-account quota is the house style is established by `AccountBlobQuota.conservative` (Sources/SwanStorage/SwanStorage.swift:23-27, 1 GiB unique bytes / 10,000 references) enforced at SwanSQLite.swift:7664-7666 — records simply never got the same treatment. Downgraded because: writes require `.accountOAuth` with `subject == author` (SwanSpaceXRPC.swift:878-882), i.e. self-authorization only, so "exhaust storage" is self-DoS; there is no permissioned-space traffic on the deployed profile; and the receipt-row component the scan folds in here is separately filed as F27.
findings.remediation: Reject the scan's "earliest unauthenticated boundary" framing — there is no unauthenticated boundary on this path. The correct control is a cumulative live-record ceiling checked inside the same transaction that already validates the batch, at Sources/SwanSQLite/SwanSQLite.swift:3474-3510, before the per-write inserts at :3531. Reuse the exact predicate the export path uses (`SpaceCARProductionLimits.maximumRecordCount`, SwanSpaces.swift:618) so the two can never diverge again, and count only net-new creates so deletes and replacements remain unconditionally accepted — an account at the ceiling must always be able to shrink. MORE IMPORTANT: apply the identical fix on the public surface, which is the one actually deployed. `PublicRepositoryReadLimits.maximumGenerationIndexEntries = 100_000` (Sources/SwanStorage/PublicRepositoryReadDirectory.swift:528) is enforced on every public read (Sources/SwanSQLite/PublicRepositoryReadStore.swift:529-534) and on projection verification (PublicRepositoryStore.swift:945-948), but nothing in `applyPublicRepositoryMutation` (PublicRepositoryStore.swift:440-697) counts live records. Exceeding it via ~100,001 createRecord calls permanently returns `resourceLimitExceeded` for getRecord/listRecords/getLatestCommit/getRepo while writes keep succeeding — a self-inflicted federation outage reachable inside the Cloudflare rate budget. Add the count check next to the record-index writes at PublicRepositoryStore.swift:574-605.
findings.risk: Introduces a new terminal error state for a previously-accepted write, so it is a protocol-visible behaviour change: pick the error mapping deliberately (SwanSpaceXRPC.swift:952-957 maps `SwanError.malformed` -> InvalidRequest, which is probably wrong for a quota — a distinct 4xx quota code is clearer). Counting live records per batch adds a COUNT inside the hot write transaction; on the public side prefer maintaining a counter column over a COUNT(*) per commit. Must not be retroactive: an existing repository already above the ceiling has to stay writable for deletes, or the fix strands the account permanently.

findings.title: public_repository_mutation_requests grows without bound, including abandoned wrong-CID reservations
findings.evidence: Row growth is real and every structural claim checks out. Each HTTP operation mints a fresh UUID (Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanPublicRepositoryMutationXRPC.swift:187, 250, 282, 319), the coordinator reserves before preparing, and reservation INSERTs a row at Sources/SwanSQLite/PublicRepositoryStore.swift:397-412. The schema (Sources/SwanSQLite/SwanSQLite.swift:448-472) has no timestamp, expiry, or retention column, and the only statement touching the table other than SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE is a migration DROP of a differently-named legacy table (SwanSQLite.swift:2197). The failed-request half is confirmed: `abandonPublicRepositoryReservation` (PublicRepositoryStore.swift:699-734) only UPDATEs status to 'abandoned' and never deletes, so authenticated failures accumulate durable rows while publishing nothing. The behaviour is a known, documented choice: docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-12-swan-read-after-write-design.md:223-227 — "RAW's dependence on `public_repository_mutation_requests` retention must be pinned by a regression test and a comment at the DDL. The table grows unbounded today; if anyone later adds the natural cleanup, it must retain at least the RAW window or the removal half stops working with no error anywhere." Downgraded because the scan's headline impact is overstated by roughly three orders of magnitude per row. It claims committed rows "retain committed_projection bytes" from "1,000,000 byte" JSON bodies and cites a fixture "committing 300 unique 900,000-byte records". `committed_projection` is not the record body: `encodeProjection` (PublicRepositoryStore.swift:1213-1231) serializes only {action, collection, rkey, recordCID, previousCID} per write — roughly 200 bytes typical, bounded by 200 writes/batch (PublicRepositoryLimits.swift:9) at ~40 KB worst case. Tests/SwanSQLiteTests/PublicRepositoryCARSpoolRSSRegressionTests.swift:172-173 is an opt-in CAR-spool RSS gate, not a ledger-accumulation demonstration. At the Cloudflare 600 req/10s ceiling this table grows ~12 KB/s; `public_repository_blocks` (F21) grows up to four orders of magnitude faster on the same requests, so this is the minor half of the same attack.
findings.remediation: Do not apply the scan's generic "prune durable ledgers" instruction directly — the design doc above imposes a hard floor on any retention policy. Concretely: add `created_at INTEGER NOT NULL` to the DDL at Sources/SwanSQLite/SwanSQLite.swift:448-472 via the existing `addAccountColumnIfMissing` migration helper (pattern at SwanSQLite.swift:2491-2495), stamp it at insertion (PublicRepositoryStore.swift:397-412) from the `wallClockMicroseconds` the caller already supplies at :310, and add the DDL comment the design doc explicitly asks for. Then prune on a policy strictly wider than the read-after-write window, modelled on `PublicFirehoseRetentionPolicy` (Sources/SwanSQLite/PublicFirehoseRetention.swift:8-49) rather than a bespoke rule. `abandoned` rows carry no replay obligation and can take a much shorter TTL than `committed` — split the two. Sequence this AFTER F21's block GC; pruning ~200-byte receipts while megabyte blocks accumulate is not worth the migration.
findings.risk: Schema migration on the live account database — needs the standard versioned-migration path, not an ad-hoc ALTER. The real hazard is stated in the design doc: pruning inside the read-after-write window silently breaks RAW deletion handling with no error surfaced anywhere, so the retention floor must be derived from the RAW window constant and pinned by a regression test in the same change. Requires a maintainer decision on the retention values and on whether `next_revision UNIQUE` (SwanSQLite.swift:453) can safely lose historical rows — deleting them frees revision values relative to the allocator's `floor` computation at PublicRepositoryStore.swift:367.

findings.title: permissioned_space_requests receipts are retained forever while the adjacent oplog in the same transaction is pruned
findings.evidence: The contrast is inside one transaction and is unmistakable. Dedup reads the table at Sources/SwanSQLite/SwanSQLite.swift:3477-3483; one row is INSERTed per successful unique request at :3648-3660; and ~20 lines later the same transaction prunes `permissioned_space_oplog` to `oplogRetention` depth at :3682-3710 (default 10,000, validated at :1718). The receipts schema (SwanSQLite.swift:991-998) has no timestamp, expiry, or quota column, and grep confirms only six references to the table across Sources/ and Tests/ — schema, dedup SELECT, INSERT, and three migration/backup name lists (:3902, :4185, :4420) — so there is no deletion path at all. Reachability is self-authorized writes only (`requireSelfWrite`, Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanSpaceXRPC.swift:878-882) through the four record-write handlers at :731-876. No design comment defends this retention; unlike F21's outbox (PublicFirehoseOutboxStore.swift:234-236) and F24's ledger (the read-after-write design doc), nothing states an idempotence-replay obligation here, which makes it the cleanest of the four ledger findings to bound. Two corrections: the scan classifies this as `secret-exposure`, which is wrong — nothing in the row or the path discloses anything; and it assigns Impact (high), which the row size does not support (~150-200 bytes: two UUID strings, a space URI, a DID, two integers).
findings.remediation: Agree with the scan's direction; reject its severity and its category. Add `created_at INTEGER NOT NULL` to Sources/SwanSQLite/SwanSQLite.swift:991-998, stamp it at the INSERT (:3648-3660) from the same `Date()` the outbox insert already computes eight lines below at :3662, and prune in the same transaction immediately after the oplog prune at :3682-3710 using the identical depth-based shape. Depth-based, not age-based: the dedup guarantee only has to outlive client retry behaviour, and matching the existing oplog retention keeps one knob instead of two. Do not add a per-account byte quota here — the row is fixed-width and a cardinality bound is sufficient and far cheaper.
findings.risk: Schema migration (versioned path required). Behavioural risk is precise and narrow: pruning a receipt makes that request_id replayable, so a client retrying a write older than the retention depth would no longer be rejected at SwanSQLite.swift:3481-3483. Set the depth well above any client retry horizon and add a negative test asserting a request just inside the window is still rejected. Note for the maintainer: the CAS/revision guard (:3487-3497) — not the receipt — is what actually prevents a stale replay from corrupting state, so the post-prune failure mode is a duplicate-rejection becoming a conflict-rejection rather than a double-apply. Worth confirming.

findings.title: Permissioned full-repository export reserves 384 MiB worst-case and never downsizes for the streaming phase
findings.evidence: Arithmetic and mechanism confirm. `SpaceCARProductionLimits.maximumWorkingSpoolBytes` = 256 MiB CAR + 2 x 64 MiB metadata = 384 MiB (Sources/SwanSpaces/SwanSpaces.swift:622-629, with `absoluteMaximumCARBytes` at StreamingSpaceCARRecovery.swift:58). It is reserved at Sources/SwanSQLite/SwanSQLite.swift:4608-4613 before any repository size is known, on `SpaceCARSpoolAdmission` defaults of 1 GiB global / 512 MiB per account (SwanSpaces.swift:666-678), and the lease travels into the spool (SwanSQLite.swift:4614-4636 -> SpaceCARBodySpool, SwanSpaces.swift:815-829) and is released only when the response writer calls `cleanup()` in the `defer` at Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanSpaceRepositorySyncXRPC.swift:542. Note the scan's numbers imply more concurrency than exists: 384 MiB against a 512 MiB per-account cap allows exactly ONE export per account and two globally, so "span across authors" needs two accounts to saturate and there is one. Downgraded primarily because the worst-case reservation is a documented deliberate choice whose reasoning holds for the phase it covers: SwanSpaces.swift:613-616 ("Swan reserves the consumer's entire 64 KiB signed-commit allowance even though ordinary P-256 commits are much smaller, so storage can reject an oversized suffix before a reader-specific envelope exists") and :623-626 ("Conservative process admission includes the final CAR allowance plus two metadata allowances: one for the encoded index during handoff and one for the connection-local SQLite projection/B-tree overhead that remains live while the body spool is assembled"). Unlike F23's blob case, the CAR's size genuinely cannot be known before it is produced, so reserving worst-case ahead of the build is correct. The gap the scan should have named is narrower and real: once the spool exists the exact size IS known — `SpaceCARBodySpool.bodyByteCount` (SwanSpaces.swift:776-778, "Exact index-plus-record suffix bytes") — and the reservation is never reduced for the slow-reader streaming phase it is then held across.
findings.remediation: Reject the scan's framing ("charge actual bytes rather than worst-case fixed reservations") as applied to the build phase — the design comment at Sources/SwanSpaces/SwanSpaces.swift:613-629 is correct and reversing it would let an oversized suffix reach disk before rejection. Fix only the streaming phase: add a `downsize(to:)` to `SpaceCARSpoolLease`/`SpaceCARSpoolAdmission` (Sources/SwanSpaces/SwanSpaces.swift:680-707 plus the lease class below it) that lowers a lease's `bytes` under the same NSLock and adjusts `reservedByAccount`, then call it once `bodyByteCount` is final — at SwanSQLite.swift:4633-4636 where `transferredLease = true` hands the lease off. Since F23 needs the same primitive on `PublicRepositorySpoolLease` (Sources/SwanStorage/PublicRepositoryReadDirectory.swift:961-982), design one shape and add it to both in a single change. Correct the metadata working set too: after the build the two 64 MiB metadata allowances are no longer live and should be released even if the CAR body reservation stays.
findings.risk: Downsize must be monotonic and must never permit a later increase, or the admission accounting stops being a bound. It must be idempotent with `release()` and safe against the `deinit`-driven release path (SwanSpaces.swift:709+ mirrors PublicRepositoryReadDirectory.swift:972). Freeing capacity mid-request changes concurrency characteristics — more exports admitted simultaneously means more concurrent SQLite read transactions — so re-verify that the read transaction is genuinely released before streaming as SwanSQLite.swift:4599-4602 claims. No wire, schema, or client-visible change.

findings.title: Public repository import retains and sorts an aggregate MST leaf array with no repository-wide leaf cap
findings.evidence: The unbounded-in-count structures exist exactly where cited: `var leaves: [RepositoryMSTLeaf]` and `var recordCIDs: Set<CID>` at Sources/SwanPublicRepository/RepositoryMSTValidation.swift:377-378, appended per leaf at :452-453 with no aggregate cap; a second `expectedCollectionsByRecordCID` dictionary built over all of them at :487-490; and `leaves.sort` at :522-524. Per-node caps at :387 (500,000 nodes) and :400 (4,096 entries) do not bound the aggregate, as the scan says. But the scan missed the control that does bound it: `reachableBytes` is accumulated through the checked `adding(_:to:maximum:)` helper on EVERY MST block at :398 and every record block at :506, against `maximumReachableBytes` which defaults to `limits.maximumCARBytes` = 512 MiB (:359-362, PublicRepositoryLimits.swift:20). Since each leaf costs ~40+ encoded bytes inside its node, the leaf count is bounded in the low tens of millions, not unbounded — real amplification (roughly 5-10x input, so single-digit GB from a 512 MiB CAR), but a bounded blow-up, and blocks are staged in SQLite rather than held in memory (Sources/SwanSQLite/PublicRepositoryImportStaging.swift:232-248). Reachability is the bigger correction. The entrypoint is `swan import-public`, an operator CLI subcommand (Sources/swan/SwanCommand.swift:5511-5514 declares it; :5664-5711 is the importer invocation), defaulting to `https://pds.test` via `SWAN_LAB_PUBLIC_REPOSITORY_URL` (:5603-5607). `RemotePublicRepositoryCARImporter` has no other caller in Sources/ — no HTTP route reaches this path. The in-process caller at PublicRepositoryStore.swift:938 is the local-verification path and is preflighted by `preflightPublicReadProjectionWithoutGate` (PublicRepositoryReadStore.swift:481-534), which caps at 100,000 index entries first. So the finding's "Impact (high)" is not supportable: the blast radius is an operator-invoked CLI process OOMing against a remote the operator chose, not the serving process.
findings.remediation: Worth fixing cheaply, not worth the scan's priority. Add a repository-wide leaf/record ceiling to `validateProjection` beside the existing node cap at Sources/SwanPublicRepository/RepositoryMSTValidation.swift:387 — check a running leaf counter inside the append loop at :452 against a new limit on `PublicRepositoryLimits` (Sources/SwanPublicRepository/PublicRepositoryLimits.swift:27-34), defaulted to `PublicRepositoryReadLimits.maximumGenerationIndexEntries` (100,000, PublicRepositoryReadDirectory.swift:528) so an import can never produce a repository the read path will subsequently refuse — that alignment is worth more than the memory saving. Do NOT adopt the scan's "admission quota at the earliest unauthenticated boundary"; there is no unauthenticated boundary on this path. Second, the sort at :522-524 recomputes `Data($0.path.mstKey.utf8)` per comparison — trivially avoidable and a larger constant-factor win than the cap itself.
findings.risk: A leaf cap makes previously-importable large repositories fail. If set at 100,000 it is exactly the ceiling the public read path already enforces, so nothing importable-and-servable is lost — but confirm no acceptance/interop fixture imports a larger repository before landing. Threading a new field through `PublicRepositoryLimits.init` (:40-78) touches its validation contract, which the type documents as "may only be tightened or enlarged within the documented construction bounds" (:5-6); follow that pattern rather than adding a bare constant.

clusterNotes:
The eight findings are three distinct defects wearing one label, and the scan's single boilerplate remediation ("use the existing active-account authorization transaction/lease pattern") is right for exactly one of them.

GROUP A — signer epsilon-race (F15, F32, F44, F45). Four copies of one 5-line body: read `account.status.authorizesAccount` + `keyReferences`, `await keyStore.key(for:)`, sign. The suspension is real in all four (ProxyServiceAuthentication.swift:152, SpaceDelegationTokenIssuer.swift:51, SpaceServiceAuthentication.swift:255, SpaceRepositoryCommitSigner.swift:58). But three controls the scan under-weighted collapse the impact:
  (a) every credential minted here is a 60s bearer token that deactivation does NOT revoke. A token minted 59s *before* deactivation is valid 59s *after* it. Perfect linearization moves the post-revocation validity window from 60s+e to 60s. The delta is the epsilon, not the 60s.
  (b) the key-rotation variant fails closed at the verifier: SpaceCredentialAuthority.swift:273-277 and :366-370 require `current.signing.generation == expectedSigning.generation`, so a token signed with a rotated-out reference is rejected, not accepted.
  (c) permanent deletion is not a racing transition at all — AccountPermanentDeletionCoordinator.swift:157-160 calls `quiescer.quiesceAccount(did:)` before PLC tombstone, key destruction, and data destruction, and the concrete quiescer (AccountPermanentDeletionRuntime.swift:28-34) calls `revokeAndDrainAccount` → `closeForPermanentDeletion()`. Only ordinary deactivate/suspend is live, and that is an operator command against the operator's own single account.
  DO NOT apply the scan's remediation here. `withActiveAccountAuthorization` documents its own contract at AccountControlStore.swift:2436-2438 ("Callers must not perform network I/O in `operation`; this is a short final publication fence, not a general-purpose transaction wrapper"). Wrapping a keystore file-read + AES decrypt + ES256 sign in the control-DB write transaction would serialize all token issuance — including the pipethrough hot path — behind the single control write gate. The correct fix is the pattern the codebase already uses on the verify side (SpaceCredentialAuthority.swift:304-317): re-read the account after the keystore await and require `currentAccount == account` before signing. Two lines per issuer, no lock held.
  Separately and independently of the security question: the comments at ProxyServiceAuthentication.swift:149-151 and SpaceDelegationTokenIssuer.swift:48-50 say "Do not perform an await after this point" and the very next statement is an `await`. That is a documentation defect that will mislead the next editor, and it is the single most valuable thing to fix in Group A.

GROUP B — durable write survives the lifecycle transition (F18, F43, F46). These are not epsilon races; the windows are milliseconds (F18, F46) to minutes (F43, a 256 MiB stream). F18 is the odd one: it is not a missed check but a deliberate, documented decision to proceed after the fence has *already rejected* (SQLitePreMigratedAccountDirectory.swift:2663-2666). F46 is the one place the scan's boilerplate is correct — `applyAuthorizedWrites` is a network-free staged mutation, exactly what `withActiveAccountAuthorization` was built for.

GROUP C — F37, which the scan rated LOW and which I think is the most substantive item in the cluster. It is the only one where I can point to an invariant that provably holds on one path and provably does not on its sibling, with the test asymmetry to match.

Ordering: fix F37 first (real firehose-visible ordering violation, 15-line fix, matching test already exists to copy). Then F46 and F43 (durable side effects after a returned error). Then Group A as one commit across the four issuers plus the two false comments. F18 last, and only after Josh answers the pre-activation question — it is the only item with a client-visible behaviour reversal.

One shared helper is worth introducing: the four Group A issuers should call a single `requireUnchangedAuthorizingAccount(did:expected:)` on DurableAccountDirectory rather than four hand-copied re-reads, since the copy-paste is what produced four identical defects and two identical false comments in the first place.

Sources/SwanOAuth/ProxyServiceAuthentication.swift:143-145 reads `account.status.authorizesAccount` and `keyReferences`; :152 is `let material = try await keyStore.key(for: references.signing)`; :159-169 signs. The comment at :149-151 ("Do not perform an await after this point") is directly contradicted by :152 — the scan is right about that. No caching widens the window: Sources/SwanAccounts/DurableAccountDirectory.swift:136-138 and :147-172 both hit the control store directly. Impact is overstated for three reasons. (1) The minted credential lives 60s (ProxyServiceAuthentication.swift:15) and deactivation does not revoke already-issued service tokens, so linearizing moves post-revocation validity from 60s+e to 60s. (2) The rotation variant fails closed at any generation-binding verifier — Sources/SwanOAuth/SpaceCredentialAuthority.swift:273-277. (3) Permanent deletion cannot race: Sources/SwanAccounts/AccountPermanentDeletionCoordinator.swift:157-160 quiesces before key destruction. Do NOT wrap signing in `withActiveAccountAuthorization` — AccountControlStore.swift:2436-2438 explicitly scopes that API to short network-free publication fences, and holding the control write gate across a keystore file read would serialize the pipethrough hot path. Instead copy the pattern already in this codebase at Sources/SwanOAuth/SpaceCredentialAuthority.swift:304-317: after Sources/SwanOAuth/ProxyServiceAuthentication.swift:152, re-read `accounts.account(did: issuer)` and require `current == account` before reaching :159, throwing `SwanError.unauthorized`. findings.risk: One extra control-DB read per proxied request on the live AppView path. Measure it — this is the highest-QPS route on swan.place and it currently does two control reads per request; this makes three. No wire-format, schema, or client-visible change. findings.title: PublicFirehoseCommitFence deliberately re-invokes the mutation after the active-account fence rejects it
findings.evidence: Sources/SwanSQLite/SQLitePreMigratedAccountDirectory.swift:2663-2666: `catch let error as AccountControlStoreError { guard case .invalidTransition = error else { throw error }; return try await mutate(nil) }`. `.invalidTransition` is thrown precisely for the inactive case at Sources/SwanSQLite/AccountControlStore.swift:2503-2505. The behaviour is deliberate and documented at SQLitePreMigratedAccountDirectory.swift:2637-2641: "An account that no longer authorizes falls back to a non-emitting mutation: pre-activation and post-deactivation commits produce no firehose event." The generation fence is NOT bypassed — AccountControlStore.swift:2506-2508 throws `PublicRepositoryMutationPublicationError.staleSigningGeneration`, which is not an `AccountControlStoreError` and therefore rethrows; Tests/SwanSQLiteTests/AccountAuthorizationLeaseTests.swift:228-266 (`testStaleSignerGenerationNeverFallsBackToNonEmittingMutation`) asserts exactly this. So the scan's "final authorization fence is not preserved" is half right: the signing-generation half is preserved and tested, the lifecycle half is deliberately waived, and no test covers the waiver. One impact claim is wrong: the scan says reactivation "can subsequently expose the post-revocation repository state" as if silently. Sources/SwanAccounts/AccountOperatorService.swift:355-365 emits `emitReactivationSync` on every reactivation, which announces the current head (Sources/SwanSQLite/PublicLifecycleEmitter.swift:99-108) — relays resync rather than diverge.
findings.remediation: This needs a decision, not a patch. My recommendation: narrow the fallback at SQLitePreMigratedAccountDirectory.swift:2663-2666 so it applies only to an account that has never been active (no `publicGenesisCommitCID`), and let a post-deactivation commit fail. I could not find a production caller that needs the post-deactivation branch: the HTTP mutation path already requires `target.status == .active` (Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanPublicRepositoryMutationXRPC.swift:340), the genesis commit is written during PLC preparation (Sources/SwanAccounts/PLCAccountPreparationService.swift:179) rather than through this fence, and key rotation requires an active account. Add the missing test as the mirror of AccountAuthorizationLeaseTests.swift:228-266. If Josh wants the fallback kept, the comment at :2637-2641 should state that this is a knowing waiver of the revocation boundary, because as written it reads as a description rather than a trade-off.
findings.risk: Client-visible: a write racing deactivation currently returns 200 and would begin returning an error. Also a behaviour reversal on a documented deliberate choice, so it must not be applied without Josh. If the pre-activation branch turns out to have a caller I did not find, narrowing it breaks account creation — verify by running SwanHTTPTests/PublicRepositoryMutationHTTPTests and SwanAccountsTests/PLCAccountRotationServiceTests before landing.
findings.needsHumanDecision: Does any production path still rely on the pre-activation (or post-deactivation) non-emitting commit fallback at SQLitePreMigratedAccountDirectory.swift:2663-2666? If only pre-activation is needed, may I gate the fallback on `publicGenesisCommitCID == nil` and let post-deactivation commits fail?

findings.title: Reactivation and activation head-sync inserts bypass the firehose authorization fence that manual sync uses
findings.evidence: This is the strongest finding in the cluster and the scan under-rated it at LOW. The asymmetry is explicit: Sources/SwanSQLite/PublicLifecycleEmitter.swift:113 wraps `emitManualSync`'s insert in `control.withActiveAccountFirehoseAuthorization`, while `emitActivation` (:69-78) and `emitReactivationSync` (:99-108) commit the control-side batch and then call `enqueueHeadSync` (:134-177) with no fence at all. The test suite documents exactly this gap: Tests/SwanSQLiteTests/PublicLifecycleEmitterTests.swift:375-409 (`testManualSyncLosesDeterministicRaceToDeactivation`) is a deterministic barrier race asserting the fenced path rejects, and the reactivation test at :451-477 is uncontended. Why the fence matters mechanically: a fenced insert lands inside the control write transaction, so a concurrent deactivation cannot create generation N+1 until the row at generation N is durable, and the sequencer's `account < lifecycle` rule (Sources/SwanSQLite/PublicFirehoseSequencer.swift:153-163) then orders correctly. An unfenced insert can be beaten by generation N+1 being created AND drained, after which `lifecycleGeneration == nil` at :151 and the stale generation-N `#sync` is chosen at :159-160 and appended — a `#sync` published after `#account(active:false)` on a firehose federated with bsky.network. The sequencer never compares the row's generation against the durable current generation, so nothing downstream catches it.
findings.remediation: Wrap the `enqueueHeadSync` calls at Sources/SwanSQLite/PublicLifecycleEmitter.swift:72-78 and :101-107 in `control.withActiveAccountFirehoseAuthorization(did:)`, taking the generation from the fence closure instead of `batch.generation` / `currentLifecycleGeneration` — i.e. make them structurally identical to `emitManualSync` at :110-132. Then handle the new failure mode at the caller: Sources/SwanAccounts/AccountOperatorService.swift:362-364 must catch `AccountControlStoreError.invalidTransition` and swallow it, because the reactivation status write at :347-354 has already committed and must not be reported as failed just because a deactivation raced the follow-up announcement (the deactivation's own `#account` batch is the correct announcement in that case). Add the mirror of PublicLifecycleEmitterTests.swift:375-409 for the reactivation path. I would NOT also add a generation-vs-durable-current rejection in the sequencer as the scan's root-cause note implies — the fence restores the invariant at the source, and a dropping rule at PublicFirehoseSequencer.swift:145-177 risks silently discarding legitimate queued commits.
findings.risk: Changes `AccountOperatorService.reactivate`'s error surface: without the caller catch, a raced deactivation would make a successful reactivation report an error. No wire-format or schema change. Run Tests/SwanSQLiteTests/PublicLifecycleEmitterTests.swift and the SwanPublicFirehoseTests sequencer suite.

findings.title: Streaming blob upload adopts into the public namespace with no post-stream lifecycle check
findings.evidence: Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanPublicRepositoryMutationXRPC.swift:78-81 checks `target.status == .active` in the preflight closure, then :103-133 streams up to `256 * 1024 * 1024` bytes (:49) through `blobStore.putStreaming`. The wrapper does delegate straight through with no fence — Sources/SwanSQLite/SQLitePreMigratedAccountDirectory.swift:2786-2800 — in deliberate contrast to :2719-2740, where record mutations go through `PublicFirehoseCommitFence`. The sink is Sources/SwanSQLite/SwanSQLite.swift:7127+ (`putStreaming`, whose own comment at :7122-7126 describes spool-then-adopt into the durable CAS transaction). So the window here is genuinely long, unlike Group A. Impact is nonetheless low: the artifact is an unreferenced content-addressed blob in the account's own namespace, public reads of an inactive account are refused at Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanPublicRepositoryReadXRPC.swift:385 (`account.status.authorizesAccount else { return nil }`), and the spool is byte-capped per account by `publicBlobSpoolAdmission.reserve` (SwanPublicRepositoryMutationXRPC.swift:92-98). Permanent deletion is not exposed — `revokeAndDrainAccount` awaits `closeForPermanentDeletion()` (SQLitePreMigratedAccountDirectory.swift:1109-1124) before `destroyAccountData`.
findings.remediation: Do not apply the scan's transaction/lease remediation — holding a control write transaction across a 256 MiB stream is exactly the abuse AccountControlStore.swift:2436-2438 forbids, and would stall every other control write for the duration of an upload. Fix at adoption instead: after `putStreaming` returns at Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanPublicRepositoryMutationXRPC.swift:133, re-resolve the target and re-check `status == .active`; if it is not, call `blobStore.remove(reference)` (available at SQLitePreMigratedAccountDirectory.swift:2782-2784) and throw `PublicMutationFailure.notFound`. The blob is content-addressed and unreferenced at that point, so removal is safe. The cleaner variant, if Josh prefers it, is to push the check inside `SwanSQLite.putStreaming`'s final CAS/reference transaction so the adoption itself is conditional.
findings.risk: Client-visible: an upload racing deactivation currently returns 200 with a blob ref and would begin returning 404. Removal must be idempotent and must not touch a CID that another record already references — verify `remove` is refcount-aware before wiring it into this path, or the fix could delete a shared blob.

findings.title: Permissioned repository sync signs a reader envelope across an unfenced keystore await, contradicting the file's stated invariant
findings.evidence: Sources/SwanOAuth/SpaceRepositoryCommitSigner.swift:49-51 checks `account.status.authorizesAccount` and reads references, :58 awaits `keyStore.key`, :65-71 calls `createReaderEnvelope`. findings.title: Permissioned repository writes commit durably before the lifecycle recheck that rejects them
findings.evidence: Sources/SwanSQLite/SQLitePreMigratedAccountDirectory.swift:1057-1082: `preopenedRepositoryDatabase` (which checks `isActiveAccount` at :2406) selects the database, `repository.applyAuthorizedWrites` at :1070-1075 durably commits through `SwanSQLite.swift:10725-10732`, and only then does :1076-1078 check `isActiveAccount` and throw `SwanError.unauthorized`. The post-commit throw cannot roll back the write. All four entrypoints share it — Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanSpaceXRPC.swift:735-764, :771-791, :798-813, :816-875, all behind `requireSelfWrite` at :878-881. The comment at :1045-1048 is honest ("rechecks lifecycle, terminal shutdown, and the resolved database path *around* the durable operation") — it claims detection, not prevention, so this is a gap rather than a false claim. Impact is narrower than "authorization bypass": the write lands in the account's own permissioned repository, is not published to the firehose, is self-write only, and is unreadable while the account is inactive because reads take the same `preopenedRepositoryDatabase` gate at :2406. The user-visible symptom is a durable side effect behind a returned error — a correctness/idempotency wart with a security shadow.
findings.remediation: This is the one finding where the scan's boilerplate remediation is correct, and the scan correctly names the API: `applyAuthorizedWrites` is a staged, network-free mutation, exactly the contract `AccountControlStore.withActiveAccountAuthorization` documents at Sources/SwanSQLite/AccountControlStore.swift:2433-2438. Wrap Sources/SwanSQLite/SQLitePreMigratedAccountDirectory.swift:1070-1075 in `controlStore.withActiveAccountAuthorization(did: author) { ... }` and delete the now-redundant post-commit check at :1076-1078. Confirm first that nothing under `applyAuthorizedWrites` performs network I/O or re-enters the control store — if it does, the alternative is to push the `isActiveAccount` assertion into `database.apply`'s own SQLite transaction instead.
findings.risk: Holds the control write gate for the duration of a permissioned write batch (bounded by `authenticatedSpaceWriteMaximumOperations`, SwanSpaceXRPC.swift:821-823). Deadlock risk if anything inside `applyAuthorizedWrites` re-enters the control store — check before landing. No wire-format or schema change; the failure response for a raced write is unchanged (still unauthorized), only the durable side effect disappears.

clusterNotes:
Single-finding cluster. The scan's own hedge ("Upstream decoding may impose its own depth ceiling") is the whole answer, and the ceiling is not speculative or third-party — it is an in-repo, hand-written, byte-level strict JSON pre-parser (`StrictPermissionedWriteJSON`, Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanSpaceXRPC.swift:1167-1263) that hard-caps container nesting at 64 for objects AND arrays, runs on the raw body before `JSONDecoder` is ever invoked, and is wired into every JSON write surface in the codebase (SwanPublicRepositoryMutationXRPC.swift:596, SwanSpaceXRPC.swift:1083, SwanSimpleSpaceXRPC.swift:558, SwanSpaceNotificationXRPC.swift:504, SwanSpaceCredentialXRPC.swift:236). The scan traced downward from the HTTP handler body into the codec but never looked at the `decode:` closure that produced the handler's input, which is where the control lives.

Two independent feeders reach `PublicRepositoryRecordCodec.publicRecord`, and both are depth-capped before it:
1. HTTP writes (createRecord/putRecord/applyWrites/deleteRecord) — capped by StrictPermissionedWriteJSON at 64.
2. Stored-block reprojection (SwanSQLite/PublicRepositoryReadStore.swift:129-131 and :224-226) — input comes from `RepositoryMSTValidation.decodeRecordBlock` (Sources/SwanPublicRepository/RepositoryMSTValidation.swift:92-106), whose parser advances depth for maps as well as arrays (`guard depth < maximumDepth` at RepositoryMSTValidation.swift:659 for arrays and :663 for maps).

The genuine residual is a correctness/maintainability inconsistency, not a security hole: the codec's *conversion* phase and its *encode* phase disagree about what "depth" means, and only the encode phase is right. Worth fixing so the package-public API is self-defending, but it is not a live vulnerability and should not be filed as MEDIUM security-control-bypass.

Citation drift worth recording: the scan's "entrypoint/wrapper Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanPublicRepositoryMutationXRPC.swift:163-177" is not the entrypoint — that range is the `applyWrites` write-loop body. The actual request entrypoint/decoder is `withPublicMutationInput` at SwanPublicRepositoryMutationXRPC.swift:565-606. Had the scan cited the real entrypoint it would have had to read line 596.

findings.title: Public record conversion does not advance the 64-level nesting bound through objects and maps
findings.evidence:
MECHANISM IS REAL AS DESCRIBED: Sources/SwanPublicRepository/PublicRepositoryRecordCodec.swift:107 (`convertObject` calls `convert(value, depth: depth, ...)` — unchanged), :130 (`convert` `.object` branch calls `convertObject(fields, depth: depth, ...)` — unchanged), :141 (`.unknownType` passes `depth` unchanged), :183 and :193 (`convertCBOR` recurses into OrderedCBORMap entries and `[String: Any]` values with `depth` unchanged). Only arrays advance: :132-135 and :212-215. The encode phase by contrast is correct: :398-399 (`.object` -> `encodeObject(depth: depth + 1)`) and :354-356.

THE CONTROL THE SCAN MISSED: every HTTP path that reaches `publicRecord` runs a strict byte-level JSON pre-parser before any decoding. Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanPublicRepositoryMutationXRPC.swift:596 `try StrictPermissionedWriteJSON.validate(data)` sits inside the `decode:` closure of `withPublicMutationInput` (:565-606) and executes *before* :597 `try JSONDecoder().decode(Value.self, from: data)`. The parser is Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanSpaceXRPC.swift:1167-1263; its depth gate is :1187 `guard depth < 64 else { throw AuthenticatedSpaceWriteFailure.invalidRequest }` and it advances depth for BOTH containers — :1191 `case 0x7b: try object(depth: depth + 1)` and :1192 `case 0x5b: try array(depth: depth + 1)`. It is therefore strictly stronger than the codec on exactly the axis the scan says is unguarded (objects). All four JSON-decoded public mutation routes go through `withPublicMutationInput` (SwanPublicRepositoryMutationXRPC.swift:470, :483, :496, :530), covering putRecord/createRecord/applyWrites/deleteRecord — i.e. all three handlers the scan names (:172, :176, :245, :275).

SECOND FEEDER ALSO CAPPED: the only other `publicRecord` callers are Sources/SwanSQLite/PublicRepositoryReadStore.swift:129-131 and :224-226, whose `ATProtocolValueContainer` comes from `RepositoryMSTValidation.decodeRecordBlock` (Sources/SwanPublicRepository/RepositoryMSTValidation.swift:92-106 -> `RepositoryRecordBlockValidator.decode`, :598-612). That CBOR parser advances depth through maps as well as arrays: RepositoryMSTValidation.swift:640 `case 4: guard depth < maximumDepth` and :659-664 `case 5: guard depth < maximumDepth ... readMap(depth: depth + 1, ...)`. There is no third caller (`grep -rn "RecordCodec.publicRecord" Sources` returns only those four sites plus the definition at PublicRepositoryRecordCodec.swift:64).

BODY BUDGET: SwanPublicRepositoryMutationXRPC.swift:23 `publicMutationMaximumJSONBytes = 1_000_000`, below `authenticatedSpaceWriteMaximumJSONBytes = 1 * 1024 * 1024` (SwanSpaceXRPC.swift:718), so validate's own size guard (:1169) never pre-empts the depth guard on the public path — the depth check always runs.

TEST EVIDENCE: the cited test at Tests/SwanPublicRepositoryTests/PublicRepositoryDomainTests.swift:288-312 (`testRecordCodecEnforcesDepthSizeAndEmbeddedLinkValidity`) does exercise only `prepare` with a mixed array/object graph, as the scan says — that part of the scan is accurate. But there is no test anywhere for `StrictPermissionedWriteJSON` depth rejection either (`grep -rln StrictPermissionedWriteJSON Tests` returns nothing), so the load-bearing control is untested, which is the real gap.
findings.remediation:
Do NOT apply the scan's remediation as written ("move the missing security check to the closest shared control, fail closed before the sensitive operation") — the check already exists at the closest shared control and already fails closed. That string is generic boilerplate and following it would add a redundant gate while leaving the actual gap (zero test coverage of the gate) untouched.

Recommended, in priority order:

1. TEST THE REAL CONTROL (this is the only item with security value). Add a case to Tests/SwanHTTPTests asserting `StrictPermissionedWriteJSON.validate` rejects a 65-level object-only body and accepts a 64-level one, and an end-to-end route test that POSTs an object-only ~100k-deep `record` to /xrpc/com.atproto.repo.createRecord and asserts HTTP 400 InvalidRequest with no durable write. `StrictPermissionedWriteJSON` is internal to SwanHTTP (Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanSpaceXRPC.swift:1167), so `@testable import SwanHTTP` reaches it. Note the enum lives in SwanSpaceXRPC.swift despite being shared by the public-repo routes — consider moving it to its own file (e.g. Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanStrictWriteJSON.swift) so the next reader looking for the public-write depth gate can find it; that move is what actually prevents the next scan from repeating this miss.

2. HARDENING, not a fix: make the codec's conversion accounting mirror its own encode accounting so `PublicRepositoryRecordCodec` is self-defending as a package-public API rather than relying on an HTTP-layer invariant. Targets: Sources/SwanPublicRepository/PublicRepositoryRecordCodec.swift:130 (`.object` -> `convertObject(fields, depth: depth + 1, ...)`), :141 (`.unknownType` -> `depth + 1`), :183 and :193 (`convertCBOR` map/dictionary recursion -> `depth + 1`), each preceded by the same `guard depth < limits.maximumCBORNestingDepth` shape already used at :132 and :212. This makes convert exactly as strict as `encode`/`encodeObject` (:398-399), never stricter, so no record that `prepare` accepts can be newly rejected.

3. Add the object-only negative case to Tests/SwanPublicRepositoryTests/PublicRepositoryDomainTests.swift alongside :302-312 — a 3-level object-only chain against `maximumCBORNestingDepth: 2` asserting `.recordNestingTooDeep` from `publicRecord`, which is what the existing test genuinely does not cover.
findings.risk: Item 1 is test-only, zero risk. Item 2 changes validation strictness on a path that also runs over ALREADY-STORED records (Sources/SwanSQLite/PublicRepositoryReadStore.swift:129-131, :224-226, the blob-promotion/reachability walks). Reasoning it through: after the change, convert's accounting is byte-identical to `encodeObject`/`encode` (PublicRepositoryRecordCodec.swift:349-400), which every stored record already passed via `prepare`, and CAR-imported blocks already passed the equal-or-stricter `RepositoryRecordBlockValidator` (RepositoryMSTValidation.swift:659-664). So no currently-stored record should become unreadable — but this is a read-path strictness change over durable data and deserves an explicit regression run of SwanPublicRepositoryTests + SwanSQLiteTests rather than assumption. No wire-format change, no schema migration, no client-visible behaviour change (deep records are already rejected at the HTTP boundary with the same 400). Item 2 does mean deep-nesting rejection would start returning `recordNestingTooDeep` from the codec instead of the HTTP parser's generic InvalidRequest in any future non-HTTP caller — a strictly better error, not a contract change for today's clients.
findings.needsHumanDecision: Should `StrictPermissionedWriteJSON` be moved out of Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanSpaceXRPC.swift into its own file? It is the load-bearing nesting/duplicate-key/trailing-garbage gate for FIVE unrelated write surfaces (SwanPublicRepositoryMutationXRPC.swift:596, SwanSpaceXRPC.swift:1083, SwanSimpleSpaceXRPC.swift:558, SwanSpaceNotificationXRPC.swift:504, SwanSpaceCredentialXRPC.swift:236) yet is defined mid-file in the permissioned-spaces module and named after the permissioned path, which is why an automated scan of the public-repo write path missed it entirely. Moving it is a pure refactor but touches five call sites; maintainer call on whether that churn is wanted now.
